### Bazaar diplomacy will bury American supremacy
*The New Indian Express · Opinion*

On Tuesday last, Secretary of State Marco Rubio with his wife and Ambassador Sergio Gor in tow landed in Mumbai. The ambience was awesome and the symbolism scandalous. Soon after their arrival, America’s 250th birthday was hosted and toasted at the Jio World Convention Centre in Bandra Kurla Complex, built by the very business tycoon Washington had come to court.

Next morning, the most powerful diplomat of the most powerful nation was keeping appointments like a salesman making a sales pitch. He along with Gor met both Gautam Adani and Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran before he began other official meetings. Neither side said a word about what was discussed.

The irony was impossible to ignore. Adani has spent two years battling an American lawsuit that almost dented his group’s global ambitions. The Tatas, whose flagship TCS developed business for American clients, watched Trump slap a punishing fee on H-1B visas that made sending Indian techies to manage those very clients prohibitively painful. The persons Trumpian establishment wounded were now being wooed by Washington. Few scripts are written with such sardonic symmetry.

And now comes the pilgrimage to Jamnagar. Gor, an envoy who strolls like a lord through Delhi’s corridors of power, had to accompany his boss across Gujarat to seek an audience with Mukesh Ambani and his son Anant. The mission was pure commerce. Both pleaded with Ambani to process Venezuelan crude, invest in America and finally facilitate the President’s refinery dreams in Texas come true.

The Ambanis, masters of message and image, orchestrated the optics with surgical skill. First came pictures of Rubio and Gor with the younger Ambanis, the patriarch pointedly absent, followed after an hour later by a frame of four before the family temple. Finally, a photograph of three of them—Rubio, Gor and Mukesh—lounging casually in a room wrapped in greenery. It was a cruel joke choreographed in pixels.

Three Indian business houses with a combined market value below a trillion dollars were setting the terms of trade for a nation with a GDP of over $30 trillion.

Equally symbolic was who stayed away from the highly-hyped event. Most of the titans who granted private audience were conspicuous by their absence at the anniversary celebration itself. The only diplomatically correct gesture came from the Indian government. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar attended with the Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and obliged his hosts with a bilateral meeting.

Yet Jaishankar delivered his discomfort with diplomatic deftness. He raised the champagne flute for the toast and placed it back on the table without a sip. Then he told Rubio, in good humour but with unmistakable sarcasm, “You won’t be counted as a friend of India until you really understand cricket,” before reminding both Indian and American guests that Saurabh Netravalkar, America’s leading cricketer, hails from Mumbai.

The message was elegant and exact. India plays both one-dayers and Test matches, Trump just plays T20.

But Rubio had nothing concrete to offer India. He repeated the familiar refrain that a trade deal with India was all but done. What India received is a temporary reprieve from punitive tariffs over Russian oil, a favour as fragile as the mood of the man who granted it. And that mood swings wildly. For years, Trump painted China as a predatory menace plundering American wealth. In September, he rolled out not one but two red carpets for Xi Jinping—greeted him on the tarmac at Andrews air base, gave him a guided tour of the National Archives and hosted a lavish State dinner. The Trump-Xi summit produced pageantry and pandas, but precious little policy.

On Russia, the reversal is even more ridiculous. The same Washington administration that punished India with a 25 percent penalty for buying Russian oil has now waived sanctions on Moscow and struck a deal for Russian diesel. When the US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, American diesel prices soared nearly 80 percent. Farmers fumed, truckers grumbled and a President facing voters suddenly discovered the virtues of Vladimir Putin’s oil fields. What was a crime for India became commerce for the US. Like an avaricious business leader, Trump betrayed even Ukraine by striking a deal with Russia.

Trump demanded that Kyiv stop striking Russian refineries. He advised Ukrainians to find a new leader through elections and nudged Zelenskyy towards surrendering land seized by Russian military. The defender of democracy demanded elections only from the democracy under attack.

Europe is the worst victim of Trumpian tantrums. Allies of eight decades are treated as foes by him, while he flirts with autocrats as friends. Israel, once the cornerstone of his Middle East policy, watched its Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fly in for the UN General Assembly and leave within hours, denied a White House welcome.

Iran, bombed in February, is now an interlocutor to be invited for talks whenever oil markets tremble. India was labelled a tariff abuser in one season and serenaded as a strategic partner in the next. The thread tying together these twists is not strategy but survival. Americans vote on November 3. Losing the House would paralyse the administration for the remaining two years. For Trump’s transactional architecture, conviction is a matter of convenience and principle a bargaining chip.

For more than 18 months, the world order has been battered into being a bazaar where loyalty is rented and alliances auctioned. The world may have to suffer two more years of these hysterics. For eight decades, the world needed America. That compulsion gave Washington its unmatched leverage. Mumbai this week revealed a reversal of roles that should alarm every American patriot.

Today, America needs the world. It needs Russian diesel to calm its pumps, Chinese goodwill to steady its markets, Indian capital to build its refineries and Indian talent to run its industries. A nation that once dispensed favours now solicits them. History offers a sobering lesson—if Trump fails to correct course, the next chapter of American history will be written not in Washington, but in the capitals that would have learned to live without it.

### Million mutinies: Little and big fires everywhere
*The New Indian Express · Opinion*

Updated on: 24 Oct 2026, 6:57 pm4 min readCopiedIn 1976, a television anchor told America to go to the window and shout that they were mad as hell. Americans did. In October 2026 the window is a touchscreen connecting rage and the outraged. in 1976 the network booked the ratings. In 2026 the platform algorithms net the eyeballs and the revenue.

France has raged for more than four weeks as students protest teacher shortages and crumbling classrooms. On Friday the government mobilised 70,000 troops to keep order. In Albania, students set fire to the education ministry. In Rome, students blockaded schools and observed a ‘No Meloni Day’. In Madrid, protests about housing, rent and wages have turned Puerta del Sol into a tented campsite. In Delhi, the young turned an insult into a movement. The Cockroach Janta Party became the platform for agitations—about paper leaks, schools and denial of voter registration. In Germany, students protested in 100 cities raising the issue of broken schools, conscription, austerity and cost of living. This is to be followed by rallies by a GenZ steht auf (stand up) on October 31. Cost of education and poor public sector pay united students and unions in Belgium. Portugal’s protesters want housing and better wages. Every protest is about access: to a classroom, a job, a lease, a vote, a voice.

Tolstoy opened Anna Karenina with the observation that happy families resemble one another, while every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. So it is with the young—their complaints differ by capital, but rhyme. The world is simmering with unattended issues. Youth unemployment is in double-digits. Immigration is weaponised.

Gen AI is retrenching early- and mid-level jobs. Interest rates are higher and promise to stay there. Sovereign debt is at an all-time high. It could be argued that Trumponomics has aggravated the conditions, yet the US has seen no youth-led wave. Not as yet.

Few of these grievances are new. Some are prime examples of wilful blindness. Troubling questions on housing, wages or condition of schools and healthcare do not sprout overnight. The harsh truth is that politicians are skilled at weaponising consequences, but have no time to address the causative factors. The student, the renter and the first-time voter are making one argument in different languages: the future has been upended, and they are left without a say. The magnitude of discontent is huge.

Nearly half of humanity is under 30. Their idiom is the online feed. Six billion people are online, and 82 percent of 15-to-24 year olds use the internet. The grammar is irony. The CJP’s Instagram account has over 25 million followers. Albanians march behind cardboard flamingos. The Jolly Roger flutters at youth rallies across Europe, Nepal and Indonesia. In Nepal, tens of thousands voted on Discord for an interim Prime Minister. Italian students urge protesters to “fare come in Francia” (do as France does), and Madrid campers hold tutorials for youths from elsewhere.

It is also a generation that lives by the lens. The march, the arrest, the baton and the burning ministry are clips before they are events, instruments of mobilisation. This is the experiential generation. It is used to answers at the tip of a finger and end of a swipe. To this cohort, the adult is insolent not only in tone but in tempo, and slowness is itself an insult. The impatience is not frivolous. A leaked paper or a deleted name is a failure of fairness, the one thing the young were promised. The adults hear tempo as disrespect and tell the young to be quiet. A placard in Nantes, copied from a May 1968 Atelier Populaire poster, with Macron’s silhouette, said, “Be young and shut up.”

The young are also told they are not the authors of their script. Typically, many regimes have triggered the ‘foreign conspiracy’ clause. Albania’s Edi Rama said, “Foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace.” Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić called the students’ movement a foreign-funded colour revolution. In India, the BJP and the RSS have blamed, named and then unnamed foreign interests behind the protests. Macron says foreign leaders, Trump among them, are using the riots for their own campaigns. Fox News Digital alleges a network of 50 groups is behind the students.

Mao said a single spark can start a prairie fire. This generation has lit many small ones. Celeste Ng put the thought in a title, Little Fires Everywhere. In 2011, a Tunisian street vendor’s self-immolation lit the Arab world. Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal witnessed violent protests and deaths that forced presidents and prime ministers to flee from their people. Serbia is the live test. Students have fielded a 250-candidate list called Students Win in Sunday’s snap election. Governments fall easily, forced by fear and fervour. What follows is the test. Will the live labs in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal deliver? Anton Jäger’s Hyperpolitics calls this extreme politicisation without political consequences. His argument, in short: mobilisation is easy, organisation is hard. Anger and motivation erode and circumstance evades promised outcomes.

The larger question, though, is not about success and failures. Democracies must reflect on the why, rather than the who and how. Far-left or far-right? The labels rarely fit. Anti-government is not a political identity; it is a mood with a megaphone. In any democracy, the ballot counts but it arrives once in four or five years, between which there is no room for questions. Democracy works only if someone in power is bound to answer. A town hall without responses and consequences is hyperpolitics with chairs.

The young are not asking for a revolution. They are asking for tenancy in their own future. Governments call it disorder. Disorder is what a message looks like when no one receives it.

Author of The Gated Republic, Aadhaar: A Biometric History of India’s 12 Digit Revolution, and Accidental India

### Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India, his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement, reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India, gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary”. From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

### Is CJP Scarier Than Congress? INDIA’s Plan To Block Delimitation
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

The manner in which the Narendra Modi government has handled the recent protests by the Congress-led INDIA bloc and the Cockroach Janta Party is a classic case of different strokes for different folks. While the Amit Shah-led home ministry made elaborate arrangements to crush the CJP leaders and their supporters demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, it was instructed to take a far more lenient view of the demonstrations organised by the Opposition for the same purpose. For instance, the INDIA bloc march to the Supreme Court was allowed to proceed without a hitch while the sit-in by Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi at Akashvani Bhawan, insisting on an appointment with the CEC, went on for the whole day though they could have easily been evicted much earlier. And now the November 1 INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Grounds has also been given the official go-ahead. In contrast, the CJP leaders were detained on flimsy grounds. The benign explanation offered here was that the Congress and other Opposition parties are political players and, therefore, have to be treated differently. The CJP, in the government’s view, is a disruptive force which has to be put down. But the reality is that the government fears the CJP’s popularity with Gen Z and its ability to influence public opinion. On the other hand, the Centre’s assessment is that Rahul Gandhi does not have the same credibility as the CJP despite his best efforts to reach out to the youth. Consequently, it can afford to be generous to the Congress.

There was a big buzz in Kolkata that Prime Minister Modi would be visiting the city for the pujo celebrations, especially since it was the first major cultural event being held after the Bharatiya Janata Party’s historic win in the Assembly polls. As it happened, it was not Mr Modi but Union home minister Amit Shah who made it for the pujo but his visit was marred by the stampede at a pandal in which 19 persons died. One of the theories doing the rounds in Kolkata is that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s state unit did not want the Prime Minister to become the focus of anti-Modi protests over the Election Commission’s controversial special intensive revision of the electoral rolls. There was a possibility the visit could lead to the consolidation of arch rivals, the Left parties, the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamul Congress and some breakaway factions of the TMC which are fragile as its members are still trying to find their footing. Though the Assembly elections are long over, the controversy over the SIR exercise has not died down and remains a potent issue given Kolkata’s reputation as a nerve centre of protests.

The Modi government has again initiated discussions on the passage of the controversial delimitation bill which was defeated in the Lok Sabha earlier this year as the ruling dispensation did not have the required two-thirds majority for its passage. Back-channel discussions with the DMK, the Biju Janata Dal and other Opposition parties outside the INDIA bloc are said to be underway. These parties are being promised that the bill will provide for a 50 per cent increase in seats which, the Centre believes, should allay fears that the southern states will lose out if population is used as a criterion for the reconfiguration of constituencies. The Congress, which wants a freeze on the current number of Lok Sabha seats, is also reaching out to its partners in the INDIA bloc to firm up its opposition to the Bill. Since it has fallen out with the DMK, the Left parties have been asked to convince former Tamil Nadu chief minister M.K. Stalin to continue with his opposition to the Bill. Similarly, Trinamul Congress leader Mamata Banerjee is to speak to former Odisha chief minister Naveen Patnaik to seek his assurance that his party will oppose the bill whenever it is debated next in Parliament. The Congress proposal to its allies is that they push for an increase in the strength of state Assemblies since it is MLAs who are directly involved in dealing with local problems of the electorate.

There is a fresh twist to the ongoing factional battle in Haryana Congress. This follows a video showing Rohtak Congress Lok Sabha MP Deepender Hooda and Rahul Gandhi atop a truck during the recent Opposition march to the Supreme Court demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. In the video, Mr Hooda is seen getting off the truck following a brief conversation with Rahul Gandhi. Mr Hooda’s detractors in the party got an opportunity to point out that the Haryana MP had been publicly humiliated and that this latest incident showed that the Gandhis had lost trust in the Rohtak MP. Mr Hooda has since clarified that he was not told to get off the truck but was instead asked by Rahul Gandhi to manage the crowd of protesters. However, there are few takers for Mr Hooda’s explanation as his opponents in the party’s state unit are using the video clip to revive their rivalry.

### Making Sense Of October, The Year’s Fastest Month
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

This October I find myself especially pressed for time.

With a near-complete manuscript to deliver to a big-name publisher, a bird you might have heard of, several new writing commissions from hither and thither, and, most importantly, two growing children with burgeoning careers who need Mommy as manager, not to mention the many domestic and admin chores that pile up, time is vanishingly small! I wouldn’t dare complain about being busy and in-demand, which is infinitely better than the reverse, but have I had time to luxuriate in it? Nup. Even this column, always an enjoyable jaunt, is a race to the finish this month!

As we try to cram everything we’d hoped to accomplish this annum into this last quarter, it invariably seems more hectic than the preceding three. October is replete with so many reminders that time is rushing forward. What festivities are all about, after all, in whichever corner of the world you reside, is marking the passage of time — the waxing of the moon, the waning of the sun, and vice versa. Whether it’s the Day of the Dead, Día de los Muertos, in Mexico, or Halloween across the Western world, it’s that time of the year that puts a nip in the air and humans celebrate closure. Durga Pujas too are homecomings, without the darker undertones perhaps, but as much of a punctuation. And what is Diwali but shining a light in the encroaching murk?

With October we arrive at the penultimate chapter to the Book of The Year; the bleaker mornings recalling the ledger that must be balanced before the sun is snuffed. These tasks we set ourselves at the start of the year, resolutions for even those who make none, stare us down in their need to be settled, making us feel inadequate and anxious. Worse, it multiplies as the year diminishes, becoming inversely proportional.

It could well be Seasonal Affective Disorder impacting you, if you live in colder climes; your mood oscillating with the vagaries of sunshine. But our perception of what time we have at our disposal is determined by the wiring of our minds.

Tick, tock, tick, tock, my neurodivergent brain never stops. Consequently, deadlines not only loom larger, they also appear closer than they are (as atypical as the next artiste, Meatloaf would’ve agreed). I am that worried that my weirdly wired brain might miss cutoff dates that I circumvent it by being miles ahead of time (yet finding space, as is our wont, to finetune every last bit). When I declare the impossibility of finishing “by the 23rd” and my editor thinks I mean the day of the month, I’m really talking about the hour before midnight on the very day of our conversation, and voilà, the deed is done!

Unlike the White Rabbit in Alice in Wonderland, I’m almost never “late for a very important date”, but equally reliant on props. The calendars, diaries, schedules and lists keeping me on track are my life’s levers. Not only that, I get great satisfaction from crossing items off my to-do list as I go along. Should I manage to complete every chore and commission within my self-imposed timeframe, I will doodle all over my obliterated inventories in a self-congratulatory gush, setting flowers blooming and birds on wing as Tagore famously had. And just as with his creations (in his case, actually art), the British Museum will want to exhibit my inky efflorescence someday, surely, but will have to prise them out of my cold, dead hands (I’d give it away happily in reality, but that isn’t the BM’s favoured modus operandi, is it?)!

Yes, time holds me in thrall, but I would rather dance to its dictates than never be in the right place, like former British PM David Cameron. Repeatedly on holiday when disasters struck the UK, akin to Nero fiddling while Rome burnt, he was also well-known for refusing to say the necessary when an occasion was crying out for it, such as the nearly-a-century late apology he FAILED to make on his 2013 India trip, to the thousand-plus victims of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre by the British. In fact, many a political heavy would benefit from taking a leaf out of my sprouting, neurodivergent diary, if all it did was give them a healthy respect for Father Time.

Yet, one must never crow about having anything remotely under control, because, of course, I DON’T. The early bird occasionally gets the worm, sure, but more often than not, time and tide wait for no man. Nor for birds (feathered or otherwise). And to the modicum of order I’ve brought to my world, why would I want to attract Trouble, that green-eyed monster rampaging through life’s minor alignments? So, to the universe, I say, look away, s'il vous plaît, I’m not so deluded as to try and make a dent on your cosmic arrangements! Leave me to my own humble micromanagement systems.

In fact, as I wrap up this piece, I will stop a moment from attempting to complete objectives, put aside even my doodling pen, to watch my children, two human and one golden retriever, loping in our rust-and-mustard autumnal garden. It...

### The Election Commission Cannot Outsource Its Defence
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

There is a curious asymmetry in the political controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Political parties are shouting themselves hoarse, allegations of institutional complicity are being traded with increasing vehemence, and the credibility of the electoral process is being questioned. Yet the institution at the centre of this storm, the Election Commission of India (ECI), seems strangely reluctant to engage directly with the questions being raised about its functioning.

The silence is all the more inexplicable because the allegations are not merely the partisan complaints of a disgruntled Opposition. An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, 2026, reported that two of the three election commissioners (ECs), Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months to decisions and procedures connected with the SIR. These reportedly concerned changes to Form 6, the centralisation of control over electoral-roll software, appeals against the restoration of voters’ names in West Bengal, and decisions allegedly taken without the knowledge or approval of the full Commission.

These are serious allegations. They may be explicable, but they cannot be wished away. When questions are raised about the integrity of the machinery through which the Indian citizen exercises the most fundamental right of democratic participation, the burden of explanation rests squarely on that machinery.

Instead, the ECI issued a press note on September 23, stating that the internal notes and observations were a normal part of institutional deliberation to improve the electoral processes. It also asserted that all decisions taken by the full Commission during the preceding year, including those relating to the SIR, had been unanimous. What the statement did not do was to explain who authorised the disputed change to Form 6, who approved the filing of appeals against restored voters in West Bengal, why concerns about an audit of the electoral software remained unanswered, or why the full Commission reportedly did not meet between May and August. Nor did it address the specific concerns in the internal correspondence.

A statement that asserts unanimity is not necessarily an explanation of how unanimity was reached. An assurance that procedures are sound is not a substitute for demonstrating that they are sound. And a general declaration of institutional rectitude cannot answer specific questions about institutional conduct.

It is imperative, therefore, for the Commission to convene a press conference at which all three commissioners are present. They should answer questions directly, explain the relevant decisions and procedures, disclose what records can lawfully be made public, and clarify how the objections raised by two of their colleagues were considered and resolved. If the allegations are unfounded, the Commission has every reason to rebut them comprehensively. If there were procedural lapses, acknowledging and correcting them would demonstrate institutional maturity, not weakness. An independent constitutional institution must possess the confidence to speak in its own voice.

The BJP is entitled to defend the Commission. It is entitled to contest allegations of electoral manipulation and to point out that electoral rolls must be cleansed of duplicate, deceased and otherwise ineligible entries. No serious democracy can object to the legitimate objective of accurate electoral rolls. But there is a distinction between defending the principle of electoral integrity and appearing to speak on behalf of the institution responsible for upholding it.

Every time the ruling party rushes to defend the ECI, it risks reinforcing the very perception it wishes to dispel: that the Commission and the government are politically aligned. The BJP has won elections and lost elections. It must expect to remain a participant in both possibilities. Its long-term interest, therefore, lies not in having an Election Commission perceived as sympathetic to the government of the day, but in having one whose impartiality is beyond reasonable suspicion. The same principle applies to every political party.

All political parties must also ensure that there is optimal confidence in the manner in which ECs are appointed. Article 324(2) of the Constitution provides for the appointment of the chief election commissioner and other election commissioners by the President, subject to parliamentary legislation. For more than seven decades, Parliament did not enact a law establishing a comprehensive selection procedure.

On March 2, 2023, in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court addressed this legislative vacuum. It directed that, until Parliament made a law, appointments should be recommended by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India. The objective was to provide a ...

### Suspended session: A question of motive
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge’s letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, highlighting the delay in proroguing the monsoon session of Parliament and urging him to hold an all-party meeting on the proposed delimitation bill, raises both procedural and substantive issues regarding the functioning of Parliament and the government. The monsoon session was adjourned sine die on August 13. Conventionally, a session is prorogued within a few days of its adjournment. But parliament is technically in session even 70 days after it was adjourned. Prorogation formally ends a session and terminates pending business. Leaving the Houses in a state of suspension goes against parliamentary norms and raises questions about the government’s intentions. The move impacts the functioning of parliament and amounts to its disrespect.

The delay in prorogation comes amid speculation that the government plans to convene a session at short notice to introduce legislation on the delimitation of constituencies. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government’s attempt to pass the bill had failed in April. Any move to reintroduce legislation involving a constitutional amendment without providing sufficient notice to the members defies parliamentary conventions. In the past, the government has hurriedly introduced bills and passed them due to its majority in the House. But a two-thirds majority is required for the passage of a constitutional amendment. The government is reportedly lobbying for support for the delimitation legislation among parties which opposed it in April. A sizeable section of the Trinamool Congress, which had voted against the bill, is now supporting the BJP.

Hinduism on path to extinction due to untouchability: Mallikarjun KhargeThe proposed bill has far-reaching consequences and will alter India’s political and parliamentary map in the coming decades. It will tilt the balance of political power among different states and regions and Centre-state relations. Such legislation should not be hurried through in a special session and requires extensive debate. Kharge has called for an all-party meeting to discuss the bill. He made a similar proposal to the Prime Minister on April 11, but the government called a special session and introduced the bill on April 16. He wrote letters to the Prime Minister again, on July 16 and August 27, without receiving a response. The government appears to be building up for an ambush with the bill, and keeping the House adjourned may serve this problematic agenda. Democracy is not about back-room deals, machinations, and mala fide number games, but about the widest consultation, participation, and good faith.

### Tradition and the missing safety clause
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The elephant that ran amok during Shivamogga’s Dasara procession has revived a question that authorities can no longer postpone: Should captive elephants continue to feature in crowded public festivities? Somanna, carrying a 650-kg silver howdah bearing the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari, panicked and bolted through the procession, damaging vehicles as spectators fled. No fatalities were reported, but this was a matter of fortune, not evidence of adequate safety arrangements. The animal was brought in after the regular lead elephant, Sagar, developed a foot injury. Crowds and loud sounds may have triggered Somanna’s panic. The episode exposes the limits of relying on an elephant’s training and a mahout’s experience when circumstances can change suddenly. In 2021, an elephant carrying a howdah during Srirangapatna Dasara panicked amid firecrackers and loud music, chasing people before handlers regained control. In Mysuru in 2024, Dhananjaya chased Kanjan through the palace grounds; Kanjan broke through barricades and reached a public road. Similar incidents elsewhere, particularly during temple festivals in Keralam, have caused fatalities, injuries, and extensive damage. The concern is especially pressing in Mysuru, where lakhs gather for the Jamboo Savari.

Animal-rights activists point to the stress caused by drums, firecrackers, crowds, and prolonged exposure to heat, as well as the physical burden of carrying a heavy howdah over hard roads. Elephants are sentient animals, not ceremonial props. Even well-trained animals can react unpredictably when frightened, unwell, or affected by hormonal changes. The danger extends to spectators, handlers, and the animals themselves. The state has defended the procession before the High Court, contending that using elephants does not constitute cruelty and that they are revered during Dasara. However, religious reverence cannot, by itself, establish that subjecting elephants to noisy, crowded processions is humane or safe.

Mysuru Dasara 2026 | Lakhs witness Jamboo Savari as elephant Prashantha carries the golden howdahShivamogga Dasara procession cut short after elephant Somanna goes berserkThe challenge is balancing cultural sentiment, animal welfare, and public safety. Mechanical elephants, already used in some temple festivals, offer an alternative. Other options include reducing the role of live elephants or restricting their participation to controlled settings away from dense crowds. Over the years, tradition itself has evolved. The king once rode in the howdah; today, it carries the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari. The ceremonial symbolism has endured despite this change – a reminder that tradition must adapt to changing realities. Mysuru Dasara’s grandeur lies in its cultural significance, not in the risks its ceremonies impose. Preserving the festival’s spirit while eliminating avoidable dangers would honour its legacy far better than waiting for a tragedy to force change.

### Frozen baselines: Who has to prove they belong?
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

What does a family in Bengaluru waiting for a BPL ration card have in common with a voter in Bihar or West Bengal asked to prove they belong on the electoral roll, or, since June, a voter in Karnataka itself? Both may meet every eligibility criterion. Yet, like lakhs of others, both are on the wrong side of a cut-off date.

Food entitlements under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) are subject to state ceilings fixed to the 2011 Census. In states that have reached their ceiling, eligible newcomers wait for a card because new households can enter largely when others leave. Karnataka, like other southern states, extended coverage well beyond its NFSA quota through its own Anna Bhagya scheme, and pays for that extra coverage itself. Unlike Tamil Nadu, Keralam, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana, it was not granted the discretionary “tide-over” allocation that has brought those states extra grain every month since the Act was rolled out. In September 2025, the state’s food minister said central guidelines required about seven lakh cards to be removed. By October, two lakh had been cancelled.

'Amid inflation, BPL income limit of Rs 1.2 lakh needs a hike': MLA Rizwan ArshadIn Bihar, the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls treated everyone on the 2003 roll as presumptively eligible; other states have used the roll from their last intensive revision. Everyone else had to produce documents. That cut-off is a frozen baseline: an old snapshot of the population, more than two decades old, fixed as the reference, with membership of the snapshot as the test.

Over the past decade, such baselines have become routine in India’s digital welfare registers. The TPDS Control Order of 2015 capped NFSA entitlements at Census 2011 figures; with no census since, the national ceiling of 81.35 crore people has not moved. Ayushman Bharat’s health cover is tied to the Socio-Economic and Caste Census of 2011; Maharashtra’s health assurance society plainly tells applicants that the data is frozen and no families can be added. The National Population Register, meant as the first step towards a citizens’ register, rests on a 2010 household frame. Even Aadhaar has closed at the adult end: since 2023, first-time enrolment after 18 has required state verification that UIDAI itself likened to a passport check.

One logic runs through them: presumption for those already in, proof for those who came later. Whoever was captured in the snapshot is treated as entitled. Whoever arrives after it must establish their claim, often with documents they never needed before.

Those who arrive later are not random. They are young people who turned 18 after the cut-off, migrants who moved for work, women who moved at marriage, households that split after 2011, and the poor missed in an earlier round: precisely the groups welfare law was meant to reach. In a system that grows, a mismatch against the baseline may reveal someone eligible who was missed. In a frozen system, the baseline is a filter, and a mismatch can only become a flag, a notice, a deletion. The burden grows with time, as every year enlarges the share of the population outside the snapshot.

The vote differs from the ration card in one respect. Aadhaar was defined as proof of identity, not citizenship, and citizenship was left to a national register that was proposed, reaffirmed by the Home Ministry in 2014, and never completed. The SIR is where that postponed question has resurfaced, not through a citizenship register but through the electoral roll, and by the method the welfare registers had already made routine: an old list, presumed correct, against which everyone else must prove they belong. Britain, by contrast, has twice abandoned national ID in the face of public resistance. India built its database first, on residence alone, and is only now asking who belongs.

This is retrenchment without repeal. No statute has withdrawn the right to food, health cover, or the vote. What has changed is the date against which eligibility is checked, how access is regulated and authenticated, and the side on which the burden of proof falls. In 2018, the Supreme Court’s Puttaswamy verdict accepted mandatory biometric authentication for welfare benefits as a proportionate means of preventing leakages, without considering the frozen baselines behind the lists.

The freezes have not gone unchallenged. During the pandemic, economists estimated that holding NFSA coverage to Census 2011 figures left roughly 10 crore people outside it. But each freeze has been contested one register at a time, in different forums, and the common design has gone unnamed. Nobody need have intended the exclusion; its consequences were foreseeable, and the registers were left unrevised.

In May 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the SIR. It held that the Commission may examine citizenship only for the limited purpose of enrolment, that a deletion is not a finding of non-citizenship, and that doubtful cases must go to the authority competent under the Citizenship Act. In practice, the line is not holding. In July, the Court had to repeat that deletion does not mean loss of citizenship, on hearing that people struck off the rolls in West Bengal were being denied welfare. Judges of the West Bengal tribunals hearing appeals have recorded that the Commission’s portal cannot restore a deleted voter, even when a judicial order requires it; by September, only 1.26 lakh of 38.31 lakh appeals had been decided. The presumption that once protected a name on the roll has given way to a demand that the voter prove she belongs. Ration card-holders have lived with that reversal for a decade.

The remedy is simple in principle. Update baselines regularly. Presume eligible those already holding state-issued documents, unless the state shows otherwise. Decide newcomers’ claims within time limits, with a hearing before anyone is removed. When the state cannot keep its own lists current, the cost should not fall on the very people those lists were meant to serve.

(The writer is Professor of Sociology at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi)

## 23 October 2026

### Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

### In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis. For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

### Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

### Prasar Bharati is not a public service broadcaster
*The Hindu · Opinion*

When the Narendra Modi government took office in May 2014, the then Information and Broadcasting Minister, Prakash Javadekar, promised to end the “government fiefdom” over Prasar Bharati and recast it on the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) model: autonomous in administration, free in editorial judgement, and accountable to Parliament.

Twelve years later that promise remains unfulfilled. The 138th episode of “Mann Ki Baat”, broadcast on September 27, 2026, is only the most visible reminder that the state still treats the public airwaves as its own platform.

Also Read | Budget 2026: ₹4,551 crore for I-B Ministry; funds for Prasar Bharati, to support radio movement

The BBC model, unfulfilledThe irony is sharp. The same political class that invoked the BBC as the template, later accused it of a “continuing colonial mindset” after it telecast the documentary in 2023, “India: The Modi Question”. From April 2024 the BBC had to split its Indian news operation to meet foreign-investment rules.

The deeper story is older than the Emergency. In 1948, Jawaharlal Nehru told the Constituent Assembly — then the only authoritative Indian statement on the British model — “my own view of the set-up for broadcasting is that we should approximate, as far as possible, to the British model, the BBC, that is to say, it would be better if we had a semi-autonomous corporation under the government, of course with the policy controlled by the government, otherwise not conducted as a government department.” Even that caveat — “otherwise not conducted as a government department” — has not been honoured.

Mark Tully, former BBC bureau chief in Delhi, put the same distinction succinctly in a conversation in 2017: public service broadcasting “is not the same as government broadcast”. It rests on two principles, he said — that the government must not interfere in the broadcaster’s autonomy, and that programmes must not be judged by commercial merit alone. Without autonomy and freedom, he added, All India Radio cannot become a broadcaster for transformative change.

The Emergency of 1975 reduced All India Radio (AIR) and Doordarshan to instruments of the regime. After Indira Gandhi’s defeat, the Janata government asked B.G. Verghese to recommend autonomy. His BBC-style model became a Bill in 1979 (Prasar Bharati Bill), but the Bill lapsed. A new version, introduced in 1989 as “a charter of freedom” under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, received assent in 1990 — as the Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act, 1990 — and was enforced only in 1997. Its Statement of Objects and Reasons said the corporation should be “a genuinely autonomous body — innovative, dynamic and flexible — with a high degree of credibility”, responsible to the people and to Parliament. Nearly three decades on, Prasar Bharati is not that body. It is a pretender, a mouthpiece of the government of the day. Section 12 of the Act is the editorial constitution that was meant to lock that intent in. The primary duty is to organise public broadcasting services to inform, educate and entertain. Section 12(2)(b) requires the corporation to safeguard “the citizen’s right to be informed freely, truthfully and objectively” and to present “a fair and balanced flow of information including contrasting views without advocating any opinion or ideology of its own”.

Also Read | Prasar Bharati drafts policy to monetise television, OTT content

At the Ministry’s mercyA truncated corporation was set up so that it cannot function independently of government. Critical Sections 13, 14 and 15 of the Act remain unimplemented. Section 13 requires a 22-member parliamentary committee, elected from both Houses, to oversee Prasar Bharati on Parliament’s behalf. No government has constituted it. Former chief executive Jawhar Sircar has explained why: Ministers insist that they alone are answerable to Parliament and therefore retain the power to summon AIR and Doordarshan officials until they succumb.

Sections 14 and 15 require a Broadcasting Council to receive complaints and guard political impartiality. That Council has never been set up, and it follows that there is no system for editorial redress. The Board, meant to be professionally managed, has been filled with pliable bureaucrats. Ownership of assets and staff was never transferred. Without its own fund, the Board remains at the Ministry’s mercy. Section 23 still lets the Centre issue binding directions on what may or may not be broadcast.

Section 10 required a recruitment board to keep appointments free of government interference. Nothing happened until July 2020, when Jagadish Upasane, who headed Bharat Prakashan, publisher of Panchajanya and Organiser, was made chairman. Autonomy was compromised the moment it was announced. A 2021 manpower audit used the BBC as the benchmark: almost half of Prasar Bharati’s then 25,000-strong workforce sat in engineering, against a little over 10% at the BBC, while content staff were under 20% against about 70%. The numbers described a transmission machine, not a Content-and-News-driven broadcaster.

UNESCO’s 2001 definition is exacting. Public broadcasting is neither commercial nor state-controlled; it speaks to every citizen. Prasar Bharati fails that test. In 2000 the government declared November 12 as Public Service Broadcasting Day to mark Gandhiji’s only AIR broadcast, made in 1947 to two lakh refugees at Kurukshetra. The day has since become tokenism. In 2022 even that tokenism turned into farce when a Christian hymn sung by school students was sought to be dropped from the commemorative national broadcast.

The social contract is simple. The broadcaster has the right to speak freely, and in return it owes the public accuracy, impartiality, and independence from both the market and the Ministry. Nehru’s 1948 formula already drew that line: policy may be set, the daily conduct of broadcasting may not be run as a government department. In 1995, Justice P.B. Sawant, speaking for the Supreme Court in Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting vs Cricket Association of Bengal, went further. Airwaves are public property, he held, and the Centre must establish an independent autonomous public authority to control their use. Public broadcasting is not state broadcasting. That direction has still not been carried out.

Also Read | Government revamping communications machinery, pushes for unified outreach

There must be political willWhat needs to be done is already known. The parliamentary committee must be constituted, the Board rebuilt as a professional body, and assets and staff transferred. The regulatory council named in the Act must be created, funding designed without government strings, and Indian Information Service officers removed from operational control. The 1990 Act must be amended where practice has exposed its traps.

None of this happens without political will. The syndrome is familiar: autonomy is criticised out of power and forgotten in power. In August 2026, the government told the Lok Sabha that it had received no formal complaints from journalists or media bodies about its autonomy in the previous year. The absence of filed grievances is not evidence of independence. The Broadcasting Council named in the Act was never created, so there is nowhere for such a complaint to go.

The Chanda Committee, appointed when Indira Gandhi was Information and Broadcasting Minister, concluded in 1966 that “a psychological transformation is necessary” in the government’s approach to broadcasting. Sixty years later that transformation has not come, and Nehru’s “otherwise not conducted as a government department” remains unkept words. The options before the people are two: approach the courts to enforce the Act and the Sawant direction, or wait for the 2029 general election and a Lok Sabha willing to turn Prasar Bharati from a government handmaiden into a public service broadcaster. Until then it remains what it has been for nearly three decades: a disguised pretender.

Suhas Borker is Editor, Citizens First TV (CFTV), and has advocated public service broadcasting since the 1990s as convener of Jan Prasar. In 2000, he conceptualised National Public Service Broadcasting Day, on November 12

It was an extraordinary week in which the slow burn of Test cricket had time to display the nuances of the game even as the brutal hitting power of batsmen in modern cricket was amplified in run chases in which the targets that seemed to test the limits of the impossible, were made to look probable and then made possible by the never-say-die spirit of today’s cavalier willow entertainers.

The South Africans, down and out in the first Test, were the first to display all the doughtiness and the staying prowess needed for five-day cricket in which they excelled despite that old enemy of the long game — rain — having robbed much of the playing time.

In tandem with the comparatively gigantic Marco Jansen, the Proteas skipper first batted Australia out of the Test before unleashing his pace battery. Jansen, who has the hallmarks to claim the title of the world’s best Test all-rounder in contemporary cricket, was the destroyer-in-chief.

As the likes of Scott Boland defied age to shine with ball and bat, hanging on dearly to play for the draw, which is also a result in Test match cricket, the tension could be cut with a knife. What a week that was for the three formats of the game.

### DC Edit | PHP Flaws, AI Prying Point At Need For Digital Security
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

Digital is the new critical superhighway for almost everything people need. It is used to fight wars, issue birth and education certificates, provide entertainment, collect road tolls and even certify a person’s death. If digital networks are compromised, essential services across the connected world could come to a standstill.

Data security, therefore, deserves the seriousness with which countries guard their physical borders. Yet recent incidents reveal elementary mistakes, inadequate safeguards and possible breaches of trust that expose sensitive information. As governments and businesses insist on taking more services online, their responsibility to protect the people using them must grow correspondingly.

The discovery of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language underpinning much of the web, is alarming. The flaws could allow attackers to seize control of affected servers, steal or alter information and disrupt services without first obtaining authorised access.

Though emergency fixes were released on October 21 to address the issue, a large number of websites — at least 50 per cent of all — being run using older software will continue to remain vulnerable. A weakness in such widely used software can endanger numerous otherwise unrelated services simultaneously.

The growing capabilities of artificial intelligence introduce another threat. CERT-In has warned that AI agents undergoing research and evaluation exceeded their assigned authority and accessed live systems of Indian organisations. These autonomous agents, which can plan tasks, invoke tools and act online, accessed confidential records through exposed credentials, application settings and excessively permissive cloud access. But none of these organisations were aware of the intrusion, until the AI model providers informed them about the breach.

The lesson is simple: Giving AI agents unrestricted access and relying on written instructions to restrain them is inadequate. Their reach must be limited through enforceable technical controls, and organisations should store crucial data from tightly controlled spaces.

The eMudhra episode illustrates how a single failure can undermine digital trust. Weak private keys associated with eight intermediate certification authority certificates created the possibility of forged website credentials and forged digital signed documents. This is an easily avoidable incident, which was caused by negligence of its staff. The government must ensure that companies, who are considered gatekeepers of digital trust, must behave with utmost seriousness.

Banking incidents expose additional routes to compromise. State Bank of India said crucial data of nearly 4,000 of its customers was available on dark net, while Bank of Baroda acknowledged unauthorised access through an employee’s compromised email account. Reports allege issues of data security at HDFC Bank, which the lender denied. These incidents show why security must extend beyond transaction servers.

India, therefore, needs measurable security obligations: prompt repairs, independent audits, strict controls over employees and vendors, and clear disclosure of what an incident has exposed. Digital expansion must also be accompanied by reliable arrangements for recovery. If a hacker wipes out a university’s records, students should not be left struggling to prove their qualifications. Governments and institutions must maintain independently secured backups, test their restoration regularly and preserve physical records of crucial events. Digital systems deliver speed and efficiency, but convenience must never come at the cost of security or the ability to recover from failure.

### DC Edit | Why Hardeep Puri Must Quit
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

At a time that the Centre finds itself on a sticky wicket over the SIR controversy, the latest photograph of the Union petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri seated across a table from the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein could not have surfaced at a more damaging moment.

It deepens the government’s credibility crisis and places Mr Puri’s earlier claim that he met Epstein three or four times in a professional capacity, as part of a delegation, under a glaring question mark.

The photograph, by itself, does not prove any wrongdoing. But it does raise some legitimate questions. Speculations will flourish if facts are withheld. The government cannot expect the public to accept a minister's version, only because he has offered one. The statement issued by Mr Puri's office, stating that the minister could not recall the specific meeting or whether others were present or not, does not make the accusations being raised by the Opposition disappear.

The issue is no longer simply whom Mr Puri met. The more serious question is whether India is being exposed to coercion or pressure by a foreign power. The timing of the photograph released by the US department of justice is also politically explosive. Washington wants India to deepen energy cooperation, buy more American energy and consider refining more Venezuelan crude at Reliance’s Jamnagar refinery. The discussions come amid tensions over India’s Russian oil purchases and negotiations towards an India-US trade agreement.

Lok Sabha Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi has linked the controversy to US secretary of state Marco Rubio's visit, asking whom the Americans are allegedly trying to blackmail. It is a serious insinuation, and that is why the government cannot treat this as a private embarrassment involving one minister.

When energy supplies, trade concessions and strategic partnerships are being negotiated, India must demonstrate that its national interests are not vulnerable to foreign pressure. Waiting for a controversy to disappear is not governance. It is evasion. And that is why Mr Puri should quit pending a credible, independent examination. Resignation would not amount to an admission of guilt. Instead, stepping aside would only enhance Mr Puri's image by showing that he dares to welcome scrutiny.

### Has America’s Model Minority Reached Its Expiry Date?
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

There was a time when ‘Asok’ (Indian intern who works in the fictional corporate environment of Dilbert), the stereotypically accented Indian worker in the largely white corporate world, occupied a familiar place in the American imagination, i.e., intelligent, industrious, deferential, faintly comical and, above all, harmless. He could write the code, solve the problem and work the longest hours. But he was rarely imagined as the person who owned the building, set the rules or decided who belonged inside it.

Today, Indian-origin corporate chiefs command global enterprises, direct technological revolutions and influence millions of livelihoods. The journey from cubicle to corner office is a remarkable immigrant success story. Yet it exposes an uncomfortable truth that the minority welcomed for being useful is not necessarily accepted when he becomes powerful.

For decades, the Indian diaspora, particularly its Hindu professional segment, occupied a privileged position in America's narrative of minority achievement. The model minority was presented as evidence that education, hard work and personal responsibility could overcome racial disadvantage. Indian success became a convenient counterpoint to the struggles of Black Americans and other historically marginalised communities.

The implication was unmistakable — if one minority could prosper, perhaps the problem lay not with the system but with those who had failed to master it. The American Right found particular appeal in immigrants who appeared to validate its preferred account of meritocracy. Bobby Jindal (born Hindu, later converted to Christianity), Vivek Ramaswamy, Kash Patel, etc., emerged as prominent conservative voices of the rightwing. Their individual trajectories differed, but their prominence helped establish Indian ancestry as compatible with American political and economic power. The reassuring proposition was that immigrants could rise, embrace conservative ideas, and embody the ‘American Dream’.

But political alignment is not permanent insurance against prejudice. Donald Trump's MAGA movement has placed immigration, national identity, and cultural belonging, at the centre of its rhetoric. Its supporters are not a monolith, and legitimate immigration debates should not automatically be equated with racism. Nevertheless, portraying immigrants as threats or outsiders can reinforce the notion that some Americans are less entitled to belong than others.

The latest hate incident in Aurora, Illinois, makes this vulnerability chillingly tangible. Nineteen-year-old Alexandros Paporakis was arrested over an alleged plan to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian people, potentially at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple, one of the largest Hindu temples in the Chicago metropolitan area. According to prosecutors, Paporakis expressed neo-Nazi and white-supremacist views, told co-workers he could not wait to kill Indian people, and shared a manifesto outlining a mass-casualty plot. Police reported recovering a rifle, ammunition and material associated with white-supremacist extremism. He has been charged, and the allegations remain subject to legal proceedings.

The alleged plot was reportedly thwarted. But the fear it exposed cannot be dismissed. A community that has invested generations in education, enterprise and assimilation must still confront the possibility that its members could be targeted simply for being Indian. This does not prove that every expression of anti-immigrant politics causes violence, or that every MAGA supporter shares extremist beliefs. But exclusionary rhetoric has consequences when it normalises the portrayal of immigrants and people of colour as threats. Political leaders cannot be held responsible for every individual's actions, but the climate their words help create deserves scrutiny.

Here the model minority bargain begins to unravel. The Indian American may be a billionaire, chief executive, conservative campaigner, or naturalised citizen. To a racial essentialist, none of these achievements necessarily erases the perceived foreignness of his name, skin colour, or ancestry. The worker once mocked for his accent and the executive scrutinised for his influence may discover that both remain subject to boundaries they did not create.

The Hindu diaspora must confront an uncomfortable contradiction. Some politically conservative Indian Americans may have believed that assimilation, economic success, and alignment with majoritarian politics offered protection from hostility directed at other minorities. But majoritarianism is transactional. It welcomes those who reinforce its preferred vision of the nation and can withdraw that welcome when their usefulness expires. No minority can permanently purchase security by demonstrating that another minority is less deserving.

Indian-American success should not diminish the struggles of Black, Latino, Muslim, Chinese or other communities. Representation at the top...

### National Tropes Work, But Bipartisan Oversight Key
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Nations have their affectations — often a narrative or a trope — that brands them. China glories in its historical tradition of unitary rule. The last Qing emperor conceded power to the nominally democratic nationalists in 1912 followed by internal strife till the Communists established full control in 1949. Top-down, single-party ideological rule was pragmatically infused in 1980 with large dollops of “capitalism with Chinese characteristics” to boost economic growth and end income poverty. China now anticipates an exclusive, superpower group of two — a G2 — with America.

America is that “shining city on a hill” redolent with promise and prospects which once welcomed the willing and the brave. Immigrants cling to that hope. But President Trump is underpinning its economy with walled up, domestic competitiveness — a substantive albeit painful transformation driven by its waning unilateral moment, exemplified by the trope, “The US dollar: America’s currency but the world’s problem”, now under threat from global pushback.

India’s national trope is “Satyameva Jayate: Truth will triumph”. And it has. Nearly eight decades after Independence in 1947, our economic “potential”, is pegged at a nominal GDP of $30 trillion by 2047, about 8x current levels. A sub-trope is the “world’s largest democracy” — a prospect which Winston Churchill mocked at the time of Independence when illiteracy and under-development — the outcomes of 190 years of British colonial rule — combined with unparalleled cultural diversity, presented formidable barriers.

India’s Constitution generated hope in 1950. It devised a unique formula for dealing with three barriers to development. It offered “inclusion” by putting citizens first via universal adult franchise — which unusually at the time included adults of both genders and judicially guaranteed fundamental rights. Second, a multiparty political model made democracy management competitive, while vertical distribution of powers assured regional aspirations were met. Third, a permanent bureaucracy ensured administrative stability. Most importantly, the convention that the military serves the people via elected civilian, executive control has endured — much to the credit of India’s military establishment.

Administrative responsibilities and the power to tax are divided between the Union and state governments. A quinquennial finance commission recommends to the Union government, a fair vertical and horizontal allocation of its revenues to ensure fiscal adequacy, for all organs of government, per their mandates. There was a curious exclusion — village and city governments where the rubber meets the road- were left as administrative subsets of the respective state governments. At the time,“trickle down” administration from state governments was deemed sufficient to develop villages and cities. It was not till 1993 — that local governments — both rural and urban, were given Constitutional status, to ensure balanced development and use of public funds. Sadly, the downward delegation of funds and functions is not uniformly adequate across state governments. It can also be argued that the Union is richly funded versus states.

Direct taxes on the income of individuals and corporations — the most buoyant revenue source — is with the Union along with import or export tax. Since 2016, other than excise duty on alcohol, and petroleum products the Goods and Services Tax mops up indirect tax and is shared equally between the Union and respective state government. Any cess or surcharge imposed by the Union is not compulsorily shared with states. This is not a bug. It is a Constitutional feature which makes the states fiscally subservient to the Union government.India is not a federation unlike the US. It is a Union of states — a more devolved multi-party version of China’s unitary state — albeit curiously, much less decentralised in practice.

Opting for a strong Union was a precautionary tactic to preserve national stability. Other artifices to the same end include the All-India Services which play leadership roles across the states and the Union. Special powers vest in the Union to override the vertical distribution of powers. Under Article 352 of the Constitution, the Union government can declare National Emergency. Article 356 allows the Union to impose emergency in states, suspending the right of self-governance and imposing direct Union control.

Abrogation of fundamental rights hits at the heart of democratic functioning. Happily, Article 352 has been used only thrice. Twice to manage external threats — in 1962 the Indo-China conflict and in 1971 the India-Pakistan war which liberated Bangladesh. The exception was 1975 — when Prime Minister Indira Gandhi used it to snuff out the widespread public opposition to her government.

In 1976 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled in her favour — Justice H.R. Khanna was the lone dissenter opposing the suspension of fundamental rights, thereby...
