### Welcome To India: Immigration Makes A Second, But A Sim Card Takes A Lifetime
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

“Why let sleeping dogs lie?

Do they compose lies in their sleep?

Why not insist they tell the truth

Or are they by canine nature sly?

And are their untruths trivial or deep —

And do dogs speak in their sleep — and why?

—From Don’t You Humsay Aagey Jao by BachchooI land at Mumbai airport and surprisingly meet with none of the bureaucracy I was expecting: forms to fill, questions about who, why and where and what my grandfather did for a living…

BUT — I came to ‘Immigration’, walked into the queue marked OCI — overseas citizens of India — and was through the gates in a second. No forms, no questions…

What the f—labbergasting

f—lummoxina? No bureaucratic forms, questions, photographs? Hang on, am I in India? I checked on Google maps and it said I was.

So the DNA of the country has been modified by AI? The institutions of the country have finally realised that the purposeless filling of forms and answering questions, which lead no one anywhere, is a waste of time and life? Whew at last!

Alas, gentle reader, nothing has changed. That encounter at the OCI was unique.

The mire into which the institutions in India are immersed has still not been drained.

A few weeks ago, in this very column I wrote about my adventures with Standard Chartered Bank. It worked. I was contacted by Standard Chartered’s troubleshooters immediately and told that everything I had complained about would be put right.

Two issues. This bank had suspended my account for no reason.

I’d asked them why, but answer came there none. The troubleshooters then asked me for the particulars of my debit card which I gave them. They said the card would be activated soon. I’ve been in India the last week — I could draw money from my account using this card.

Dream on. The ATM declared my card invalid.

Hello Standard Chartered, what’s this about? Oh, they said by email, you will be issued a new card, go to the central Mumbai office and get in touch with a named person. I did.

This person understood my problem: I was in India and wanted to use money from my totally legitimate account. So yes, I was, there and then, allowed to withdraw a restricted sum. But the card?

The kind operative heralded me into an office and sat me down to fill out forms! Only one of these forms was to do with applying for a new debit card.

The rest were six duplicates of forms I’d filled out several months ago called KYC applications. I had, as I wrote in this column some weeks ago, an up and down correspondence about these eight forms. All I wanted was my account restored to normal. I hadn’t laundered any money, hadn’t borrowed even a rupee from the bank, had never had an overdraft, had regular deposits in payment for this very column etc. — so why block my account, or suspend it, or whatever the banking jargon is?

I don’t suppose I’ll ever find out.

But enough about the bank, let’s move to the process of getting an Indian sim card in my phone. I was told I couldn’t just pay for one and have it fitted into my spare mobile iPhone. I had to take my passport and my OCI card to the Vodaphone store, which I duly did.

Yes, they told me and calculated the charges I would incur and then photographed my docs three separate times. Then I had to pose for a photograph against a white background. All the photographs were then submitted to some remote official or agency via computer.

I was asked to wait for 20 minutes for some confirmation. Twenty minutes turned to forty. I paced about the store and came back to the desk of the operative who was dealing with my request for a sim card. He was on the phone. He motioned me with a raised hand to be patient. When his call ended, he started some business on the computer. Then he called someone.

After a few minutes of spirited discussion, he asked for my documents again. The young lady with the mobile phone camera was summoned again. My passport and OCI card were subjected to the same triple-photograph treatment, and I had to pose without my spectacles for more photographs.

I surmise that all these were sent again to remote control. Another half hour and I was then asked for the name and address of a close relative who lived in India. I wrote down my niece Niharika’s particulars. They wanted her phone number and they asked me to call her and tell her to expect an SMS. I didn’t know quite what they wanted me to say, so they took the phone from me and spoke to her.

In the next half hour, they must have phoned her four times. Then remote control was on the phone again. ‘Remotus’ said the were not satisfied with the photographs of myself or my documents. I said there seemed to be some misunderstanding. I hadn’t come there to buy the Taj Mahal — I only wanted a sim card in my phone. The sarcasm was wasted and so was my time. They returned the money and asked me to come another day.

### Inflation warrants early distress control
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

With retail inflation touching 5.54% in September, India’s inflation tolerance – as defined by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) – is close to its 6% threshold. It is at a two-year high and has been above 4% for four consecutive months. Food inflation was 7.74%, and rural food inflation touched 8.06% in September. The wholesale price index registered a high of 11.39%. According to data released by the Consumer Affairs Ministry, onion prices have risen nearly 113% over the last 12 months, sugar prices by 22%, and sunflower oil prices by 18%. Retail prices of most essential, government-monitored household items have gone up, with 41 of 42 items recording rises over a year. Inflation has steadily increased since January, and consumer prices increased by 0.69% between August and September.

The rise in inflationary pressures is traced to the increase in crude prices due to the war in West Asia, a depreciating rupee, and a deficient monsoon that has affected agriculture and created drought-like conditions in many parts of the country. While the rise in oil prices has raised transport costs, contributing to a general price escalation across commodities and services, a weak rupee has imported inflation. Weather disruptions could continue as the El Niño is expected to extend to the next year. Winter crops are also likely to be affected. The RBI has predicted higher inflation levels for the remaining months. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned of renewed inflationary pressures in India if the West Asia war keeps energy prices high. It also warned that higher energy prices could worsen fiscal balances in the region, making it more difficult for governments to support vulnerable households while maintaining fiscal sustainability.

Tamil Nadu government steps in to curb food inflation, fine rice to be sold at Rs 30 per kiloThe central bank has increased interest rates and may raise them again. While it is the standard monetary response to tackle inflation, it may still prove insufficient. Since food inflation can severely hit weaker sections, especially those in rural areas, the Union government should take steps to contain distress. Buffer stocks should be released in time to reduce shortages and prevent price rises. Administrative action should be initiated to prevent artificial scarcity. Imports should be considered when necessary. Farmers will need assistance for their crops in adverse circumstances, along with compensation and insurance payments for their losses. The poor, in both towns and villages, will be the worst-affected, and the government should prioritise policies to help them overcome the challenge.

### Sugar prices: A pause for solutions
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The temporary suspension of the agitation by sugarcane growers in north Karnataka offers the Centre and the state a window to address their grievances before the situation escalates again. The protest had intensified from highway blockades to a march from Belagavi towards Hubballi, where farmers planned to lay siege to the residence of Union Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution Minister Pralhad Joshi. The march was halted after the Centre announced a committee headed by former NITI Aayog member Ramesh Chand to examine the issues raised by the growers. Having given the governments time until November 26, the farmers have warned that they will resume the agitation if their demands remain unresolved. The growers are demanding Rs 5,500 per tonne for sugarcane, a minimum selling price of Rs 60 per kg for sugar, better prices for sugarcane-based ethanol, and implementation of the M S Swaminathan Commission's recommendations, among other measures.

The discontent stems from a widening mismatch between costs and returns, causing financial suffering for both farmers and sugar mills. While cultivation costs and the fair and remunerative price of sugarcane have risen substantially, the Centre's minimum selling price of sugar has remained unchanged at Rs 31 per kg since February 2019. Chief Minister D K Shivakumar’s letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi rightly points out that several crucial decisions lie within the Centre’s jurisdiction. Any further delay will deepen growers' losses, as unharvested cane steadily loses weight and sugar content. Karnataka has indicated its willingness to provide state-level assistance while awaiting central decisions.

Jaggery price rises as sugar becomes costlierThe dispute might not have escalated this far had the Union government responded earlier to the farmers' requests for a meeting. Notably, Belagavi Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Roshan engaged with farmer leaders and helped prevent an escalation. The immediate priority is to ensure a remunerative price for the current crop and the timely commencement of crushing operations. If the Centre's price proves inadequate, Karnataka should consider a state-backed top-up while enforcing timely payments. The Centre must revise sugar and ethanol pricing and establish a credible mechanism for periodic reviews. Several countries have support programmes that protect farmers against price fluctuations and income losses, offering useful lessons for India. A permanent forum involving growers, millers, and government representatives could help resolve disputes before each crushing season. November 26 must be a deadline for action, not another date for deliberation. Farmers cannot be expected to keep their crops and livelihoods on hold indefinitely.

### RSS Chief’s Dussehra Delusions | Foreign conspiracies without evidence, foreign funds without scrutiny
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) Chief Mohan Bhagwat alleged that “demonic forces” from the West were trying to “destabilise India” in his annual Dussehra speech to the organisation. He also claimed that “regime change will not happen” in India like in France (sic), Albania, Bangladesh, or Nepal.

Like the Narendra Modi government at the Centre, Bhagwat offered neither evidence of foreign interference nor of a conspiracy to force regime change.

On the other hand, there is no dearth of evidence of both RSS-affiliated organisations and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi receiving support from foreign donors.

The latest evidence comes from a US publication, Bellingcat. It shows that US donor-advised funds channelled millions of dollars in grants to RSS-affiliated NGOs in India. Donor-advised funds are a US charity-giving arrangement — individuals contribute money or assets to a charity they want to sponsor through these funds, receive a tax deduction, and can remain anonymous.

'Regime change won't happen in India': RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on 'storm blowing in from West' opposing order and propriety The investigation by Bellingcat, published on October 6, shows that two US-based charities, Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of USA (Ekal USA), and Sewa International (Sewa USA), received $24.4 million from organisations managing donor-advised funds between 2020 and 2024. Together they received contributions and grants of $117.8 million. The ultimate donors remain anonymous, and are not part of the public records.

Both Ekal USA and Sewa USA have close links with the RSS. Ekal USA began as a programme of the Vishwa Hindu Parishad of America. In India, Ekal Vidyalaya schools have been criticised for indoctrinating poor children with Hindutva ideology. The Sewa USA website also points to its RSS connections and describes Seva Bharathi in India, an RSS-sponsored group, as its sister organisation.

The investigation found that both were funding sister organisations, also affiliated to the RSS in India. The Ekal Vidyalaya project — an RSS affiliate — received $33.7 million in foreign grants from Ekal USA. Similarly, Sewa USA reported giving foreign grants to India and South Asia amounting to $29.7 million. It is not known how much was given to its sister organisation in India, Seva Bharathi, during this period (2020-2024).

Both Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of India and Seva Bharathi have FCRA clearance from an RSS-friendly Modi government. Logically, however, merely on the basis of these organisations receiving foreign funding, can it be said that either they or their parent organisation, the RSS, have automatically become agents of foreign powers?

How is it then that the RSS readily accuses those who challenge the Modi government as operating under foreign influence (having not even provided evidence of foreign funding), while financial and ideological networks located abroad who fund its associates in India are considered beyond suspicion.

The same standard should be applied equally to both those who are critical of the government and those ideologically aligned to it. It should include full disclosure of funding, transparency about the organisational relationships with the funding agencies abroad, disclosure of the purpose of the expenditure, and production of evidence of any improper influence.

As for the Modi government, rallies abroad, at Madison Square Garden in New York, Wembley Stadium in London, or ‘Howdy, Modi!’ in Houston — are foreign-funded events and a form of transnational political interference because of how they impact domestic politics in India. Through these events, foreign citizens, albeit of Indian origin (PIOs), pool millions of dollars that indirectly influence Indian elections and the domestic political atmosphere through image-boosting campaigns for Modi.

These events also interfere in the domestic politics of the host country, such as in Modi’s partisan sloganeering for local political leaders, as in ‘Abki baar, Trump Sarkar’. The events also turn Indian community organisations in the host country into a lobby, to press Western political leaders, as in pressing them to overlook human rights or democratic backsliding within India.

So, neither Bhagwat nor the Modi government have a leg to stand on when they talk of foreign forces interfering in Indian domestic politics.

Bhagwat’s second proposition in his Dussehra speech was that it is a “wrong perception that problems get solved only through agitation”.

Of course, problems also get resolved through dialogue, negotiation, and parliamentary debate. However, when people feel that these methods have failed repeatedly to make those in power listen — as in the case of voter exclusion through SIR — are citizens not free to force negotiation with the State through peaceful resistance in the indigenous manner blessed by Mahatma Gandhi?

'Communist-Islamist cabal' running protest industry to undermine Brand Bharat, says RSS-linked magazine Organiser Bhagwat’s statement that “regime change won’t happen in India” is wishful and inaccurate. Sudden upheavals may be harder in India because of its size and established institutions, but they are not impossible. India’s history is replete with examples where mass agitations forced the removal of chief ministers (Chimanbhai Patel’s ouster in 1974), contributed to the electoral defeat of governments (the J P Movement in 1974-1975), made governments reverse policy (farmers’ movement in 2020-2021) and altered the balance of power in Parliament (fall of the Morarji Desai government in 1979 after the disintegration of the Janata Dal).

The fall of a government does not mean a collapse of the political system. Hypothetically, the Modi government could fall if the National Democratic Alliance coalition breaks down, or if a mass movement leads to an early general election.

Bhagwat has conflated a number of contemporary examples of protest to create a scary picture of political anarchy worldwide waiting to overwhelm India. In truth they are all different. The French government of Michel Bernier fell in 2024 after losing a vote of confidence — through a constitutional parliamentary process without an overthrow of the French State. The current protests in France by students and labour unions have not led to the fall of the French government either. The ongoing protests in Albania demonstrate the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama is under pressure, but it has not yet fallen.

Bangladesh and Nepal demonstrate a quite different pathway where political channels had become ineffective or inaccessible and the State’s political institutions lost their capacity to negotiate with the mass movement. It is reasonable to think that based on India’s size, its federal structure, its strong institutions, and military traditions that will not be the trajectory of Indian politics today.

With the long tradition and maturity of mass movements in India, the government and the RSS chief ought to take a lesson from that history instead of branding the demand for rethinking current policy changes in the electoral system as a foreign conspiracy.

Bharat Bhushan is a New Delhi-based journalist.

### Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

### Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
*The Hindu · Editorial*

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

### DC Edit | There Could Be A US Trade Deal, After All
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

Now that it has come in the US President’s words, a US trade deal with India is in the offing. Given the protracted nature of the negotiations and a few heavy red lines drawn by India that could not be crossed, the deal has been in the pipeline for far longer than anticipated. But then global geopolitics, as redefined by Mr Donald Trump’s policies have been shifting so much as to have hampered not only the trade deal on the anvil but also sent the US-India ties on a decline.

What has changed between the time that the US President hit India with 50 per cent tariffs, threatened to raise them to 100 per cent for buying Russian oil and then changed his tune to leave them with only a mild tariff for using child labour is a power that gained in importance due to the oil supply crisis through the straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb before strikes on Russian and Saudi Arabian oil refining facilities throttled more than a fifth of the supply chain.

The soft power, or should one say a refined prowess, lay in India’s capacity to process oil in its public sector and private refineries which the US President, who now plays the role of global oil overseer after having first created the crisis by starting the Iran war, has spotted. And he sent his Secretary of State to personally suss out Reliance’s facility in Gujarat’s Jamnagar, home to the biggest single site refining facility that can process 1.24 million barrels a day.

Word on the street is the US, in a bid to use the vast Venezuelan oil resources, even if they are of an inferior grade, would like to rope in India as the refiner and global supplier of Russian oil, now free of sanctions and tariffs for at least for two months, and oil from Venezuela to be carted across the world, which could still be worthwhile as the basic oil costs about 80 percent less than the average prices around $100 a barrel ruling today thanks to the Strait of Hormuz imbroglio.

The proof of the pudding is in the eating, they say, and it remains to be seen if India can use that one weapon in its armoury to extract a trade deal from its tortuous dealings with the Trump administration which glamorised its ties with Pakistan to the detriment of relations with India. It also remains to be seen at what cost the US trade deal will fructify for India as there were suspicions about giving away too much ground.

Going by Mr Trump’s description of the deal going to be “different”, it can be surmised that India-US may sign an initial trade deal covering areas it can agree upon while leaving the sticky points like agriculture and dairy for later. Any trade deal breakthrough will be important as it would be a vindication of India’s strategic autonomy principle applied to foreign affairs and the fact that it stood up to Mr Trump when he was pushing hard on various fronts like H-1B visas and green cards that may affect Indian IT professionals the most.

The trade deal in any form could be the harbinger of a more balanced approach from the White House regarding India and the old Asian binary of India-Pakistan. It appears it may have dawned on a transactional US President that India’s oil refining capacity could be the card that finessed his plans in the prevailing global scenario much as China’s hold on crucial rare earth minerals proved to be.

### A flawed measure of backwardness
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The Supreme Court’s verdict that a person belonging to the Backward Classes who converts to Islam is not entitled to reservation based on their pre-conversion status does not answer all questions about linkages between caste, religion, backwardness, and reservation. The Court dismissed the Tamil Nadu government's appeal against a Madras High Court order, which held that a person converting to Islam cannot claim reservations under the Backward Class (Muslim) category solely based on conversion. A bench of Justices Prashant Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar ruled that backwardness suffered in the antecedent social order cannot by itself be carried forward to the religion to which the individual has converted. The case concerned a person who converted to Islam and sought to be identified as a Muslim Lebbai, a backward community. After the local revenue authority turned down his application, he approached the Madras High Court, which, too, rejected his plea.

Questions remain about the Court’s view that a person does not carry their backwardness when they move from one religion to another. Backwardness is a social and economic condition. Many sections among Muslims have been declared backward and are entitled to reservation benefits. Seven communities designated as Other Backward Classes (OBCs) constitute the majority of Muslims in Tamil Nadu. The Rajinder Sachar Committee of 2006 had found that the Muslim community has suffered from social, economic, and educational backwardness similar to the Scheduled Castes and Tribes. The Court said the TN government's order wrongly treated a person's historical disadvantage in one religion as sufficient proof of membership in a particular backward class in another religion. The contention here is that social backwardness is tied to a caste structure and that when an individual converts to a non-Hindu social order, that backwardness ceases to exist.

Constitutional provisions regarding reservation for backward classes are based on social and economic backwardness, not on religious status. Article 15(4) and Article 16(4) allow the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes of citizens without reference to any religion. While reservations based on Scheduled Caste status are only available to those belonging to the Hindu, Sikh, and Buddhist religions, backward and OBC reservations are religion-neutral. When both the communities in question are backward, why should religious conversion be a measure to deny a person’s entitlement? That might amount to discrimination based on religion and a restriction on the right to practise any religion.

### Criminal apathy to a known danger
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The electric shock injuries suffered by two children near Rajanukunte on Bengaluru’s outskirts point to another systemic failure that continues to place lives at risk. Thirteen-year-old Sanvi and her five-year-old brother, Ayaan, were seriously injured when a metallic measuring tape they were playing with came into contact with a high-tension wire running alongside their rented house. Their ordeal calls for an inquiry and action against those whose negligence allowed the danger to persist. The parents have held both the landlord and Bangalore Electricity Supply Company (BESCOM) officials responsible. The family had recently moved into the property to educate their children. Aware that the high-tension wire ran close to the balcony, their father had formally raised safety concerns with the landlord, who allegedly dismissed his warnings.

When narrow roads and dense urban layouts bring houses dangerously close to power lines, assigning blame becomes a complex issue involving multiple authorities and actors. Legally and practically, accountability is shared across several levels. However, even where physical space is a constraint, utilities have a statutory obligation under the Electricity Act and safety codes to prevent hazardous conditions by replacing old bare wires with insulated cables that significantly reduce electrocution risks. While property owners and landlords maximise every square inch of constrained plots, ignoring statutory safety clearances to add balconies or floors, municipal bodies frequently look the other way as sanctioned plans are blatantly violated. Across Bengaluru and elsewhere, thousands of homes stand dangerously close to overhead electrical lines, exposing residents to a risk that has been normalised for far too long. Tragic accidents involving electrocution occur with distressing frequency, both in Bengaluru and across the country. Yet, once the outrage subsides, matters return to square one.

Siblings suffer shock from overhead power line in North Bengaluru, criticalAfter every such incident, authorities focus on compensation and suspensions. While necessary, these measures do not prevent the next accident. Power utilities should conduct comprehensive audits of high-risk residential zones and replace vulnerable overhead conductors with insulated cables. Municipal authorities must strictly enforce minimum safety clearances and take action against unsafe constructions. Landlords and builders must be held liable for renting properties that violate safety norms. Most importantly, complaints from citizens should trigger corrective action within fixed timelines. No family should have to gamble with the lives of their children. Unless governments, utilities, and property owners act decisively, this tragedy will not be the last. The question is not who alone is to blame. It is why known dangers are still allowed to exist.

### The memory of water: Why India needs to understand its dams better
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

From ‘assuring’ at the end of a monsoon season to ‘alarming’ before the beginning of the next, the unfailing trajectory of media headlines about India’s water reserves also lays bare the precarity of supply. For example, the country’s 166 major reservoirs with a combined live-storage capacity of 183.56 billion cubic metres saw water levels plummet from 87.83% of capacity in late November 2025 to a worrying 26% by early July this year.

According to the National Register of Large Dams, India has 6,628 specified dams – 6,545 operational and 83 under construction – that can store about 330 billion cubic metres of water. Yet India’s ever-larger reservoir system, which includes the world’s third-highest count of large dams after China and the United States, hasn’t necessarily translated into greater water security. Much of the pressure on India’s reservoirs, already beset by increasingly uneven rainfall and inflows, stems from additional capacity being quickly absorbed by the raging human, agrarian, industrial, and hydroelectric thirst for water.

Reservoirs that fill up after intense or concentrated rainfall lose water almost as rapidly to drier and hotter weather conditions. Sharp regional swings in rainfall and water storage further undermine national averages. The challenge becomes many times more complex in El Niño years like this one.

A user plan to unlock new water: Managing demand in India's big citiesFor long, India’s reservoirs have been treated as mere storage tanks rather than interconnected systems with the power to influence floods, droughts, and everything in between. After all, water held back or released from a reservoir can have a significant bearing on downstream extremes. The annual dilemma of whether to view the country’s reservoirs as a glass half-full or half-empty makes water management an uphill task, further complicated by the dearth of historical data needed to make sense of changing water dynamics and plan for a future under climate change.

The Central Water Commission monitors water levels in only 166 of India’s large dams, and even for these, systematic daily observations are only available from around 2000 onwards, which hinders efforts to fully assess climate risks, plan for droughts and floods, and represent reservoirs more realistically in water-management models.

Researchers from IIT Gandhinagar recently rebuilt daily storage records for 75 major Indian reservoirs across 15 basins, from their commissioning year up to 1999. They did this by using a mix of weather data, computer simulations of water movement through rivers and reservoirs, and machine learning to predict patterns based on existing data.

Major reservoirs in Karnataka report second-lowest storage in 6 yearsThe study, led by Vimal Mishra and Urmin Vegad of the Department of Civil Engineering at the institute, also examined changes in reservoir storage over time and across regions, and identified the specific times of a year when most changes occur.

Filling in the historical gaps has revealed surprising facts. India’s reservoir capacity may have grown with the construction of massive new dams, but normalised storage levels show a moderate long-term decline, indicating how factors like rising water withdrawals offset the increase in capacity. The researchers report rising storage trends in 68% of the reservoirs during pre-monsoon months (March-May), and in 64% during post-monsoon months.

According to the research, changes in reservoir storage are greatest during the peak of monsoon rains from late July to mid-August, and again around January when seasonal drawdown and water demand for irrigation surge. Many reservoirs in central and western India, for example, show larger swings between monsoon filling and dry-season drawdown.

The researchers also found fewer low-storage events in 67% of the reservoirs and more frequent high-storage conditions in 64%. This may be good for drought resilience, but it calls for greater caution in managing flood risks.

Deciphering the water ledger

Improved understanding of reservoir levels relative to their historical capacity can enhance the ability to monitor droughts, plan support measures, adjust water releases from dams, and preserve space for flood control ahead of extreme rainfall events. It can also help improve crop planning, irrigation, and hydropower generation, while identifying basins in need of new storage or other interventions, and enabling better-coordinated, evidence-backed water-sharing between states.

The IIT study underscores that boosting water security is as much about building more dams as it is about improving data-driven measures to retain water, reduce losses, control demand, and handle uneven inflows. This requires India’s water and flood models to become more realistic.

First, they must accurately represent the water that reservoirs can actually hold, accounting for factors such as storage lost to sedimentation, and the capacity and operating limits of gates and spillways across all major reservoirs.

Second, models must represent how dams are operated in practice, encompassing seasonal water-level rules followed by operators, irrigation, drinking water, and hydropower requirements, emergency water releases, and real-time forecasts of rainfall and inflows.

And third, water, flood, and inundation models must continually exchange information to enable better insights into how one dam’s releases affect downstream areas and how multiple dams operating together can reduce or intensify flood risks. This matters because a 2011 study published in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences found that larger hydrological models often leave out or oversimplify dam operations.

Without long-term records, it is hard to assess seasonal patterns, distinguish temporary water shortages from longer-term variations related to climate change, strengthen early-warning systems, and guide decisions around vast new investments. Combining the crucial dynamics of reservoir storage with rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, and demand management can help India reduce its dependence on new dams.

The writer is an independent journalist and commentator.

### Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
*The Hindu · Editorial*

When Emmanuel Macroncame to power in 2017, at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire, including the 19th-century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews. The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

### Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.

### The RSS at 101, between change and continuity
*The Hindu · Opinion*

As the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS)concluded its centenary celebrations on Vijayadashami (October 20, 2026), the organisation that began in 1925 as a cultural response to Hindu subjugation has grown into one of the most influential socio-political forces in the country. It runs 88,949 daily shakhas at 55,683 locations, while one of the 32 organisations it has inspired, the Bharatiya Janata Party, governs India. Yet, its legacy remains deeply contested. For many liberals and secularists, the RSS evokes a history of exclusion, communalism, and ideological bigotry. For its supporters, it represents discipline, service, and a proud assertion of Hindu identity. The question now is twofold: whether the RSS is evolving (whether there is, in fact, an RSS 2.0); and whether the rest of us, secular Indians, can find a modus vivendi with it.

Infographics | RSS: Mapping the saffron empire

A dualityThe discomfort of secular and liberal Indians with the RSS is not without foundation. The organisation’s early years were marked by conspicuous silence and distancing from the freedom struggle. While Congress leaders courted arrest and endured colonial repression, the RSS abstained from anti-British agitation. Its tactical accommodation with the British Raj, and the Hindu Mahasabha’s with the Muslim League in the government of Bengal, in the waning years of Empire, reflected its prioritisation of Hindu consolidation over Indian nationalism.

Walking a thin saffron line Post-Independence, the RSS’s image was indelibly stained by its association, however indirect, with the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi, which many of its cadres celebrated by distributing sweets. Though the organisation was banned and later exonerated, the ideological proximity between Nathuram Godse and the Sangh Parivar left a lasting scar. In subsequent decades, the RSS and its affiliates were frequently accused of complicity in fomenting communal discord, from the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992 to the Gujarat riots of 2002.

Its intellectual canon, too, has been appalling: M.S. Golwalkar, the second Sarsanghchalak from 1940-73, praised Nazi Germany’s racial policies and commended Hitler’s treatment of the Jews as a model for Hindus in dealing with Muslims. His writings, once central to RSS pedagogy, portrayed minorities as threats to national unity, Mahatma Gandhi as an un-Hindu pacifist, the Constitution as divorced from Indian roots, and secularism as a western import. Even in more recent years, the organisation’s stance on women, emphasising domestic roles, child-bearing and cultural preservation over autonomy, has been labelled regressive, misogynist and patriarchal, and not only by women.

The message in the RSS chief’s speechYet, to reduce the RSS to a stereotype of intolerance is to ignore its vast and varied social footprint. During the Partition riots, RSS volunteers played a critical role in protecting, rescuing and rehabilitating Hindu and Sikh refugees, especially in Punjab. In times of national crisis — wars, earthquakes, floods, landslides — the organisation and its social service arm, Seva Bharati, have mobilised swiftly and effectively, often outpacing state machinery. Its educational initiatives, through Vidya Bharati schools and Ekal Vidyalayas, have brought basic literacy to remote tribal areas. Its health camps, blood donation drives, and charitable outreach have earned praise even from ideological opponents. For many Indians, especially in small towns and villages, the RSS is not a political entity but a provider of tangible services and moral discipline.

Signs of a ‘shift’This duality — ideological bigotry on one hand, genuine civic engagement on the other — has long confounded observers. But recent years suggest a shift toward a more conciliatory posture. Under Mohan Bhagwat, the RSS has adopted a noticeably softer tone, publicly affirming Islam’s place in India (“Islam arrived in India and will remain in India”) and cautioning Hindus against religious provocation, famously urging Hindus to “stop looking for a Shivling under every masjid”, a notable departure from earlier combative rhetoric. The leadership now reinterprets “Hindu Rashtra” not as majoritarian rule, but as an inclusive civilisational ethos, quietly omitting from new editions Golwalkar’s most incendiary views in favour of appeals to national unity and service. Outreach to Dalits and tribals has expanded alongside cautious interfaith dialogue; during an August 2026 visit to the United States, Mr. Bhagwat championed pluralism, declaring that excluding Muslims contradicts Hindutva itself. Concurrently, the RSS frames its link with the BJP as hands-off: “We only give suggestions,” Mr. Bhagwat has said, distancing the organisation from the day-to-day decisions of government. “Things cannot be achieved through politics alone.”

Still, there is a widespread view among secular liberals that Mr. Bhagwat’s recent remarks are a tactical manoeuvre to make Hindutva acceptable to a broader, international audience rather than a fundamental change in core RSS ideology, which endorses or condones exclusionary and bigoted conduct in practice. To dispel such misgivings, we argue, the RSS chief must address critical issues with solid institutional and public messaging within India rather than relying on platitudes abroad. In particular, Mr. Bhagwat should clearly oppose any initiatives that violate the spirit of the Places of Worship Act, 1991 (particularly regarding temple reconstruction in Mathura and Varanasi, causes which Mr. Bhagwat says the RSS itself would not back while swayamsevaks are free to join them). He should deplore how anti-conversion legislation in Maharashtra shifts the burden of proof onto minorities during ordinary acts of worship, prompting churches in Mumbai to require self-attestations before permitting entry to non-Christians. He must demonstrate moral leadership by actively opposing physical attacks on Christian churches, priests and nuns, prayer meetings and burial grounds, while ensuring that the law is not weaponised against minorities, especially Muslims, through selective first information reports for offering namaz or the hasty use of bulldozers against religious structures without due process or appeal.

A picture of Islam that is quite differentInstitutionally, Mr. Bhagwat and the RSS should sanction leaders of the BJP and Sangh Parivar organisations for engaging in hate speech, while expressing his own anguish over why India’s communal atmosphere has become increasingly toxic despite a decade of inclusive public rhetoric. Without such concrete measures, Hindutva continues to align with a majoritarian understanding of democracy, with Hindus alone seen as the primary owners of the nation, making truly inclusive dialogue difficult. That would require the RSS to renounce and denounce vigilantism unequivocally, to uphold constitutional pluralism and inclusion, and to treat disagreement and dissent not as betrayal, but as proof of India’s democratic vitality, in its civilisational tradition of samvad (dialogue/conversation/discussion).

The next generation is watchingThere is also a generational test here, and it may well prove a decisive one. A majority of Indians are under 35 years, and they will judge the RSS by what they see it do on the street and on their phones. By that measure the record is thin: meme pages, troll armies and vigilantes who act against everything Mr. Bhagwat has said, and do so in Hindutva’s name, have only multiplied, and it is hard to point to any instance of the RSS publicly disowning, let alone disciplining, any of them. If his words are meant, young Indians will expect to see them enforced. If they are not, the young will draw their own conclusions, and an organisation that has always prided itself on shaping the character of India’s youth will have failed the one audience that will decide its second century.

At 101, both the organisation and the nation stand at a political and civilisational crossroads. While its tone is softer and outreach broader, elements within the Sangh ecosystem still traffic in hate and exclusion. As the RSS’s influence grows across institutions, secular Indians face a profound dilemma. Acknowledging that cultural nationalism is now entrenched does not warrant embracing it, but it does demand engagement. Rather than seeking reconciliation at the expense of principle, secular liberals can challenge its inconsistencies, insist on inclusive governance, and achieve coexistence without surrender.

Shashi Tharoor is a fourth-term Member of Parliament (Congress party) from Thiruvananthauram, and the Sahitya Akademi Award-winning author of 29 books, including ‘Why I Am a Hindu’ and, most recently, ‘The Sage Who Reimagined Hinduism: The Life, Lessons and Legacy of Sree Narayana Guru’. His forthcoming book is ‘The Fight for Indian Liberalism’ (January 2027)

### DC Edit | CJP Arrests Blow to Our Legacy
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

One of the unique features of the Indian independence movement was the civil disobedience movement where people would non-violently break the law which curtailed their basic democratic rights such as the right to assembly. It caught the imagination of the world so much it had takers in several countries. The Defiance Campaign of 1952 in South Africa by the Black people where they gathered violating the segregation law and the civil disobedience movement, again, of the Black community in the United States in the sixties, were two such movements which ultimately triumphed. It may come as a curious piece of information that the latter took place in a country whose Declaration of Independence insisted that “all men are created equal”.Making salt was no criminal act, but the Dandi march and the boiling of sea water to precipitate some salt violating the law shook the moral foundation of the British Raj. True, it took several more years and several editions of the movement for India to attain independence but its ethos continue to reverberate in the country’s conscience and are shared by all those who have at least a distant idea of the national movement.Prime Minister Narendra Modi often tells the world that India is the mother of democracy, and he may have a point: we have democratic traditions in our past. But incarcerating people who violate simple laws for days together and burdening them with cases misusing the laws available in the statute book cannot be a democratic practice. CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were given bail by a special executive magistrate after spending eight days in jail for entering Jantar Mantar. Of course, the government had indeed denotified the place as a designated protest site in the nation’s capital but to jail them for entering the spot and waving national flag as a mark of protest and in furtherance of their political campaign against the special intensive revision of voter rolls do not exactly brighten India’s image as a democratic country. As for the CJP leaders, they can take assurance in the words of Martin Luther King Junior, the leader of the American civil disobedience movement: unlearnt suffering is redemptive.

### DC Edit | Europe Is Burning and Politics Is Adding Fuel
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

It is almost as if a third of EU nations are going through the early stages of a European Spring as protests have broken out. France, with its long tradition of street protests, saw peaceful demonstrations transform into riots as cars were set on fire, public buildings stormed and a looting spree engulfed various cities of the old Republic.The Arab Spring was said to have leapt from a humble Tunisian cart pusher standing up to authority. Things appear far worse in France today that is experiencing one of its worst civil unrests in years after a peaceful student-led protest movement against deficiencies in the school system and infra ran for weeks.The anxiety around everything concerning the present and the future — cost-of-living indices defying gravity with petroleum and energy prices constantly rising due to the Iran war, lack of satisfying job opportunities for youth starting out on their life journey and general discontent — has been energising far-left protests even as a confrontation between the far-right and the far-left is looming electorally as the curtain begins to descend on the President and his era of Macronism.The blame game is on as leaders in power take potshots at insurrectionist elements and radical far-left groups, as Macron did. That he was cavorting in an event with Celine Dion while protests were raging may not have drawn much public sympathy for one of the imposing political figures of Europe in the last decade and more.The pattern is visible in other European nations too where political contests are brewing between the extremes and economic hardship, more than deprivation, which is rarer in welfare states, is driving the young onto the streets, as in Belgium, Italy, Greece, Ireland, Spain, Germany and Austria.Much of the unrest has had to do with inadequate education funding, school conditions deteriorating to the extent of rats running around classrooms, fuel prices and urban housing crises, with shouts of political grievances emerging conveniently at what some deem as an opportunity to put pressure on the regimes of the day.Whatever be their political sympathy towards protesters who may be mostly from the deprived classes, there is no government that will not act to keep order and protect the trust in the administration as capable of protecting property even if criminal gangs are the ones inspiring the riots against symbols of power, essentially of capitalism and the looting aimed at commercial enterprises.The world economy tanking at this juncture is not helping as it takes hits from wars causing disruption of global supply chains. However, at its heart, this is a display of public hyper-anxiety about their lot in life today, clearly being flamed by political clashes everywhere, including in India where students protesting corrupt exam practices as in the leaking of question papers began a movement that has taken off to highlight the right to vote.Democracies must attempt a delicate balancing act between giving space for dissent and sustaining public order, between sympathy for the protester and contempt for the unruly, between human rights and authority. And regime changes do happen periodically in polls in which the public still has a say unlike in nations where the right exists not at all or stays only on paper.It is a difficult time politically for the world, but there is no guarantee that victory for the far-right, as predicted in France and Brazil, will help stem the discontent nor can victory for the liberal and the far-left guarantee a solution to problems. What with the centrists seeming to fail too, today’s world remains the biggest challenge for leaders.

### Abhijit Bhattacharyya | Beware the October Shock As China Moves Signal Threat
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Come October, come China and Pakistan in tandem. On October 22, 1947, a murderous assault on the independent Kashmir state by Pakistani army-supported irregulars paved the way to Srinagar acceding to sovereign India on October 27, within five days. Next, the Chinese annexation of a free and sovereign Tibet between October 6, 1950, and October 24, 1951, shook India’s security system to the core. And, finally, came the worst of all:

the naked two-front Chinese invasion of Kashmir and NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh) on October 20, 1962, shattered Prime Minister Nehru’s dream of an enduring India-China bilateral. Hence, every October, expect the unexpected. India should be prepared to face the October shenanigans of the Dragon not excluding diplomatic harassment. The pattern is so deeply ingrained in the psyche of the rulers of China that it would be surprising to see the recurring failure of India to give due importance to their diabolical designs over more than six decades. India must not forget that the first assault by the Communist Party of China’s People’s Liberation Army, akin to organised crime, occurred on the Indian patrol of Thag la ridge when “50 odd men were heavily attacked 5 am Wednesday 10 October 1962 by 800 men supported by heavy mortars” at Tseng-Jong in the remote corner of then NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh). What followed 10 days later on the Saturday of October 20 is part of the most inglorious chapter of India’s history showing the results of misreading the Dragon’s mind. Then PM Nehru continues to be the villain till date. Regrettably, however, none of the successors of Nehru could reverse the losses. China rules the roost and Indians cannot tackle its powers in any way whatsoever.Now, 64 years after the Tseng-jong assault, along the 15,000-foot snowline, China has once again descended to the sea level on October 10, 2026, tying up a US $335.78 million agreement with Bangladesh to expand and modernise the Mongla port, 80 kilometres from the Indian (West Bengal) border. Make no mistake; its arrival at the eastern door of India through Dhaka is straight out of The Strategy of Indirect Approach by Liddell Hart. And if that were not enough, the first ever joint Sino-Pakistani army exercise began on the “forbidden” land of Xinjiang, not far from the Karakorum tri-junction with India and Afghanistan within 96 hours.

A clear signal of deepening military trust, weapons inter-operability and joint command and control (as last seen in May 2025 during Operation Sindoor) against India. Yet, there’s no Indian reaction. Why? When a free and sovereign Tibet was brutally conquered by the Communist Party of China in 1950, Home minister of India Vallabhbhai Patel did point out the grave threat to India’s sovereignty and security. However, today’s India lacks the Sardar’s wit, wisdom and courage. Today the Dhaka-Beijing-Islamabad combo has created another October headache for New Delhi without doubt. Nevertheless, a section of India’s ruling class is clearly in “olive branch” mode. On October 14, the Indian minister of commerce and industry, Piyush Goyal, said, “India is working to rebuild its relations with China.” However, the same day, Ashwini Vaishnaw, the electronics and IT minister, said that “India’s critical minerals are among the biggest vulnerabilities in its push for tech sovereignty”. True, the world knows how heavily dependent India is on China in this subject. And the world also is seeing how China takes full advantage of this to keep India on leash. But the last of the three statements, the one made by the foreign minister, was the clearest in conveying New Delhi’s intent. He said “any disturbance along India-China border will have consequences, as the LAC (Line of Actual Control) has to be stable for normalising relations between two countries”.

This writer, too, has been of same view, that ceaseless territory violation of India by China is non-negotiable. All things, economics, trade, commerce, diplomacy, banking and politics- can continue only if Indian land is intact and not being snatched away by a purported ‘friend’ who says, “let’s talk on convergence, divergence can wait”. That’s the classical duplicity of the Dragon, the misreading of which led Nehru to become the object of criticism by his successors that continues to this day. But did Nehru or Indira Gandhi ever invite China to exploit the Indian market to make money in the heartland and massacre our military at the outpost in a one-sided deal?

What makes the task of Indian diplomacy more complicated is the ceaseless undiplomatic, and at times uncouth, unprovoked salvos fired at New Delhi by MAGA-inspired Donald Trump administration officials everywhere. Consequently, India today faces an unprecedented two-front flank assault, from the US from the west and from China from the north and northeast. But while the United States’ misdemeanours are a comparatively new trend, the Chinese shenanigans have been chronic and unrelenting....

The crucial issues Mr Rubio discussed with the Indian foreign minister S. Jaishankar was to nudge India to sign a bilateral trade deal. “We’re very, very close,” said the American about it. The other issues on the agenda were American tariffs and bilateral energy interests. The US wants India to buy less of Russian crude and rely more on supplies from America and Venezuela. Diplomacy links with economics, trade and commerce. Energy is where Reliance Industries matters. Its Jamnagar refinery is one of the few in the world that can handle the complex Venezuelan crude. After 2022, the numbers within AGMUT are 65 for J&K, and 10 for Ladakh in case of IAS. The IPS figures are 70 and 10, respectively. These obviously do not denote the total strength of AGMUT. Another lesser-known impact is the arrival of new IAS and IPS in J&K, and Ladakh from other parts of the country. They are part of AGMUT, and can be transferred. “The local administrative fragrance is slowly disappearing,” remarks a source familiar with the bureaucracy. This is crucial because the three regions of the old J&K state are distinct in terms of geography, culture, languages and politics. Understanding their fault lines requires more acumen than the abilities to read official briefs. An officer describes the new revolving door culture. A few newly posted AGMUT officers treat their assignments as interim ones, like visits of guest lecturers, before the plum postings in Goa or Delhi. This is not a verdict on every officer but raises a serious question: Can continuity survive when officers think of themselves as temporary visitors? Supporters of joint AGMUT argue that a centralised cadre will shake the grip of local networks. Sources agree that patronage and corruption in parts of J&K and Ladakh need strong checks. But AGMUT must bring impartiality without alienation, and accountability without erasing local knowledge. Bureaucratic flower power A senior secretary based in Delhi discovered a novel way to practise austerity without sacrificing aesthetics. The PWD used to decorate his office with fresh flowers, which were replaced on alternate days. But winters came with a problem. The flowers refused to wilt on the second day, and remained fresh. But they had to be thrown away. Rather than allow healthy blooms to meet an official death, the secretary took them home. His office remained decorated with new flowers. His living room acquired fresh colours. The flowers worked overtime. It was a unique arrangement to transfer the flowers without a formal order. Call it recycling, resource optimisation or jugaad, but the civil servant ensured that ‘state’ flowers enjoyed a second innings in private surroundings.

## 20 October 2026

### A familiar script after a tragedy
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

Everything that goes wrong at large congregations and leads to a stampede was present at the pooja pandal in Kolkata, where 19 people were killed and at least 25 were injured on Saturday. The tragedy at the Chorbagan pandal was foretold but ignored by both the organisers and the authorities responsible for ensuring safety. Reports indicate that the entry and exit points were too narrow for emergency movement, security personnel were far fewer than what was required, and announcements meant to guide the crowd only added to the confusion. As often happens, showers triggered a rush; a sudden downpour forced some visitors to seek shelter inside an already crowded pandal, while others tried to leave. An announcement suggesting that the structure might collapse increased the panic. A VIP gate may have constrained effective use of the limited space. The competitive zeal among Durga Puja organisers to outshine one another has often come at the expense of safe and efficient pandal design and crowd management.

The day after the tragedy also has a familiar script: condolences, ministerial visits to the venue, compensation announcements, arrests, safety audits, formation of a special investigation team, blame games, and whataboutery. Questions about why temporary shops were permitted in a narrow lane, and why basic safety protocols, crowd management guidelines, and emergency rescue norms were not followed, will likely remain unanswered. Rain or other natural events, the sudden arrival of a vehicle, or sheer crowd size are often cited as causes of the tragedy. There have been findings that blamed the victims or the inability of the crowd to follow directions for the situation ‘going out of control’ and causing deaths and injuries.

Kolkata stampede: A shoe mark on a child’s face, a father’s wail — ‘No Puja for us again’Last year alone, stampedes at different venues claimed over 127 lives. According to the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), India has witnessed 3,935 stampede incidents between 1996 and 2022. India is a country with a huge population where large numbers of people congregate on various occasions. Most stampedes have happened at places of worship. It is administrations at all levels, especially at the local level, and organisers of events where crowds gather who should ensure that safety protocols are religiously enforced. It is unfortunate that India has not learnt the necessary lessons from the thousands of stampedes it has seen.

### Metro’s costly drift from timelines
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

Bengaluru’s Pink Line has become an expensive illustration of what happens when infrastructure planning and execution drift far from their timelines. The 21.26-km corridor, linking Kalena Agrahara in the south to Nagawara in the north via M G Road, was originally estimated at Rs 8,730 crore and scheduled for completion by March 2016. Construction commenced only in 2020, by which time the revised cost nearly doubled to Rs 17,346 crore. Tendering delays, bureaucratic red tape, complex tunnelling, escalating material prices, and steep land costs all played a part. Meanwhile, the estimate for Phase 2 has increased from Rs 30,695 crore to Rs 40,425 crore. This is not an isolated setback. Bengaluru began planning its metro in the early 2000s, with approvals granted in 2006. The first 6.7-km stretch of the Purple Line opened in October 2011, but the line connecting Whitefield and Challaghatta became fully operational only in October 2023. The Green Line began operations in March 2014, while the Yellow Line now links R V Road and Bommasandra. The Pink Line and the airport-bound Blue Line remain under construction. Future projects include the proposed Red Line from Sarjapur to Hebbal and the Orange Line in western Bengaluru. Once all sanctioned phases are completed, the network is expected to extend to around 220-225 km.

By comparison, Kolkata introduced India’s first metro in 1984, while Delhi’s network now exceeds 350 km. Bengaluru, a later entrant, has widened the gap through delays in execution. The airport shows the consequences of poor planning clearly: Kempegowda International Airport opened in 2008, yet nearly two decades later it still lacks metro connectivity. A rapid-transit link should have been planned and delivered alongside the airport rather than treated as an afterthought.

Pink Line: BMRCL files compliance with CMRS's observationsThe larger problem is a persistent failure to anticipate future demand. Projects are conceived to address current congestion, but by the time they are completed, they fall short of the needs they were intended to meet. In this context, proposals such as the 60-km Bengaluru-Tumakuru metro, expected to cost over Rs 20,000 crore, raise legitimate questions about priorities. Announcing ambitious new corridors while existing ones remain unfinished risks stretching finances and administrative capacity even further. Before announcing new infrastructure projects, the government must complete works underway, with firm deadlines, regular progress reviews, and clear accountability for delays. Bengaluru is Karnataka’s largest economic contributor and one of the world’s fastest-growing metropolises. It needs infrastructure that anticipates growth, not a succession of delayed projects that struggle to catch up with it.

### Elon Musk’s promise to give SpaceX stock to kids is no gift
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

One of the great joys, but also miseries, of following business news over the past decade or so has been riding the dodgy roller coaster of the Elon Musk experience. He has gone from a guy people considered a real-life Tony Stark to something more like a modern-day Henry Ford, in the worst possible way, with countless gut-wrenching twists in between.

At no point, however, did anybody think: “Hey, you know who’s missing out on this? Children.” Until today.

SpaceX Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk pledged on Monday to donate one share of his company to each of America’s 72 million children, vowing it would be the first such gift “of many.” If you had just this morning traveled here from another planet, then you might consider this a reasonably generous gesture from a near-trillionaire. The stock has been a bit stagnant since its June IPO, sure, but the company has billions of dollars in US government contracts, and Musk has promised its revenue will soar from less than $19 billion last year to $1 trillion by 2030.

Such a gift would barely trouble Musk’s vast wealth and power. It would cost about $10.5 billion, shaving Musk’s net worth to $889.5 billion. And as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Liam Denning points out, it would cut his SpaceX voting power, currently at 82% because of the stock’s dual-class nature, by just 0.1 percentage points.

But even a passing familiarity with Musk’s whole vibe should raise many immediate concerns about this “promise.” For one thing, it was made on his social media app, X, formerly known as Twitter, on which Musk has promised many things, a large percentage of which have never happened. Most famous was his 2018 declaration that he had “funding secured” to take Tesla Inc. private at $420 a share. It got him in serious legal trouble when it turned out not to be true.

If you have several hours to kill, you can peruse this website for a long list of other unfulfilled Musk promises, including a “cross country summon” feature that would let your Tesla travel the continent by itself, Incredible-Journey style, to find you; half-hour rocket trips from New York to London; 1 million robotaxis; and seafaring Teslas, to name a few. Buying stock in Musk is less an investment than it is subscribing to a streaming service for increasingly ridiculous science fiction.

Elon Musk announces to gift SpaceX shares to all American childrenAlso, it doesn’t seem as if Musk spent long hours conferring with lawyers and accountants planning for this gift. Rather, the timing and Musk’s track record suggest he saw SpaceX’s AI rival, Anthropic PBC, making its own charitable pledge on Sunday and felt the urge to one-up it. The maker of Claude vowed to donate 5% of its shares, potentially worth $75 billion (if the company is worth $1.5 trillion), to a fund that will benefit the “public good,” including AI’s destruction of jobs that kids want.

Musk replied to Anthropic’s X post making this announcement with a curt “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” suggesting he’s just better at doing charity. His detail-free promise of one share per child followed hours later. How will children receive these shares? Nobody knows, and the odds are very good that nobody will ever have to find out.

Anthropic’s offer seems to be an olive branch to AI’s large and growing contingent of haters and skeptics, including most of the American public, ahead of its IPO. Maybe it will also deflect some of the pressure to impose actual government regulation of the technology.

Musk could use some good publicity, too, and not just because SpaceX is a growing AI giant. He has embraced White nationalism and let SpaceX’s Starlink service undermine Ukraine’s effort to defend itself from Russia’s invasion. He manned the Department of Government Efficiency that slashed government jobs and offices without care for the repercussions, including the 700,000 people who have already died because of DOGE’s assault on USAID.

His behavior affects everyone invested in his companies, for better or worse, including those theoretical 72 million children. For a long time, “worse” has been a no-show; his fans have helped Tesla’s stock price defy traditional market logic for years. How long can the magic last? As tough as children have it these days, with the climate in chaos, war in Europe and the Middle East and AI threatening to take all of the jobs, do they really need the headache of finding out?
