### France comes unglued, again
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

American liberals have often looked to France for a model of what they would like to see in the United States: universal healthcare; low-cost daycare; affordable universities; strong worker protections; sacrosanct social benefits; high taxes; large investments in green energy; a secular republic in a multicultural society; constrained defense budgets, modest economic growth but lots of joie de vivre.

For a long time that model seemed almost plausible. Not anymore.

What has unfolded in France in recent weeks -- student protests against deteriorating schools turning into mass demonstrations against deteriorating economic conditions turning into violence and rioting against the state itself on a level not seen in years, and all this ahead of presidential elections that could wind up pitting the extreme left of Jean-Luc Mélenchon against the extreme right of Marine Le Pen -- are scenes from a country coming unglued.

It’s not just France. Europe’s political center is crumbling.That's not because its finances or politics are broken, although both are. More deeply broken are the promises that were supposed to hold the country together: that the young would find opportunity and the old would have support; that the country could carry on as a vast entitlement state without having to compete as a nimble and enterprising one; that France would maintain its identity and its security within a peaceable Europe open to itself and to the rest of the world.

Those promises were never really tenable, though it's remarkable how tenaciously the French have held on to them.

A succession of French prime ministers have struggled to enact a reform raising the retirement age to 64 from 62, which would bring it more in line with the European Union average and help address the crushing fiscal burden of paying generous pensions in an aging society. Yet the measure is a political nonstarter, which has now been kicked past the next election so the current prime minister can hold on to his job.

France's youth unemployment stands around 20%, nearly three times the rate in Germany. Yet statutory social costs for employers are higher in France -- about 45% of gross salary -- than anywhere else in Europe, discouraging hiring.

A whopping 57% of the country's gross domestic product is spent by the state. Yet the quality of France's public schools, hospitals, policing and other social services is in manifest decline, not because the government spends too little but because it tries to do too much.

France is hardly the only country in which people are unwilling to let go of government benefits for the common good. But its problems are compounded by its elite traditions of étatisme, even under Emmanuel Macron's supposedly reformist presidency, and deep-seated hostility to free markets and enterprise. One recent survey of 34 countries put French attitudes toward economic freedom in the bottom quarter of the table.

Of course the French are fully within their rights to distrust or repudiate what they call, usually as a slur, "neoliberalism." But they should accept the consequences that come with that distrust.

Average annual wages in France, measured in U.S. dollar purchasing power, are over 30% less than they are in the United States. The last time the World Bank published its "ease of doing business" rankings, in 2020, France came in 32, in league with Turkey. That may explain why France gets relatively little foreign direct investment -- only 15% of what tiny Singapore takes in.

In a list of the world's 100 largest companies as measured by market capitalization, 62 are from the United States, 11 are from China and Hong Kong, and just four are from France. Last year, Le Figaro reported that "nearly 15,000 recent graduates from French engineering and management schools choose to begin their careers abroad each year," the primary reasons for wanting to go being France's low salaries.

Policies of national self-impoverishment have broader effects on social cohesion and national security. Resentments against migrants inevitably fester when people feel they are sharing dwindling national resources with newcomers. So do most other resentments -- of class and age and religion and race -- when people are fighting over how to divide those resources rather than thinking about how to grow them.

Demographic forecasts expect net immigration to jump an additional 50% in the coming decades compared with the net increase over the past 30 years. Barring draconian immigration restrictions or a miracle of economic growth, this is a recipe for civil strife, if not outright war.

It's also a formula for a different kind of danger. Though they are ostensible opposites, both Le Pen and Mélenchon oppose military aid to Ukraine and want a partial or full withdrawal by France from NATO. To the extent that the protests and riots have boosted their presidential chances, they've also made it likelier that Vladimir Putin will eventually win his war, especially as the Trump administration turns, shamefully, on Ukraine.

It's always possible that the weekend's spasms of violence will remind the French, some of whom are now under curfew, that their politics tend to end badly when taken to the streets. There's a warning there for all the naifs who used to extol the virtues of a country that thought it really knew how to live.

### The US-Iran war is making world hunger much worse
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Step away from the minute-by-minute news cycle for a moment and consider what two of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council have wreaked: Russia and the United States, with their illegal wars against Ukraine and Iran, share much of the blame for reversing a whole generation’s progress in the fight against hunger.

According to the new Global Hunger Index, released last week just before World Food Day, the combined scourges of undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — all symptoms of relative starvation — have become worse, halting a two-decade trend of improvement.

The numbers in this year’s index reflect hunger conditions in 122 countries during the years 2021-2025. But as the report’s experts make clear, the war that US President Donald Trump launched against Iran in 2026 will exacerbate the deterioration, condemning tens or hundreds of millions to hunger in the years to come, in addition to the estimated 645 million who were “undernourished” in 2025.

The spread of hunger of course has many causes in these times of “polycrisis,” ranging from factors beyond human control, including weather patterns such as El Nino, to disruptions in which we humans had an unhelpful hand, such as climate change.

The crucial addition to those problems, though, is the increase in wars. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program, which collects such statistics, counted 65 state-based armed conflicts in 2025, the most since World War II.

Wars are deadly in many ways, but one of them is keeping food away from civilians. That’s true from Sudan to the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Gaza Strip. Last year, for the first time since the UN developed a ranking method for hunger crises, catastrophic famine was declared in two places at once, Sudan and Gaza.

But if all wars starve, some starve a lot further afield from their battlefields than others. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is an example. Before Moscow’s invasion, those two countries accounted for roughly 30% of global wheat exports. When those shipments, largely through the Black Sea, were disrupted in 2022, food prices spiked and the people worst affected were in poor countries in Africa and Asia.

This year’s US-Israeli war against Iran is a similar shock, which will show up in the next hunger index. Consumers in America, Europe and other rich countries feel the war’s effects mainly at the pump, through higher fuel prices caused by oil being throttled on its way through the Strait of Hormuz. People in poor countries also suffer from more expensive energy.

Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of HormuzBut they face a bigger problem. Before the war, about 30% of the world’s fertilizer exports traveled through the Strait of Hormuz — everything from urea and ammonia to phosphates and sulfur. Those flows stopped for a while, and are now returning to trickles. The World Bank projects the price of urea, for instance, to spike by 60% this year, before stabilizing only in 2027 (provided the war doesn’t flare up again).

Farmers in poor countries are in effect priced out. In that way the shortages of fertilizer caused by the war directly cause starvation and child stunting and wasting elsewhere. (Stunting refers to children being too short for their age, wasting to being underweight.) These shocks typically persist long after hostilities end, because agricultural markets take time to recover, and farmers have already missed entire planting and harvesting seasons.

Even a rise in food prices of 1% correlates with higher mortality of children under the age of five. Households that struggle to afford food tend to cut back on the most nutritious meals first, with lifelong effects for the children. (For example, Indonesians who were children of poor parents during the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98 are on average shorter and more obese than those in other age cohorts.) The Iran war of 2026 will stunt many Africans, Asians others for decades to come.

The overall scale of suffering is in fact impossible to quantify. Moses Chrispus Okello, an Ethiopia-based researcher at the Institute for Security Studies, points out that the new food crisis caused by the Iran war hits countries in Africa all the harder because they have no money but a lot of debt and refugees, and are already reeling under droughts caused by climate change.

Hunger caused by a distant war also tends to ignite new conflicts, which then lead to even more instability and starvation. Abdoulaye Mohamadou at the Permanent Inter-State Committee for Drought Control in the Sahel argues that the relationship between hunger and war in that African region is “circular.” War restricts access to agricultural land and pastoral mobility and also disrupts markets, supply chains, humanitarian access and trade. The absence of fertilizer and the arrival of famine then worsen war.

And how is the United States under Trump responding to this hunger crisis? Certainly not by attempting to slow climate change — Trump pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement that’s meant to limit global warming.

Nor by sending humanitarian aid. The administration dismantled what used to be the US Agency for International Development. Those cuts demonstrably led, among other effects, to spikes in violence and conflict in Africa. America, along with other countries, has also slashed funding to the UN’s World Food Program, and ordered the WFP to stop work on specific projects it had financed, from Yemen to Sudan and Haiti. Such defunding will result in additional millions of deaths, especially of young children.

So much for the second of the UN’s 17 so-called sustainable development goals, which was to achieve “zero hunger” by 2030. Trump, who disdains the UN, will no doubt blame this failure on that institution rather than his own policies, or the war of choice he launched in the Middle East.

### What a young India can learn from Gandhi, Jayaprakash Narayan
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Recent events in Delhi deserve to be seen beyond the immediate confrontation between the government and the Opposition. Something deeper is taking shape in India — a crisis of trust between citizens, particularly the young, and institutions meant to stand above day-to-day politics.

The Election Commission of India is a constitutional institution, and the National Testing Agency was created as an autonomous body to conduct examinations. Yet controversies over electoral rolls and NEET have contributed to a growing perception, especially among the young, that institutions on which their future depends are not sufficiently transparent, accountable, or independent. Whether every allegation is eventually proved is important. But the larger question is: why so many young people doubt the fairness of the system?

Youth anger meets State repression: How CJP and resurgent protests are testing the Modi governmentThe State’s response to youth protests is, therefore, significant. Barricades, restrictions, heavy police deployment, and detention may control a demonstration, but they cannot restore trust. A democracy cannot police its way out of a crisis of confidence. When peaceful protest is treated primarily as a law-and-order problem, the State may win the day but lose something more valuable — the confidence of citizens.

There is also a difference between a protest led by political parties and a mobilisation of young citizens who do not see themselves as extensions of any party. Governments understand political parties — their leaders, structures, and compulsions. A spontaneous youth mobilisation is more fluid, less predictable, and potentially more enduring.

I would hesitate to say that the government is ‘afraid of Gen Z’ while taking the Opposition lightly. That is an interpretation, not a fact. But independent youth mobilisation does present a different challenge. The young people protesting today will form a substantial part of India’s electorate in the coming years. They can be offered employment, entrepreneurship, technology, and development. They can also be dispersed through political co-option or fear. But one thing is harder to manage: a generation that loses trust in democratic institutions themselves.

Here Mahatma Gandhi, and later Jayaprakash Narayan, offer important lessons. Gandhi never regarded opposition to British rule as the whole of the freedom struggle. Satyagraha and non-cooperation were accompanied by a Constructive Programme: communal harmony, removal of untouchability, village industries, education, sanitation, health, work among peasants and labourers, Adivasi welfare, and the rebuilding of village societies. Constructive work was not an adjunct to political struggle; it was the preparation for Swaraj. Gandhi understood something contemporary politics often forgets: it is easier to mobilise people against something than to mobilise them for something.

Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) carried a related idea into a different historical moment through his call for Sampoorna Kranti (Total Revolution). His movement united students, citizens, and political groups against corruption, authoritarianism, and the erosion of democratic institutions. The restoration of democracy after Emergency was a great victory for India. JP showed that citizens, when morally mobilised, could challenge an overwhelmingly powerful political establishment.

Yet history leaves a difficult question: why did India, after such a powerful nationwide movement, return so quickly to many of its familiar political and social ways? This is not to diminish JP or the achievement. Precisely because the achievement was so great, the question must be asked. The movement defeated authoritarianism, but Sampoorna Kranti did not become a sustained, nationwide, non-party constructive programme through which citizens could practise democracy in their daily lives.

Political parties eventually occupied the space the movement opened. Governments changed, but many deeper structures of inequality, corruption, centralisation, and dependence on political power remained. The lesson is uncomfortable but necessary: a nationwide andolan can remove a government; it cannot by itself reconstruct a society. Political victory without social reconstruction leaves political culture largely unchanged.

This is where Gandhi’s Constructive Programme regains relevance. Why should young people only protest? If they distrust the ECI, let them create non-partisan Citizens’ Election Watch groups to verify electoral rolls, explain correction procedures, and document irregularities. If they distrust examination systems, let students study how examinations are conducted and demand institutional reforms that protect millions of candidates.

If unemployment concerns them, let them work with communities to develop livelihoods, skills, and enterprises rather than waiting solely for government recruitment. If climate change concerns them, let them restore water bodies, regenerate degraded land, and work with farmers on ecological livelihoods. If the condition of villages concerns them, let every college adopt a cluster of villages and make health, education, sanitation, digital literacy, and local economic development part of student citizenship. This would not mean withdrawing from protest. It would mean giving protest a constructive foundation.

The same principle applies to India’s forest regions. The defeat of Maoist violence is important; no society can permit armed violence to decide its future. But the end of insurgency cannot be a licence to transfer forests and natural resources to corporations without considering the rights and livelihoods of forest-dwelling communities and ecological consequences. Gandhi would ask: development for whom, and decided by whom? A constructive programme would unite gram sabhas, Adivasi communities, young people, ecological knowledge, and responsible investment. Development need not reject industry, but it must enlarge the capabilities, livelihoods, and dignity of local people rather than merely transfer their resource base elsewhere.

How inexperience, strategic missteps hobbled the CJP's anti-CEC protestsThe Opposition, too, has responsibilities. It should not merely inherit youth anger or convert every youth mobilisation into another political rally. Nor should it assume that defeating the current government equals changing India. The lesson of JP is that political victory is not social transformation. If the Opposition wants to become a credible alternative, it must demonstrate what different politics would mean in education, employment, institutions, villages, forests, and the everyday lives of citizens.

The young need not become another Opposition. They could become an independent democratic force that questions every government, but belongs to none; that protests when necessary, but constructs continuously; that demands accountability from institutions, while practising accountability itself. This is what Gandhi understood by Swaraj. It was not simply the transfer of power from British rulers to Indian rulers. It began with self-regulation, extended to the capacity of communities to govern themselves, and required citizens capable of resisting domination without becoming instruments of domination themselves.

The writer is former vice chancellor of Gujarat Vidyapith, founded by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920) (Syndicate: The Billion Press.

## 19 October 2026

### Developing minds in a digital world, a changing India
*The Hindu · Opinion*

Each evening, a familiar scene unfolds in homes around the world. A teenager sits hunched over their smartphone, seamlessly moving between chats, videos, social media, and games. Homework is completed with the help of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) platform. Engagement with the world increasingly gives way to time spent on screens. While this may appear routine today, it could represent a profound change in how children — and their developing brains — experience the world, learn, and grow.

These changes have particular significance for India, with approximately 65 crore people under the age of 25 and one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing digital ecosystems. Each day, millions of Indian children and adolescents spend significant time on digital devices, a trend accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic as education, recreation, and social interaction moved online.

Children have fundamental right to access and use internet: Supreme CourtEasy access to the digital world has brought undeniable benefits, from unprecedented access to information and educational resources to new ways of communicating, creating, and learning. The recent remarkable advances in AI, performing tasks that once required sustained mental effort, have expanded these possibilities even further. Nonetheless, these digital environments have also introduced a powerful and largely unregulated force into children’s lives—one we are only beginning to understand.

A brain under constructionTo be clear, technology itself is not the problem. The concern is what happens when powerful digital tools and devices become a constant companion in the lives of young people during a period of critical brain development. Cognition, emotion, and behaviour depend on brain systems that undergo profound developmental changes in childhood and adolescence. The prefrontal cortex — central to sustained attention, working memory, planning, decision-making, and impulse control — continues to mature into early adulthood.

Does Article 21 include right to digital access? | ExplainedDigital environments provide an unusually dense and repetitive stream of experiences that may engage the brain in distinctive ways. Over time, these experiences could influence how the brain’s structures and circuits are organised and connected —strengthening some pathways, while others remain underdeveloped. Because the brain is highly plastic during early life, such patterns of engagement can have lasting effects, potentially shaping how young people think, feel, and act across the lifespan.

Indeed, emerging research has linked high levels of screen time with alterations in the brain’s structural development and connectivity. While suggestive, such findings do not prove that digital technologies cause harmful changes in the developing brain. They do, however, underscore the need to better understand the digital experiences of today’s youth and how, for better or worse, they may affect critical functions such as attention, reflection, self-control, and creativity.

Supreme Court address a parental anxiety: How to keep the Internet safe for children | ExplainedReinforcement shapes attentionA large proportion of Indian young people use social media, with Instagram among the most popular platforms. Adolescence is a period when belonging, peer evaluation, and social approval are especially important, making the rewards of social media engagement particularly seductive and salient.

Many digital platforms are designed to capture and sustain attention by exploiting basic features of cognition, emotion, and reward. Short videos, autoplay, infinite scroll, algorithmic recommendations, and social feedback create reinforcement loops in which novelty and rewards — likes, shares, and comments — are delivered rapidly and unpredictably.

These variable patterns of reinforcement can encourage repetitive checking and rapid shifts of attention, keeping users in a continual state of anticipation for the next reward. As a result, many young people may become highly adept at rapidly shifting among multiple sources of information yet may still find it difficult to sustain attention on a single task or topic.

Beyond the amount of time spent online, we must also consider how digital reinforcement can shape young people’s expectations of everyday life. When online reinforcement is imminent and constantly accessible, ordinary experiences — having a face-to-face conversation, practising a skill, or simply sitting with one’s thoughts — may feel less rewarding by comparison.

Offloading mental effortThe speed with which generative AI has emerged and transformed how we engage with the world is astonishing. Unlike many earlier technologies, however, AI does not just assist with mental effort; it can supplant it. To be clear, humans have always used tools to reduce cognitive load. Taking a photograph in a crowded parking lot, for example, means we do not have to later remember where we parked. There is nothing inherently wrong or problematic with this kind of cognitive offloading.

The concern arises when AI begins to replace, rather than support, the mental effort necessary for learning. Students can now use AI platforms to generate ideas, organise arguments, write essays, and summarise material. Used thoughtfully, these tools can enhance the learning process. Used as a substitute for independent thinking, however, and AI can undermine the cognitive effort through which knowledge and skills are developed.

Puzzling over a challenging question, struggling to find the right words, making mistakes, and revising an argument are not obstacles to learning — they are central to it. If AI routinely eliminates these experiences, we should rightly ask what the impact will be on young people’s ability to think critically, use informed judgment, and persevere when answers are not immediately available.

The problem is not just learning. There is another cost that is easy to overlook: boredom. Rarely welcomed, boredom creates space for imagination, reflection, creativity, and the development of a rich inner life. When every idle moment is filled with constant stimulation, young people have fewer opportunities to think, wonder, daydream, or reflect on their experiences.

The adaptive brainThere is another way to understand how young minds may be shaped in today’s digital world. Neuroplasticity is the brain’s lifelong capacity to adapt in response to experience, learning, and the environment. The modern digital environment is almost certain to influence the growth of young people, but not necessarily in a harmful manner. Rather, as some scientists argue, their brains may be adapting to function in a world that is very different from that of previous generations.

To be sure, many young people exhibit impressive abilities to filter information, navigate complex digital environments, and switch among multiple sources of information. Perhaps, then, the changes observed in young people reflect cognitive adaptation — novel ways of thinking and processing information based on the demands of a digitally saturated world.

Yet, adaptation need not be always beneficial; it may also constrain how other capacities are expressed or used. Given the significance of the issue, we must therefore consider what may be gained — and what may be lost — as young minds adapt to increasingly digital environments.

In effect, young people around the world are participating in a vast, largely uncontrolled experiment in how sustained exposure to digital technology may shape developing brains and minds. At the same time, the corporations responsible for designing many of these digital technologies have strong financial incentives to keep young people — their current and future users — engaged.

Safeguarding the futureIndia’s youth are growing up in an environment that was unimaginable until quite recently. Whatever concerns we may have, we cannot simply ignore or reject digital technology. Children will use it. Our responsibility is to help them use it capably, thoughtfully, and responsibly.

At the family level, parents need practical, evidence-based guidance. Children should have device-free times and places, protected study periods, healthy sleep routines, and opportunities for unstructured time. The objective is not to eliminate screens, but to ensure that they do not occupy every available moment.

Schools have an equally important role. Education must preserve what might be called productive struggle — the effort involved in thinking, writing, reasoning, solving problems, and working through uncertainty. Digital tools, including AI, can support analysis, revision, and feedback without replacing original and critical thinking. Greater emphasis should be placed on independent cognitive engagement, including oral examinations, supervised writing, and applied problem-solving.

At the policy level, digital platforms — especially those targeted at young people — should face far greater scrutiny and accountability. Policymakers must demand technology companies provide stronger evidence about how their products affect the cognitive and emotional development of children and adolescents. Governments must also support independent research capable of informing policies and regulations as these technologies continue to evolve.

We should not wait for definitive evidence of harm before asking whether the digital environments we are creating are conducive to healthy development. A young mind needs stimulation, but also silence; information, but also reflection; assistance, but also struggle. We can embrace technological progress while still protecting the experiences through which children and adolescents learn to think, imagine, reflect, and grow.

Derick H. Lindquist is Dean of the Jindal School of Psychology and Counselling at the O.P. Jindal Global University, Sonipat, Haryana

### DC Edit |Bridge Ladakh’s Trust Deficit
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

Ladakh stands at a defining moment in its modern political history. Massive infrastructure projects, unprecedented strategic investment and growing national attention have placed the region firmly at the centre of country's development and security calculus. Yet, beneath this promise lies a widening trust deficit between Ladakh’s representative leadership and the Union government, one that cannot be ignored.

The Centre’s rejection of demands for statehood or a Union Territory status with a legislature has made one thing clear: Ladakh is unlikely to follow the constitutional road travelled elsewhere in the country. Instead, the Centre is proposing a unique model, tailored to the region. While innovation in governance is not inherently problematic, any framework imposed without broad local acceptance risks deepening political alienation.

The concerns raised by the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) cannot be dismissed as mere questions of nomenclature or administrative design. At their core lies a demand for meaningful democratic participation, constitutional safeguards and a greater voice over land, resources, culture and development. For a region with fragile ecology, distinct cultural traditions and sensitive demographics, these aspirations are legitimate and deserve serious consideration.

At the same time, Ladakh’s leadership must recognise the strategic realities that inform the Centre’s approach. Bordering China and Pakistan, Ladakh is not an ordinary administrative unit. Its geopolitical significance makes stability, institutional clarity and national security paramount concerns. A prolonged confrontation between local stakeholders and the Centre serves neither purpose.

What is needed now is not maximalism from either side, but statesmanship. The Centre must engage with Ladakh’s representatives in a spirit of trust, flexibility and transparency. Equally, LAB and KDA should remain invested in dialogue rather than outright rejection. Constitutional innovation can succeed only if it carries democratic legitimacy.

The stakes are far greater than a constitutional formula. Development can build roads, airports and power plants. Only consensus can build durable institutions. For Ladakh, and for India, the challenge is to ensure that strategic importance is matched by political accommodation. A peaceful, empowered and confident Ladakh is not merely a regional aspiration; it is a national necessity.

### DC Edit | State Must Break Gangs, Not Simply Nab Gunmen
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

The firing on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff’s car in Mumbai’s Juhu on Sunday evening is an open challenge to the authority of the state and the rule of law. Though the actor escaped the firing with minor injuries, his driver and a bystander were injured. The fact that gunmen opened fire in a public place, endangering everyone present highlights the need for a sustained campaign against organised crime and accountability for the failures that allow armed criminals to strike.

In a sound clip released on social media, two persons who claimed to be members of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, accepted the responsibility for the attack, accusing Shroff of ignoring their earlier warnings. They also threatened attacks on Salman Khan and those working with him.

A social media declaration cannot substitute for evidence. Police must establish its authenticity and identify the people who commissioned, financed and facilitated the shooting and act against them. Mumbai knows the damage organised crime can inflict on its economy, institutions and public confidence. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, who also holds the home portfolio, must ensure that India’s financial capital does not become a lawless land once again.

The government’s objective must be the elimination of criminal cartels. Arresting the shooters is essential, but insufficient. Investigators must pursue recruiters, weapons suppliers, financiers, extortion collectors and those arranging transport, accommodation and reconnaissance. Every payment and communication should be traced until the chain of command is established and attached.

Another important aspect that requires attention is the motive behind attacks on film personalities and celebrities. An attack typically will have two broad motives — extortion or publicity. Established gangsters attack celebrities or business persons for extortion. The attacks on T-Series founder Gulshan Kumar and producer Rakesh Roshan fall into this category. Criminals seeking to establish themselves as gangsters carry out attacks to gain publicity. Attacks on celebrities generate publicity, which criminals can exploit to intimidate and extort money from others.

While extortion is an area that only law enforcement agencies need to deal with, the government needs a different strategy to deal with newbie or aspirational criminals, who need publicity to establish themselves as gangsters. The government needs to work with media organisations to evolve a policy or standard operating procedure which denies publicity to criminals by not identifying them. This may not end the emergence of gangsters, but it will remove an important motive behind the attacks on celebrities.

The government should also look at organised crime differently from individual crime because the unstated goal of the former is to enforce its writ, which challenges the sovereignty and authority of the state. When gangsters seek to settle disputes, they challenge the authority of courts and the rule of law. A challenge to the state amounts to sedition and insurrection, and such crimes should be treated as acts of waging war against the state and offenders must face exemplary punishment to deter criminals from joining crime networks, which operate on a franchise model.

### Gen Z Needs To Regroup, Pick Issues That Matter
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

It is clear to everyone around that the fight over the special intensive revision (SIR) carried out by the Election Commission under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is not going to be a T-20 contest. It is going to be a long-drawn-out one.

There is little doubt that the SIR was not carried out fairly. It is a legal issue, and it would need hundreds and thousands of people to step forward to make their complaints over the arbitrary way the state election commissions have carried out the exercise.

The Supreme Court can only judge the issues concerning SIR based on specific instances. There need not be many examples. a single instance of violation of a rule or procedure is sufficient to hold SIR to be null and void.

There is enough room to assume that CEC Kumar is not above suspicion of acting improperly. The court can suggest revisions and give directions for remedial measures. That will still leave Mr Kumar the choice to complete his term in the face of protests. So the objections to SIR and nailing Mr Kumar’s responsibility can only go so far and no further. Armed with a possible negative view of the Supreme Court over SIR, the Opposition can initiate the impeachment process against the CEC.

If the Opposition manages to establish the wrongdoings in the execution of SIR, it will be both a political and a legal victory. In the political arena, moral victories do not matter much. It is also clear that the Opposition’s main target is not Mr Kumar but Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his chief collaborator in the decision-making process, Union home minister Amit Shah. Even if Mr Kumar is nailed for his legal faux pas, Mr Modi and Mr Shah can shrug their shoulders and remain cynical bystanders. It is hard to imagine that either the Prime Minister or the Union Home minister will take moral responsibility for the illegalities found in the implementation of SIR.

So those who have filed the case against SIR will have to be content with tactical victories. This will be a crucial political gain no doubt. But as in the case of Neet and the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmender Pradhan, the Modi government will divert attention by talking about the economy though it is not doing too well in real terms.

Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman appears acutely aware of these economic challenges. She has been speaking in sombre tones about the rupee’s declining value against the dollar and rightly attributing it to external factors. And unlike Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal, who has been unduly optimistic and even exuberant, she referred to India-United States trade talks in guarded tones. She remarked that both sides have reached a plateau in the talks, and neither side has any scope for yielding ground.

The sale of majority stake of the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) is not the gleeful development that innocent people in and outside the government are making it out to be. It is not a trophy for that illusive and elusive thing called economic reforms. Instead of creating public sector banking giants, as China has done, India has opted to bring in a foreign partner.

It makes sense if India’s private banks were to create partnerships with global private banks. For the government to seek a foreign partner for a bank is a declaration of failure. So the economy is facing tough challenges. The comfort zone for the Modi government is shrinking.

Neither Andhra Pradesh chief minister and Telugu Desam chief Chandrababu Naidu nor former Bihar chief minister, Rajya Sabha member and Janata Dal (United) leader Nitish Kumar are inclined to demand their pound of flesh from Mr Modi’s BJP which is in a minority and which they are propping up. The large-scale defection from the Lok Sabha contingent of the All India Trinamul Congress (AITMC) is still up in the air.

The not-so-happy situation in which the Modi government finds itself seems to be a natural consequence of a government that has been in power for 12 years, and it is running out of ideas and programmes that can impress people. There is a sense of fatigue both in the government and the people. Even Mr Modi who is forever high on optimism, is subdued. It does not mean that the government is at the end of its tether. There is enough to do even to keep things as they are.

The Opposition has reasons to be cheerful. The government is literally with its back to the wall. But it might have to widen its agenda. The individual issues like the leakage of Neet examination papers or the foul play in the SIR are effective protest issues, but they may not sustain. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Leftist student organisations like the All-India Students Association (AISA) have played a stellar role in putting an arrogant government in the dock. But it may not be sustained over a long stretch.

Even as the BJP hopes the unfriendly gale would blow over, the idealistic protesters who have breathed new life into the dead polity may have to...

### Is Protest Only Means Left To Us To Take Back Democracy?
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

The three democratic tools available to us are the vote, the courts and protest. The only one over which Indians have real agency is protest.Voting is considered to be the same thing as democracy, as if democracy vanishes between elections. For decades, the election process in India has been accretive in adding prestige and credibility. That phase is behind us.

The Constitution says that every Indian aged 18 or above, who is not “disqualified under this Constitution or any law made by the appropriate legislature on the ground of non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime or corrupt or illegal practice”, shall be entitled to be registered as a voter at any such election.

This direction is more like a suggestion to the present Election Commission. It assumed, no doubt on the orders of the government, that its exercise to gratuitously put crores of people through trauma would carry on undisturbed.

A survey of how many rollbacks and clarifications it has issued over the last four weeks throws up a list of about one dozen.

These include a “special enrolment drive” to bring in people left out by the previous special disenfranchisement drive. Then there is the removal of a declaration for some people, a waiver for in-person appearance for other people, a review of flawed software, limiting (but not ending) the malicious practice of objections being filed by third party individuals against voters, mostly Muslims of course.

Then there is the introduction of searchable voter lists after resisting them all this time for no reason other than opacity. And now private school teachers being made to do the extracurricular work that hapless public school officials have been running door to door doing, and other things besides.

The number of measures shows the sloppiness with which this adventure was embarked upon. The speed at which the measures are coming betrays the panic. The disclosure that the commission’s majority was being disregarded in decisions taken would have surprised few. Will these subsequent corrections, rollbacks and reviews resolve the mess? Of course not. We have already been divided into several tiers of Indian citizens: some voters, some struck off, some in appeal, some without information about their status, some beyond care, others awaiting judgment.

This steaming pile of excrement cannot be solved by anything other than a full rollback. Alas, now with elections already having taken place, even this action will lead to problems of electoral legitimacy, for instance in Bengal.

So, no. This mess is of a scale that could only have been erected by the architect of minimum government, maximum governance.

The second democratic tool we have is the courts. Article 32 says our right to move court for the enforcement of fundamental rights “is guaranteed”. Note that what is guaranteed is the liberty to move court. What follows from there in proceedings is something we can witness daily in this country and need not be expounded on further. Our finest lawyers have already spoken about where things stand. As with the Election Commission, there has been erosion here also.

The third democratic tool, the only one over which we have real agency, is protest. Showing up to tell the state that we feel violated and it must stop. The government can mess around with our vote, as it is doing, and the justice system can toy with us as it does in service of the executive. It is harder for it to force itself on our bodies, though it tries.

Protest is our most effective tool at getting the state to stop misbehaviour. This is why there is such energy expended by the government in attempting to curb it, limit it and throttle it.

The farm laws, once Indians were mobilised in the tens of thousands and arrived in Delhi, were dead. It took a full year for the government to finally strike them down, and those months were wasted because the monarch did not want to be seen as surrendering to the people. But it was immediately clear to many the moment the mobilisation happened, that the people would win. Deliciously, this victory was accompanied by an apology. An apology that was a qualified one, as may be expected from the person offering it, but an apology nonetheless.

The brave Muslim women who led the protests against the National Register of Citizens succeeded in halting what has happened in Assam from happening elsewhere in India. Yes, it is true that the road this SIR has put us on ultimately takes us to the same destination, but recent events show that this will not be easy for the government to do uncontested no matter how much the BJP leadership salivates at the thought of crores of disenfranchised, disentitled and interned.

Peaceful assembly (Article 19) is a fundamental right, meaning one that enjoys a high degree of protection from encroachment by the government. But in practice, the encroachment has exceeded the freedom over the decades. And there it will remain, caged in designated areas and subject to...

### ECI’s U-turn cannot erase its crimes
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s decision to initiate a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and UTs, including Bihar, West Bengal, and Tamil Nadu, where it has held the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, is an admission of guilt and defeat. Last year, the ECI skipped this regular annual exercise to launch the SIR, rewriting electoral rolls in its own way, questioning voters’ rights, excluding large numbers of voters, and inflicting tension and trauma on citizens. With this latest measure, and others announced last month after revelations about its functioning, the ECI may be attempting to undo some of the wrongs done through the SIR. While the SIR required every voter to fill an enumeration form to make it to the draft roll, in the SSR all existing voters will automatically make it to the draft roll. The ECI has said it will enrol new voters, re-enrol those left out using the original Form 6, and disallow mass Form 7 objections. Crucially, it will also release searchable election rolls in text-based PDFs to parties and candidates.

For over two years now, the Opposition has demanded digital, machine-readable rolls. The ECI had rejected it, claiming that the Supreme Court disallowed it and that it would violate voter privacy. If so, why has the ECI allowed it now? It should explain why it has changed its position on this and other matters. It must also explain whether the new enrolment drive will cover voters deleted in West Bengal, and whose cases are pending before tribunals. It should also publish separate lists of fresh voters enrolled and voters re-enrolled after deletion.

The CEC must go and it’s time to abandon SIRThe SIR amounted to a violation of rights and denial of voting rights to millions through arbitrary and prejudicial use of power. The question now is whether reversing many of its provisions will restore the pre-SIR rolls. Clearly, the ECI’s rethinking and reversals have been forced by the protests. The idea may be to claim that protests are unnecessary because the ECI’s unacceptable actions have now been reversed. But these are not mistakes to be forgiven once corrected; they are crimes that demand accountability. In any case, the result of the exercise remains uncertain. The system of appointing ECI members and the law granting them legal immunity must be reviewed. The SIR violated basic democratic and electoral norms. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who orchestrated the vile attempt to scuttle India’s electoral system, should resign — or be made to resign.

### Laws must punish conduct, not identity
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The Bengaluru City Police Commissioner’s circular regulating the activities of transgender persons in public spaces has drawn criticism for stereotyping and targeting a historically marginalised community. Complaints of aggressive solicitation, intimidation, extortion, and obstruction of traffic by some members of the transgender community are real and cannot be ignored. Citizens have a right to move freely and feel safe, and the police have a duty to act against unlawful conduct. The question, however, is whether an entire community can be singled out for special scrutiny when existing laws already address such offences, regardless of who commits them. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) provides for action against criminal intimidation, extortion, and related offences, while traffic and public-order laws address obstruction and nuisance. There is little justification for creating a separate enforcement framework for transgender persons when the same legal provisions apply to all citizens. A circular that grants wide discretion to regulate their presence and activities risks encouraging profiling and selective enforcement.

Policing must be guided by conduct and evidence, not

Many transgender persons lack access to regular livelihoods in a society where barriers to education, employment, and social acceptance persist. While intimidation or coercion cannot be condoned, the line between lawful conduct and criminal behaviour must remain clear. The circular’s emphasis on respecting transgender rights and dignity is welcome, but it cannot substitute for safeguards against arbitrary enforcement. Karnataka’s transgender policy of 2017 envisages inclusion through education, healthcare, skill development, employment, and social security. The state’s decision to provide 1% reservation for transgender persons in public employment reflects an effort to expand opportunities and reduce exclusion. A policing approach that reinforces stigma would sit uneasily with these measures. Constitutional guarantees of equality before the law under Article 14 and the right to life and dignity under Article 21, extend fully to transgender persons. In National Legal Services Authority vs Union of India (2014), the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a distinct third gender and affirmed their constitutional rights.

Bengaluru Police to act against transgenders blocking traffic, harassing publicThe government should review the circular in consultation with transgender representatives, civil society groups, and legal experts. Clear safeguards against profiling, proportionate enforcement, and effective grievance-redress mechanisms are essential. Public complaints of harassment and intimidation must be addressed firmly, but this is best achieved by enforcing existing laws against offenders. Misconduct must be punished, but identity cannot become a basis for suspicion.

### Apples, oranges, and illusions. Behind the hype of India’s IMF-certified GDP growth
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

On October 13, the IMF released its latest World Economic Outlook (WEO). For 2026 (India’s FY2027), the IMF has projected India’s real GDP growth at 7%. Economists and commentators keen to sing the government’s praise (the Stutians) lapped it up. Many declared victory, particularly against the backdrop of nationwide doubts raised about the reality of India’s projected 7.6% real GDP growth in the first quarter of FY2027.

The IMF WEO database provides two types of GDP estimates. First, the estimate of real GDP growth. Second, comparable worldwide GDP in current US dollars. Curiously, no one in India has talked about GDP growth in current USD.

What do the two GDP estimates released by the IMF say for global and India GDP growth in FY2027? How has India fared? What is the reality of India’s GDP growth story and contribution to global growth?

The IMF has developed a system for GDP and other economic data collection from all member countries using a general data dissemination system (e-GDDS since 2015) and special data dissemination standards (SDDS).

All member countries provide their GDP data following this protocol, which the IMF uses for its WEO, without modification or judgement. The 7% real GDP growth for FY2027 is based on India’s data — and not that of the IMF.

Using the same protocol, it projected the global GDP growth for 2026 of 3.1%, China 4.5%, and India 7%. The IMF’s India growth projection is as robust or weak as the GDP growth estimates provided by the NSO/government.

GDP growth in current US dollars

The IMF projects the global GDP in current USD for 2026 at $128 trillion, with US GDP at $32.64 trillion, China at $21.55 trillion, and India at $4.06 trillion. This results in a global GDP growth for 2026 at 8.03%, the US at 5.59%, China at 9.78% and India at merely 3.87%.

India had set a goal of reaching $5 trillion GDP by FY2025 and becoming the third-largest economy in FY2029. Germany and Japan, the countries ahead of us in the race to become the third-largest economy, have a GDP of $5.47 trillion and $4.34 trillion in 2026, respectively, and generated growth of 6.95% and (-)2.5%. Despite the negative growth, Japan stays well ahead of India. The United Kingdom, which we left behind in 2022, has surged ahead of us with a GDP of $4.27 trillion and a growth of 6.39% in 2026.

In current USD terms, the largest six economies (barring Japan) have a GDP growth rate higher than India’s in 2026.

India’s GDP growth (in current USD) is one of the lowest in the world.

India’s contribution to global growth

Prime Minister Narendra Modi keeps highlighting India as the largest contributor to global growth (while experts say India contributes 20% of global growth). This claim is based on India’s real GDP growth data submitted to the IMF.

Delegates walked out of IMF steering committee meeting when Russian official spokeThe position of the US is quite peculiar. As the USD depreciates, its real GDP growth is subdued (2.3% in 2026), whereas in current USD (making it comparable with the rest of the world in the same currency), the US recorded a much higher growth of 5.57%.

The scenario of IMF member countries’ contribution to global GDP growth changes dramatically when GDP and their growth are considered in current USD.

The global economy is estimated to grow by $9.52 trillion in 2026 (from $118.49 trillion in 2025). The US contributes $1.78 trillion (18.71%) and China $1.92 trillion (20.17%). India is contributing only $0.15 trillion (a mere 1.59%).

The top six economies will contribute 48.43% of the global growth, with the rest of the world contributing 51.57%.

This is extremely underwhelming. India’s share of the global GDP in current USD terms in 2026 is 3.17%. Our growth contribution is much less than our share of global GDP.

Instead of false celebrations, this should be a cause for serious worry.

Modi government continues to underperform

India’s GDP (current USD) was only $0.608 trillion in FY2004 when the UPA government of Manmohan Singh took charge. It grew to $1.848 trillion in FY2014 when it demitted office, generating a GDP growth of a massive 11.76% (despite higher inflation).

The Modi government took it to $3.512 trillion in FY2024 and to $4.060 trillion in FY2027.

Since 2014, the Modi government has generated a GDP growth of 6.24% in current USD — that’s barely more than half of the growth rate during the UPA years.

In three years of its third term (from 2024-2025), the Modi government has achieved a GDP growth (in current USD) of only 4.96%. This is pathetic. It is also less than the global GDP growth of 6.05%, China’s growth of 5.47%, and the UK’s growth of 7.56% in these three years.

Look at the full glass

Real GDP growth and GDP growth in current USD can be considered as apples and oranges. These two can also be viewed as the two halves of a glass.

Prabuddha (balanced, wise people) will see both apples and oranges and the two halves of the glass to get a real sense of how India is doing in the global GDP and growth race.

The picture is more sombre than rosy.

Subhash Chandra Garg is former Finance & Economic Affairs Secretary, and author of ‘The Great Indian Budget: How the Government of India Spends Your Money’, and ‘We Also Make Policy’.

### Beyond religiosity: on the Kolkata pandal tragedy
*The Hindu · Editorial*

This year’s Durga Puja in Kolkata was meant to be truly special. The first after the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government in West Bengal, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari wanted the pandals to showcase his party’s commitment to Hindu religiosity as well as to demonstrate the efficiency of the administrative machinery under him. He made it a point to highlight that the number of pandals in the State had increased by 25% over last year to more than 57,000. He was a visible presence at pandals across the city. Union Home Minister Amit Shah was in Kolkata as well to add heft and leverage to the puja’s popular appeal. But disaster struck at Kolkata’s Girish Park area on Saturday, as 19 people lost their lives in a stampede that could have been avoided with better organisation and crowd regulation. Both the police and the puja organisers failed to anticipate the sudden surge of the crowd at the venue.

Puja pandals, just like Mumbai’s Ganapati installations, are often sites of creativity and festivity; they have generally been accident-free despite the participation of a large number of people. The Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotstab’s theme this year was Beyond Sound. With a narrow entry and exit, the creators apparently sought to give an experience to visitors that involved controlling the light falling inside. The surrounding lanes were narrow city gullies that cannot hold two cars at the same time. Unanticipated too — at a time of retreat of the monsoon — was the rain that struck India’s east coast with heavy thunder and lightning in the evening. As people barged into the pandal seeking safety — visitors keep moving inside the Durga Puja pandals typically — the organisers requested people to leave fearing that the structure might collapse. Packed crowds can be incident-free only if sudden surges of movement, often triggered by panic, are avoided throughout. In Kolkata, panic apparently stemmed from the announcement regarding the safety of the structure, though the fear about the structure’s safety was justified. The effort should have been to wean the crowd away in a regulated manner. The government has promised an inquiry and deterrent follow-up action. There is the question of whether in the government’s drive to make the celebrations spectacular and grand, safe management practices got ignored at the event. Although Mr. Adhikari said the police helped rush the victims to hospitals, he also indicated that only temporary home guards had been posted at the pandal. Effective deployment of experienced police personnel may have helped avoid the tragedy.

### Treacherous waters: on the Bihar boat tragedy
*The Hindu · Editorial*

River crossings on stretches of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are notoriously unsafe as poorly lit, unregistered boats ply with bare access to lifesaving equipment. Overcrowded vessels, operated by untrained or underaged people, add to the risks, and enforcement action only follows an accident. These boats are not the preserve of the poor but are also used by government personnel, teachers, and bank employees: many areas lack reliable alternatives, making the riverine journeys the sole option. On October 13, at least 13 children drowned when a country-made boat capsized in Raghopur, in Bihar’s Vaishali district, after setting off at 8.30 p.m. for a memorial feast in an adjoining village, even though rides are prohibited post sunset. The boat was visibly dilapidated, including a hole in the deck through which it drew water, and was being operated by a young boatman. There were at least half a dozen other people on the vessel when it capsized despite its reported capacity having been five. The riverine tract in Raghopur is continuously shaped by sediment deposits and has historically been hard to access, especially during the monsoons. Raghopur lacks all-weather roads, and has a history of being isolated during floods. The first section of the Kachchi Dargah-Bidupur bridge, between Patna and Raghopur, was ready in June 2025, but the monsoons still flooded the approach road and blocked access. The overarching motif across these episodes has been a consistent lack of safer alternatives, including the general paucity of public transport. A chaotic regulatory framework, including the Model Rules 2011 under the Bengal Ferries Act 1885 and the Inland Vessels Act 2021, has also not prevented training programmes and inspections from lagging behind the proliferation of unsafe transport practices.

That all those who drowned on October 13 were children deepens the sense of tragedy. In general, children warrant additional, more sensitive socio-economic support. The Bombay High Court had recently upbraided the Maharashtra government for failing to arrange transportation for over 200 children from villages near Chandoli National Park and Sahyadri Tiger Reserve; they had to walk several kilometres to reach school, braving the risk of wildlife encounters. Such precarity persists in Hingoli, Palghar, and Nashik in Maharashtra alone; similar situations have also been created by school reorganisation programmes that do not sufficiently account for children’s safety when shuttering infeasible facilities. The children who drowned in Vaishali were not headed to school, but the risk exposure is paramount. The ultimate tragedy is that access to ordinary childhood activities remains contingent, in so many economically disadvantaged communities, on accepting dangers that public institutions already know how to prevent.

### DC Edit | Trump Ditches Ukraine For Diesel
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

Granting a 60-day waiver from sanctions on Russia and proposed 100 per cent tariffs on five countries including India, US President Donald Trump will be hoping the Russian President, Mr Vladimir Putin, will organise millions of tonnes of diesel to help bring down quickly the “gas” prices at American petrol pumps. But in doing so he will be feeding billions of dollars into the Russian war machine while throwing Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukraine under the bus.

One authoritarian President’s largesse in supporting the economy of another warmonger must rank as the worst strategic decision of the decade as European unity is undermined and the gate is wide open for Mr Putin to attack energy sites and such civilian infra targets inside Ukraine in a war that he has been unable to make any progress in after ingress into the Donbas region in February 2022.

India can act relieved and keep importing Russian energy, and even process some of the crude to export back to Russia, while Mr Zelenskyy defies Mr Trump’s selfish idea of a unilateral declaration of an energy ceasefire that the combatants had not been consulted about. If the world situation were not so dire because of the Iran war that Mr Trump began waging at Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu’s behest, India might even smile at the turn of events that allows it to keep sourcing its oil at reasonable prices from Russia and elsewhere, including possibly Venezuela.

The principles, which bound the West together in a common cause against the “Soviet” threat during the Cold War, have been given short shrift by a US President who has sacrificed the honour code at the altar of personal and party convenience. Doing so at a perilous time is worse as Mr Putin has been fulminating against European powers thus adding to the prevailing uncertainty caused by the two wars in Europe and West Asia.

Mr Trump may have reason to worry over the results of the midterms, the forecasts for which are projecting the loss of control of the Senate and the House for Republicans. He risks casting away all the values that bound the free world together just for giving Russia a free pass to come back to the mainstream, all in the hope that its President will respond positively to trading avenues being opened again.

### Vote Deletion & ‘Infiltrators’: Amit Shah’s Great Diversion
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Fighting the damaging optics of the ongoing mass agitation against alleged manipulation of electoral rolls through the SIR exercise, Union Home minister Amit Shah has gone on the offensive. He described the Rahul Gandhi-led Opposition movement as an “action plan to protect infiltrators”.

Like a ventriloquist’s doll, BJP president Nitin Nabin, has echoed Mr Shah, claiming that Mr Gandhi was “engaged in protecting infiltrators”.

The accusation is more than political rhetoric. The Union Home ministry has launched a portal allowing members of the public, NGOs, government bodies and even “international organisations” to report unnatural demographic shifts and abnormal settlement patterns across India. Such “crowdsourcing” of information about “abnormal settlement” could potentially be weaponised to target minority communities, fuel social polarisation and to purge names from voter lists.

Mr Shah’s ministry has no centralised list of infiltrators detected in the last 12 years and no comprehensive information on the subject, leaving state governments to deal with it. So such an initiative will strengthen Mr Shah’s argument against the Opposition although it remains to be seen whether it produces usable information or not.

With elections in Uttar Pradesh and other states in sight, the BJP is also preparing a public campaign hyping up the infiltrator argument to rebut the Opposition’s questions about the SIR and the conduct of the Election Commission.

On the SIR, an administrative and institutional issue, the Narendra Modi government and the Election Commission are vulnerable to questions about whether eligible voters were deliberately excluded, whether deletions were properly verified, and whether the procedure and software used to remove names were reliable.

Framing the controversy in terms of “infiltrators” shifts the frame of discussion away from the accountability of state institutions. When Mr Shah talks about the security of the nation, the narrative acquires an emotional urgency. And accountability takes a backseat.

This reverses the direction of scrutiny as it turns the accusers — Rahul Gandhi, the broader Opposition bloc, supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party and other youth voices — into the accused. By his accusations, Mr Shah wants to divert the political energy of those protesting to defending themselves rather than keeping public attention focussed on voter-roll manipulation.

He seems to believe that an emotionally charged narrative connecting SIR to nationalism, national security and fears of a changing political balance between communities will resonate more with the public. In contrast, the Opposition is trying to communicate the technicalities of how voter deletions have occurred which could be less compelling.

Mr Shah is not dubbed as a modern-day Chanakya by his acolytes for nothing. His infiltrator narrative also links easily with BJP’s attempt to delegitimise the protestors by portraying them as anarchic and foreign-instigated.

These strategies taken together, hope to dull the sharp questions of the Opposition. It is a playbook that the BJP has used successfully time and again against the Opposition.

However, unless Mr Shah and the BJP provide evidence to support their claims, these will remain convenient bogeys. So far, they have failed to provide any evidence of inclusion of infiltrators in previous voter lists which have now been removed through SIR. In fact, in the seven years Mr Shah has been Home minister, his ministry has failed to maintain any systematic record of infiltrators identified, arrested and deported. Between 2014 and 2024, Parliament was told that 3,568 Bangladeshi nationals were formally deported. This was a significant decline from the 82,255 deported during the preceding decade, 2005-2013, when Congress-led governments were in power.

State-level figures, where available, are disjointed and episodic. Assam reported in its Assembly that 1,72,673 illegal foreigners had been identified up to May 2026. Earlier data showed that the state’s foreigners tribunals identified 47,928 illegal foreigners between 1971 and 2014, with several thousand processed in subsequent years.

West Bengal deported 4,800 illegal Bangladeshi migrants in early 2026. Delhi Police identified 1,589 Bangladeshi illegal migrants and 55 Rohingya nationals, handing them over for deportation between June 2025 and February 2026. In an earlier drive in 2025, Delhi deported more than 120. Gujarat accounted for nearly 1,500 non-border detentions of illegal immigrants from mid-2025. Maharashtra deported more than 110, Haryana 80, Rajasthan 70 and Uttar Pradesh 65. Taken together, although strictly they cannot be added, do not amount to a large number.

### With Another Bill On Anvil, Should Education Return To The State List?
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Education has been on the Concurrent List since 1976, when the 42nd Amendment moved it from the State List. Parliament is now considering the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, which would replace the UGC, AICTE, and NCTE with a single regulator. A joint parliamentary committee is examining it. The Neet paper leak and education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation have renewed the debate, while Tamil Nadu has again demanded that education return to the State List. The larger question, however, is whether the present division of powers gives governments enough authority and clear responsibility for education.

Finance is a useful starting point. The latest comparable ministry of education figures, for 2022-23, put Centre / State / UT budgeted education expenditure by all departments at about Rs 10.67 lakh crore on the revenue account. States and UTs accounted for Rs 7.81 lakh crore, or 73.2 per cent. This is budgeted expenditure, not actual spending. States run most school education and a large part of higher education. However, central laws, regulators, national schemes, and Union-framed standards increasingly shape what they can do. This creates an accountability problem. A government that pays for and implements a policy needs enough authority to shape it and should be answerable for its results.

Neet illustrates the problem, although it does not settle the federal question. The Neet-UG examination held on May 3, 2026, was cancelled after an alleged paper leak. More than 22 lakh candidates were affected, and a re-examination was held on June 21. A failure in a national examination, therefore, affected students across the country simultaneously. Centralisation also has a clear advantage: it provides a common eligibility test and a common benchmark. State-level examinations have also faced malpractice. The issue is therefore where national uniformity is necessary and where states should have greater room to decide.

Tamil Nadu’s experience deserves attention here. The Justice A.K. Rajan Committee reported that after Neet, the share of rural, Tamil-medium, lower-income, and State Board students among medical admissions in the state declined. These findings cannot establish that Neet caused all the changes. Coaching access, school choices, and other factors may also have played a role. The findings are relevant to the question of whether a single national examination works equally well for students from different educational backgrounds.

The Supreme Court has upheld the Neet framework, and any case for decentralisation must address the reasons for a common examination. Does a single test correct differences in the quality and comparability of state examinations? If so, which part of that standardisation requires Union control? These questions point to a more precise division of powers. National standards can coexist with greater state authority over implementation and educational priorities. The constitutional position also sets limits on a simple return to the State List. Entry 66 of the Union List gives Parliament power over coordination and determination of standards in higher education and research institutions. The Union can also provide grants for public purposes. These powers mean that even greater state autonomy would not end central influence. The real task would be to define the boundary between setting national standards and regulating day-to-day education.

The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill makes this issue more immediate. It seeks to replace the UGC, AICTE, and NCTE with a single Commission and three councils that handle regulation, accreditation and standards. Medical and legal education are excluded. The Bill raises a wider question about the concentration of regulatory power in higher education. The Joint Parliamentary Committee has heard state governments and other stakeholders. It is an opportunity to examine how much regulation needs to remain with the Union.

Employment provides another reason to give states greater policy space. The State of Working India 2026 reports graduate unemployment of 39.33 per cent among those below 25 and 20.04 per cent among those aged 25-29 years, using PLFS 2023-24 data. It also shows that the transition from education to stable employment remains difficult. Education policy cannot solve this alone. Industrial growth, labour demand, and local economic conditions also shape employment. States with different economic structures should therefore have room to align curricula, vocational education and higher education with local needs.

States may, therefore, need greater policy space, but greater decentralisation also raises practical concerns. Different state rules could complicate degree recognition, credit transfer, student mobility and the enforcement of minimum standards. Fiscal capacity also differs sharply among states. More autonomy without adequate resources could increase inequality. These concerns require safeguards. A national ...

### Dead novel in its afterlife: How contemporary fiction confirms what everyone says
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Responding to rumours about the death of the novel that surface from time to time, Milan Kundera wrote about the dead novel—novels that ‘add nothing to the conquest of being. They discover no new segment of existence; they only confirm what has already been said, furthermore: in confirming what everyone says (what everyone must say), they fulfil their purpose, their glory, their usefulness to that society. By discovering nothing, they fail to participate in the sequence of discoveries that for me constitutes the history of the novel; they place themselves outside that history, or, if you like, they are novels that come after the history of the novel’. This is, of course, from The Art of the Novel, published in the mid-1980s, and the emphases in italics are Kundera’s. Re-reading it a few days ago, I was surprised that it read as much like a prognosis as it did of a diagnosis of the contemporary novel.

‘I have already seen and lived through the death of the novel, a violent death (inflicted by bans, censorship, and ideological pressure), in the world where I spent much of my life and which is usually called totalitarian... the novel is incompatible with the totalitarian universe,’ he writes in the preceding paragraph. Its tragicomic phrasing might make us gloss over an important word hiding there – ‘outside’, ‘outside that history’. And what kind of novels are these novels outside that history? ‘They are novels that come after the history of the novel.’ Perhaps because of our conditioning in such a category, we might think that this ‘outside’ would be a minor tradition. But it isn’t; I’m surprised by the recognition that such a novel is actually now the majoritarian tradition.

Think of the novels that have won awards and appeared on bestseller and critics’ lists. Stay with two or three of these titles as you run the Kundera test in your head. Did your favourite novel from last year or the year before that ‘confirm what everyone says’ or ‘what everyone must say’? Why did you like the novel? Was it because the novel you liked ‘holds up a mirror’ to ‘the problems that beset contemporary society’, as reviewers praise these days: war, inequality, patriarchy, racism, casteism, climate change...? Did the novels give you any new insight, did they just ‘fulfil their purpose, their glory, their usefulness to that society’?

Moodboard: Three novels that remind us why teachers matter The prize-winning novels of our century seem to me to be what Kundera characterises as dead novels, novels that have come after the history of the novel. It’s an odd phrasing and might seem confusing at first. Stay with it for a second – replace ‘novel’ with, say, ‘human’ – and you get what he’s doing there. ‘Humans that come after the history of the human’. What Kundera means by ‘history’ is, I suppose, evolution, not progress but deviations and adjustments and responses to contingencies that keep a species – in this case a genre – alive and energetic. It’s the mid-1980s, and Kundera is already bewailing the solidification of the conventions of the novel that will come to be feted. He doesn’t know it yet, of course, that what he calls the dead novel would become the most venerated kind of novel after the fall of the Berlin Wall and a warfaring globalisation.

Something tragicomic would happen to the genre. Every iteration of the same syntax – and formula – of this kind of novel would be called ‘original’ by publishers, reviewers and, consequently, by readers. They were called original because they were not original, because the endorsers knew that Brutus was not an honourable man. The constitutional function foisted upon the novel—that it must present a moral universe without variation, a kind of moral totalitarianism, as it were—has deadened the novel. When a deviation is noticed, it is at first celebrated and soon diagnosed as a malfunction. That is perhaps why, say, ‘autofiction’, now celebrated in capitalist countries for what Kundera would, in a heightened expression, characterise as a ‘sequence of discoveries’, a necessary feature of the ‘history of the novel’, is seen as self-indulgent when it comes from writers in former colonies. This is because it does not fulfil what Kundera calls ‘usefulness to that society’. Such novels are kept ‘outside’ the emerging canon, a sad and ironic reversion of what Kundera understood as ‘outside the history of the novel’.

(The writer is an author and poet. Her books include How I Became a Tree and Provincials.)
