### Profiles in cowardice: How world leaders and tech CEOs evade responsibility for their actions
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Published seventy years ago, Profiles in Courage presents short biographies of eight United States senators who voted against special interest groups which were intent on preserving their power in the halls of Congress. The book, which won a Pulitzer Prize for Biography, was supposedly penned by then Senator and future US President John F. Kennedy (JFK).

Given his wealth and political connections, JFK was able to either directly or indirectly influence key members of the prize board into picking his book for the Pulitzer. Despite questionable scruples and ethical considerations, JFK is still revered around the globe.

The Kennedy family established the Profile in Courage Award to honour individuals who have exhibited the same type of courage as identified in the book. It would have taken a lot of courage for JFK to step down, courage which he did not possess. While JFK would have never found a place in his own book or merited, albeit posthumously, the courage award his family established, he would be a prime candidate in any book devoted to identifying cowards in our midst, especially those in whom power is concentrated, be it in media or the political, corporate, and academic arenas.

Quote of the day by John F Kennedy: “Change is the law of life. And those who look only to the past…”Donald Trump got out of the Vietnam-era draft by claiming a ‘bone spur’ in his heel rendered him medically unfit for military service; yet, he has had no hesitation in blowing up fishing boats in international waters, ‘suspected’ of ferrying drugs, kidnapping foreign leaders, and attacking weak, poorly defended countries across the globe.

Of the eight senators discussed in JFK’s book, only one truly deserves to be included: George W. Norris of Nebraska. Norris believed in a government which was truly secular and non-autocratic at any level, and he fully understood what it takes for a country to stay neutral in times of war.

If, in the foreseeable future, a book titled Profiles in Cowardice does get written, since there are any number of candidates across the world who could conceivably be included in the book, we need a set of criteria to justify their inclusion. For example, when a country’s leader is accused of accepting bribes or committing genocide, and there is conclusive evidence supporting the allegation, how the leader responds is a clue to whether they should be included in the new book.

Likewise, when the CEO of a social media company or AI company is asked, “Is your company product harmful to children?” or “Is your product harmful to humanity?”, any equivocation on the part of the CEO is a clear indication that they are trying to extricate themselves by offering noncommittal responses. One can envisage any number of scenarios involving politicians of whatever party in whatever nation who have been compromised. The result in all of the above situations is the company’s bottom line for the CEO, and success at the ballot box for the politician. Taking full responsibility for one’s actions does not make a man a hero, but wilfully absolving himself of any blame for seeking to harm humanity does make him a coward.

Trump and his Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, have yet to even acknowledge the wanton killing of about 120 children by dropping a bomb on a girls’ school in Iran. Dropping a bomb from 35,000 feet to wipe out a school is a display of cowardice, not heroism. In a similar vein, when dozens of journalists and hundreds of women and children were deliberately targeted for elimination in Gaza by the Israel Defence Force, Benjamin Netanyahu brushed aside criticism from numerous world leaders.

Have Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk done anything meaningful or significant to control the spread of false information and misinformation intended to cast doubt on legitimate election results in various countries? I didn’t think so. Why would Sam Altman and Dario Amodei change their existing AI algorithms or discontinue working on newer AI models which pose an existential threat to humanity, especially when untold riches are at stake, either for themselves or their company shareholders? The argument that ‘if we don’t do it, China certainly will’ simply does not wash, and it would be foolish and dangerous to believe otherwise.

Trump and the leaders of the free world he has terrified are all cowards, save Mark Carney of Canada. The 1965 movie The Mouse that Roared is worth watching, especially now.

The writer is a computer scientist, a newly minted Luddite and a cynic.

### The verdict-first dissent: India’s politics of negation
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

The dramatic street theatre playing out across the capital – marked by Opposition marches to the Supreme Court, symbolic satyagraha at Rajghat, and viral standoffs with law enforcement – highlights a shift in modern political dissent. In The Revolt of the Public, Martin Gurri analysed how the digital age empowers the Public to rapidly mobilise, not to build alternative institutions, but to aggressively challenge and dismantle existing centres of authority.

The ongoing protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls serve as a textbook manifestation of Gurri’s thesis. By declaring the referee guilty before any judicial or institutional verdict has been rendered, a disparate collective of opposition interests is testing the boundaries of democratic accountability.

A central feature of Gurri’s framework is that the modern Public operates primarily through negation. It is defined by what it opposes rather than what it proposes. In the current controversy, the Indian National Congress and its regional allies have levelled severe allegations of ‘vote theft’ and systematic disenfranchisement. They point to the removal of over 13 crore names from draft rolls as definitive proof of manipulation. Conversely, the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the ruling dispensation maintain that this is a routine administrative cleanup aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased, and ineligible entries.

The striking feature of this standoff is not the disagreement itself, but the structural refusal to wait for evidence. In a traditional democratic setup, complex administrative disputes are channelled through institutional arbiters – the Parliament, the judiciary, specialised committees, or independent audits. However, the Opposition’s strategy bypasses these deliberative steps entirely. By demanding the immediate resignation of the CEC, the protest movement operates on a “verdict-first” logic. Guilt is established by public proclamation, and the street becomes the court of first and final resort.

Supreme Court seeks replies from CEC Gyanesh Kumar, others on plea filed by Rahul Gandhi, oppn leadersCritics argue that this rush to judgment stems from the political frustration of an Opposition repeatedly bested at the ballot box. When conventional institutional avenues feel blocked, the motivation to delegitimise the institutional framework grows. Gurri’s framework expands this observation beyond mere partisan sour grapes, recognising it as a systemic shift in how political actors seek relevance.

This dynamic is further complicated by the emergence of decentralised, highly online actors who lack traditional political stakes but possess immense disruptive power. The prominent role of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – a satirical movement turned protest catalyst – perfectly illustrates the concept of the ‘borderlands’ of authority.

When mainstream political heavyweights like Rahul Gandhi march alongside internet-native satirists and student unions, it signals a highly disparate coalition. Bound together not by a shared blueprint for governance but by a common target of grievance, this collective thrives on performative disruption. Because their primary currency is attention and the erosion of the Centre’s credibility, the burden of proof becomes secondary to the immediate impact of the spectacle.

The long-term danger of this trend is the systemic erosion of institutional trust. As 42 retired judges noted in a public letter, continuously branding constitutional authorities as compromised without substantiation risks deeply damaging public confidence in the democratic process itself. When the referee is delegitimised before the game even begins, the entire democratic contest is brought into disrepute. If the Public is conditioned to believe that every electoral roll revision is inherently fraudulent, no future election outcome can ever be accepted as legitimate.

This is the exact trap citizens must guard against: the descent into political nihilism. Dissent without a commitment to institutional truth does not reform democracy; it hollows it out. When Chief Justice of India Surya Kant declined to meet with Opposition leaders, explicitly stating that grievances regarding the voter lists must be pursued through established judicial proceedings rather than political representations, he was attempting to reassert this traditional institutional boundary. The CJI’s message was clear: accountability requires adherence to a process, not just the volume of a crowd.

For a democratic polity to remain stable, the right to protest must be balanced by a foundational honesty of purpose. When grievances are weaponised as political theatre, the social contract begins to fray. The Opposition must act as a credible guardian of democracy; it must anchor its dissent in verifiable facts and respect the arbitrating role of the courts. Those in authority must ensure transparency in extensive exercises like the electoral roll revision, and not give ammunition to political opportunists looking to exploit public anxieties.

The meaning of the current fractious politics is simple: when the ballot loses meaning, the street gains it. Street protests have the power to disrupt; they cannot govern. By replacing the rule of law with rallies, dissent loses legitimacy.

The writer is the former civil servant enjoys traversing the myriad spaces of ideas, thinkers, and books.

### Regime change: Ballot box or street
*The New Indian Express · Opinion*

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh is not a man given to theatrical outbursts, which is precisely why his charge landed with the weight of a warning. Last week, when he accused Rahul Gandhi and his allies of taking to the streets to topple a popular, elected government, he was not merely scoring a point in the daily duel of Delhi politics. He was naming a fear that has quietly crept into the corridors of power—the fear that the street, long dismissed as noise, may yet become a verdict.

The chorus followed with drilled precision. Several BJP leaders including its President Nitin Nabin sharpened the same sword, accusing the opposition of plotting to seize through agitation what it could not win through the ballot. The most combustible charge was reserved for the end. The BJP alleged that the opposition was importing the Bangladesh and Nepal models, where governments crumbled before violent crowds, and transplanting them onto Indian soil.

The Congress refused to surrender. Its leaders claimed that to oppose and to depose is the basic right of every citizen in a democracy. They reminded the ruling party that the very same methods had been used to remove Congress governments in the past. The Congress reminded that the BJP’s own leaders had marched at the front of those processions. Street protest, they argued, is a tried and trusted tool of democratic change all over the free world. The real question is not whether citizens may seek change, but how they go about it.

Indian history of political protests bolsters the argument. During the mid-1970s, Jayaprakash Narayan turned a student agitation in Bihar into a national movement against corruption and the abuse of power. The then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi responded with the Emergency. The Indian voter responded to her draconian regime by ousting her from power in 1977.

Again, in 1987, the then Defence Minister V P Singh walked out of Rajiv Gandhi’s Cabinet with the Bofors scandal as his weapon. During the 1989 Lok Sabha elections, Rajiv was voted out. Once again, the pattern was repeated in 2012 at Ramlila Maidan, where Anna Hazare’s fasts drained the moral standing of the Manmohan Singh government and set the stage for Modi’s rise in 2014. In each case the target was the Congress. Each agitation also had four vital ingredients: corruption, a credible leader, a slogan that touched the heart, and a common cause that rose above party lines.

Rahul Gandhi has spent the better part of a decade trying to build a similar wave against Modi, with uneven results. He took up one issue at a time, first Rafale, then Adani and Ambani, and most recently the charge of vote chori. Each campaign made an impact, but none grew into a mass movement, because these issues reached the minds of informed voters but rarely entered the homes of ordinary families.

In 2026 came the most unlikely spark. A young man in his thirties, living in America, picked up a word used by the Chief Justice of India and launched the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). But Abhijeet Dipke, its founder, chose his cause with great cleverness. The NEET paper leak had hurt more than 20 lakh families who had spent their savings, their sleep and their hopes on a single examination. The CJP became the outlet for their anger, and that anger produced results. Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned and several senior civil servants were moved out. It was a small yet symbolic regime change achieved without a single seat changing hands in Parliament.

Having tasted blood, the protesters went looking for new causes to keep their spirit alive. Rahul wisely turned his attention to Gen Z. From examination reform to unemployment, his Chhatron Ki Goonj campaign struck a chord and carried the concerns of classrooms and coaching centres into the national debate. However, the strongest weapon arrived when the SIR exercise’s manipulations were exposed. What had been a lost argument in the courts became a real grievance in towns and villages. The opposition parties that had long guarded their own territory suddenly found themselves marching together against a single target.

The government finds itself on unfamiliar ground. It knows how to fight political parties. Each new protest weakens the carefully-built story of good governance. This standoff raises a larger question that India has never fully answered. B R Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly in 1949 that once constitutional methods were available, civil disobedience and street agitation were nothing but the grammar of anarchy. Ram Manohar Lohia held the opposite view, insisting that living nations do not wait five years. Peaceful protest is the lifeblood of a free society, but road blockades that bring cities to a halt and violence that frightens ordinary citizens destroy the very cause they claim to serve.

The government, however, must resist the temptation to answer dissent with force. A ruling party that faces serious charges of weakening constitutional institutions can least affords to be seen using police, agencies and prisons to silence its critics.

The wiser course is to discover or invent outlets through which the opposition and the young can vent their grievances, whether through meaningful debate in Parliament, open hearings by committees, or regular dialogue with student bodies. The opposition, in turn, must accept the reasonable restrictions that the Constitution itself places on protest, so that the right to dissent does not become a licence to disrupt.

The movement has not yet spread across the whole country. But it has certainly given the government sleepless nights. India may well be on the threshold of a revival of democratic protest as a means of changing governments. Karl Popper, an Austrian philosopher, argued that the true strength of democracy lies in allowing citizens to remove their rulers without bloodshed, yet removal is only half the task.

The alternative must be better than what it replaces, and strong enough to govern a nation of 140 crore people. Until a united opposition finds a cause that unites, a face that inspires and a structure that lasts, they will remain a nuisance to the palace rather than a threat to its foundations.

### ChatGPT’s billions meet bubble babel
*The New Indian Express · Opinion*

Updated on: 17 Oct 2026, 7:16 pm4 min readCopiedWhen ChatGPT went live on November 30, 2022, Nvidia was best known for gaming chips. The company was worth $420 billion and Jensen Huang under $20 billion. This month, Nvidia closed at a record $5.77 trillion, and Forbes puts Huang at $199 billion.

The builders of Babel, Genesis 11:4 records, set out to “make us a name”. Today, billionaire lists are where names get made. Forbes’s 2023 annual census of the Richie Riches counted 2,640 billionaires worth $12.2 trillion. The 2026 edition found 3,428 worth over $20 trillion. Elon Musk, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg went from $514 billion between them to $1.78 trillion.

The divergence between AI and not-AI tells the post-ChatGPT story. Value exchange-traded funds have struggled returning about 47 percent in three years, whereas the VanEck Semiconductor ETF returned 327 percent. Below the billionaires there is the salaried millionaire gentry. At OpenAI, more than 75 employees sold $30 million each in one tender. SK Hynix is on course to pay its average worker $547,000 for 2026. In Bengaluru, India’s five biggest IT firms shed 57,891 jobs in two years. Icheon gets rich; Bengaluru gets thin.

India’s family offices are funding homegrown AI, but it has yet to show up on the global radar, and fund managers lament India’s underperformance and thin AI presence. Distance from AI costs money. Bernard Arnault, the richest man alive in 2023, is poorer than he was. In 2023, the richest man in China sold bottled water. Zhong Shanshan is still worth $68 billion. ByteDance’s Zhang Yiming has gone past him, from $45 billion to $69.3 billion. Tencent’s Ma Huateng has climbed from $35.3 billion to $53.8 billion.

Wall Street has always toned up its walk and talk for the season: Atkins and power yoga in the dot-com years, the Peloton through the pandemic. This era’s diet is a weekly GLP-1 jab that kills the appetite, though not for AI-adjacent stocks. The with-it crowd has moved from Zone 2 cardio to tai-chi, which seeks stillness in motion. The talk has followed the body into verbal calisthenics. Huang says compute is now revenue. Alphabet spends and warns, in one breath, that cash flow will stay under pressure. In March, with Nvidia down 11 percent for the year, the question was whether AI would pay. It is back in circulation.

Consensus has it that AI is real. There is no consensus on whether the valuations are. The result is babel about the bubble. This week the IMF warned AI could threaten financial stability. It counted 14 publicly disclosed circular deals worth $1.4 trillion and flagged “wrong-way risk”: the report warned that stakes that lose value just as the revenue tied to them is impaired. At best it signals scepticism; at worst, trouble ahead.

Gravity arrived soon enough at the stock markets. The S&P500 notched its worst week since June and the Nasdaq fared worse. The core of the AI build-out, the weave that ties Nvidia chips to labs, is stitched with borrowed money. The fabric has begun to unravel. The fall of CoreWeave symbolises what could be—its bonds have sunk below 80 cents on the dollar, yields are at 15 percent and its shares tumbled 17 percent in four days. Bonds of data centres leased to Meta and Microsoft slipped and Nvidia shed about $270 billion of market value in a week. The index is still near its record, and opinion is stranded between wobble and correction, between correction and crash. John Templeton said memorably, “Bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on scepticism, mature on optimism and die on euphoria.”

There is rationale scaffolding the AI story. Gordon Moore saw in 1965 that chips would keep doubling in capacity; the corollary was falling cost. Stanford’s AI Index says running a model with GPT-3.5-level capability fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024. Jevons named the paradox in 1865: the more efficiently Britain burned coal, the more coal it burned. Ditto with tokens. ChatGPT had 900 million weekly users by February. Nvidia booked $215.9 billion in revenue in the year to January; Anthropic was billing at more than $30 billion a year by April. Somebody is paying these invoices.

The earnings are visible. Are they enough? Gartner reckons AI data-centre owners need $8.5 trillion of revenue by 2030 to cover their costs, and forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion. OpenAI has pushed its listing to next year, after its annualised revenue was pegged $20 billion short of what it had signalled. Nvidia held $99 billion of stakes in AI companies by late July, against about $7 billion a year earlier.

At a macro level the promised land of productivity comes at a cost. Loss of jobs equals loss of consumption and growth. The ILO estimates unemployment among the 15-24 age cohort is at 12.4 percent. It is over 9 percent for the youth in the US, 16.1 percent for the 16-24 group in China and 9.9 percent of the 15-29 cohort in India are out of work. The white-collar worker forms the spine of the middle class—in India the IT is the largest exporter, the largest formal employer and a multiplier of consumption. AI is already busting business models.

Jules Winnfield, in Pulp Fiction, quotes Ezekiel 25:17 on “the inequities of the selfish”. Ezekiel did not quite say that; Quentin Tarantino wrote most of it and probably meant iniquities. The slip fits. A growing share of retirement savings sits in index funds, and 10 companies make up 37.8 percent of the S&P500. The consequences will be K-shaped either way. If it isn’t a bubble, the gains stay with a few. If it turns out to be a bubble, billionaires lose paper; everyone else feels the pain.

### A Brief History Of Student Movements
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

The recent cross-country protests by students and their organisations since June 2026 coupled with the heavy-handed response of governments have once again focused attention on student movements and their outcomes.

A brief history of student organisations and movements may, therefore, just be in order.

An All-India Conference of student activists was convened in Karachi on March 26, 1931, to establish an All-India Students Federation. Over 700 students from across India attended it. The objective being the mobilisation of young people against British imperialism. As a consequence, the first formal conference marking the incubation of the All-India Students’ Federation (AISF) was finally held in Lucknow on August 12, 1936.

Nehru inaugurated the proceedings while Jinnah presided over that conference.

Speaking on the occasion, Nehru cautioned, “When you are trying to build up a students’ federation you cannot afford to make it narrow and shut out persons holding different views.”

In less than a year the national student movement splintered along communal lines. The Muslim Students Federation under the patronage of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Muhammad Iqbal came into existence in 1937.

On December 25, 1940, at its Nagpur session, the AISF split on the existential question of what took precedence — Indian Independence or the global struggle against Nazism and fascism.

This split led to the formation of the National Congress Student Organisation (NCSO), also known as the All-India Student Congress (AISC). The inaugural Conference was held in Patna in 1943 and Ram Sumer Shukla was elected as its first President. The priority of NCSO-AISC was naturally to prioritise the Indian Independence.

Post-Independence at the initiative of the RSS, the Akhil Bhartiya Vidyarthi Parishad came to be established on July 9, 1949. Balraj Madhok and Yashwant Rao Kelkar were the moving spirits behind its inception. Its main objective was to counter Communist influence on university campuses.

An All-India Socialist Youth conference held at Kashi Vidyapeeth in Varanasi, from April 27-30, 1953, under the presidentship of Dr Ram Manohar Lohia. A student organisation named as Samajwadi Yuvak Sabha was founded. When Dr Lohia formed his own socialist party on December 31, 1955, a student organisation called Samajwadi Yuvjan Sabha (SYS) was concurrently constituted.

Finally, the National Students Union of India (NSUI), the student organisation of the Congress, was established on April 9, 1971.

The decades from 1960s to the1990s saw student protests around the world. In India, too, there were movements by students, some secular, others sectarian or linguistic.

The Paris student revolt of 1968 caught the imagination of young people of Europe. It represented a yearning among young people for a change in the “status quo”. It mainstreamed left-wing politics, anti-war sentiment, the thrust on civil rights and the institutionalisation of a counter culture that found expression in the hippie movement of the 1970s.

The upsurge in Paris coincided with the Prague Spring — a brief window of freedom in Czechoslovakia. It came 12 years after the revolution of 1956 in Hungary against Communist misrule. Both these protests were put down brutally by the erstwhile Soviet Union with Soviet tanks rolling into their respective capitals.

From Mexico, Brazil and Argentina to Chile across the Latin and South American continent in the 1960s and 70s, students rallied and railed against their respective governments on issues ranging from university autonomy, free speech, police repression, military dictatorships. Asian campuses were also on fire against US imperialism.

Post-Independence, India saw four major student movements with four very unique outcomes. The anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu in 1965 was supported by C.K. Annadurai, Muthuvel Karunanidhi (Kalaignar) and other leading lights of the Tamil intellectual and cultural community. It led to the ouster of the then Congress government and the establishment of a Dravidian dyarchy that was broken only six decades later by the victory of actor C. Joseph Vijay in the 2026 Assembly elections.

Conversely, the anti-English agitation in northern India called “Angrezi Hatao Andolan”, supported by the likes of Dr Ram Manohar Lohia and Atal Behari Vajpayee, brought the socialists and the right-wingers together. It paved the way for the establishment of the first Samyukta Vidhyak Dal (SVD) governments in the 1967 state Assembly elections.

In 1974, the Navnirman movement in Gujarat saw the ouster of the Chimanbhai Patel government. It soon dovetailed into the Sampoorn Kranti — total revolution agitation led by Jayaprakash Narayan. Emergency in 1975 and the establishment of the Janata Party government in 1977 followed.

In the 1980s, a powerful movement against immigrants from Bangladesh by the All-Assam Students Union (AASU) led to the formation of the All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad (AGSU). It ...

### Is The Art Of Critiquing Disappearing?
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

In current times, people around us don’t seem to engage much in critical thinking. Indeed, people appear to be happy to get by with exercising their minds as little as possible. I am not too sure of the origin of this malaise, but I find evidence of lazy minds everywhere.

What we see happening on a large scale is perhaps a manifestation of “collective representation” which is defined by Émile Durkheim as the “shared beliefs, values, symbols, ideas, and cognitive categories that are produced by a society rather than any single individual”. Sometimes I wonder whether it is the growing dependence on devices (that do much of our thinking for us) which is at the root of the problem. There is also the factor of a prescriptive government which would rather deal with compliant citizens than questioning ones. People become habituated to just following orders and of course there is always the fear of being penalised if they don’t.

Instead of trying to analyze the reasons for the current state of affairs I will just narrate my observations of the young. I find that as a rule; few students know how to critique. They either “like” or “dislike”, “love” or “hate”. With regard to literary works, they study ready-made critiques and are unable to give a balanced view of any issue independently. Leave alone students, even teachers do not like commenting on any colleague’s work, and if a teacher is required to do so, her account never reflects an honest opinion. I don’t think people realise how important it is to hold a balanced view of an issue or of a topic and to be able to express it clearly when required.

Then there is this confusion between opinion and fact. All the time we are subjected to opinions being paraded as facts. Hans Rosling’s Factfulness propagates the theory that you can live in hope if you develop “the stress-reducing habit of only holding on to opinions for which you have strong supporting facts”.

Any statement — especially a sweeping one — uttered without any evidence does not deserve serious consideration. For example, we often hear people say that women are better at multitasking than men. What is the basis for this claim? Or X is the best restaurant in town or Y is the best school in the country. Even if rankings of institutions are published, we should know how they were arrived at. Also, we should be suspicious of statements beginning with “everybody” or “nobody”.

It is a fact and not an opinion that criticism is required for any kind of improvement. This factual statement can be proved with simple logic. If flaws are not pointed out, how can they be rectified? Of course, the will to improve has to be there and perhaps it is not desirable that one to should be content with whatever one does.

The above point brings me to another feature of the society we live in: People in general have become overly sensitive. It is seldom that you come across people who respond robustly and constructively to criticism or even take kindly to it. As a consequence, people have stopped criticising altogether; the tendency is to please everyone. In the social media culture of “likes”, you are obliged to register your “like” for every post that is put up by your acquaintances. If you don’t, they will be offended and some may even ‘unfriend’ you. People seem to be confusing criticism with disapproval.

In school, I have noticed that teachers are reluctant to criticise in a straightforward manner. Their words are couched in euphemisms and terms of kindness with the end result that the student is not clear about the shortcomings of her work.

When we criticise, it should not be from a position of bias. And though it is difficult, we should critique dispassionately, that is, without letting emotions get in the way.

Some of the principles of balanced critiquing require us to be objective, specific and constructive. The critic must be respectful, clear and empathetic. Effective criticism requires the critic to recognise and acknowledge strengths as well as weaknesses. As stated earlier, personal feelings have to be consciously kept out, in order to arrive at a fair assessment of the object of criticism.

It is because we have lost the art of elegant critiquing, that we tend to demonstrate an all-or-none approach towards any individual, political party, a new idea and so on. Instead of expressing an opinion objectively, people have taken to making caustic remarks and personal attacks. I happened to listen to the American vice-president, J.D. Vance, telling an opponent to keep his (Vance’s) wife’s name “the hell out of his mouth”. There is nothing wrong in what Vance was wanting to say but the way it came out indicated an immature outburst.

The use of foul language just shows an absence of sound points of criticism. In any case, we live in an age when criticism is not tolerated. We witness syrupy and sickening sycophancy all around. Employees wish to please their boss, party members flatter their political leaders,...

### When Books Were Our Map To A Wild, Hazy World
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Clearing out some of my old papers, I found a diary I used to keep in my early teens. It was a thing in those days, before you had to chronicle your whole life on social media. People wrote down what happened to them in the days, their thoughts, ideas, passions and secrets, if you wanted to be part of a murder mystery. They were also called journals and this is before journaling became a 21st century thing, together with “gratitude”.

Some boring minutiae of daily life of a school-going girl in the 1970s aside, I found I had also made a list of my favourite tennis stars and most significantly, books that had made a difference to my life. How would they compare today? Does the mind of that 14-year-old match what I am now, 40 years later?

In a judgmental fashion, I was appalled to find some popular fiction. My mother, as I remember it, was very strict about reading habits and was very clear that I had a whole lifetime to read rubbish, so I didn’t have to start young. And yet I find Colleen McCoullough’s Thorn Birds in my list. Perhaps, and this is my excuse, I was allowed to read it after we had watched the American TV series. Who knows. I do remember being deeply embarrassed by the idea that I had even watched it, some years later. Although Richard Chamberlain was quite dishy.

I was amused to find George Eliot’s The Mill on the Floss on the list. I studied that in school a couple of years after the list was made, and quite disliked it. Of the great British Victorian writers, Charles Dickens and George Eliot remain my least favourite. And many of those turgid texts that were gifted to us as birthday presents: beautifully hardbound classics which remained unread on the shelves.

It occurred to me to explore the pretentiousness of a teenager. I was very pretentious as a teenager. Or so I thought. But apart from Thorn Birds, I also found Mario Puzo’s The Godfather. What?? How did I sneak that past my mother? Maybe like I quietly read Stardust when she was sleeping in the afternoon?

Some of the books reflect the talking points of the time. Like Sybil by Flora Schreider, an apparently true story about a young girl with multiple personality disorder. It caught the public imagination, and these were times when mental health and mental wellness were rarely spoken about. Sigmund Freud, from what we could glean from our parents’ conversations and the media, was all about blaming your parents and problems with sex. It was Freud and Carl Jung in those days, as far as I can remember.

And then there’s Jonathan Livingston Seagull. Much as it was discredited later, it was a book of the times. Richard Bach, I think, went out to rewrite the book several times under several names, each time reducing the impact and his own reputation. Does anyone still read it today? There’s Pearl Buck’s Hidden Flower in my list. I cannot even remember what the book is about, but I knew the writer was my grandmother’s favourite. I was shocked to the core when my mother gave me Buck’s Pavillion of Women, where a wife finds a concubine for her husband. The notion was too much to handle for my romantic teenage heart. Buck brought China to life for many; but did the Chinese see her as appropriating their culture? Could one do that today?

Thankfully, there is redemption in some choices, to feed my current ego if you will. Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice of course. William Shakespeare. Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyaya’s Pather Panchali. Rabindranath Tagore’s Gitanjali. George Bernard Shaw. Jean Anouilh’s version of Sophocles’ Antigone. Jean Paul Sartre’s play, No Exit. Albert Camus’ Caligula. Edmond Rostand’s Cyrano de Bergerac.

Shockingly, there’s so much missing. Where is Alice in Wonderland? Where is J.R.R. Tolkien? P.G. Wodehouse? And there is also something intriguing. So many playwrights. Is it because I was still in school? Why do I not read playwrights any more?

This rabbit hole also reminded me how little I read now compared to even a few years ago. I stopped reading fiction over a decade ago, and thus shut the door on so much entertainment for myself. I have gained some, though, especially in popular science. A degree in English literature means that you left the sciences behind somewhere around the time I made this list. But I have returned to it in some way. Natural history, geology, cosmology they test my skills and my brain.

Don’t worry, I take revenge on my pretentious side by reading endless murder mysteries. Although, I say this emphatically, I have not delved into the money-making game of the descendants of crime writers like Agatha Christie, where they get people to write in her name. Yuck! Now don’t try and convince me otherwise!

What I have had to remind myself is that reading is a privilege and it should not be. It should be a pleasure available to everybody. The repository of human imagination is massive and probably insurmountable, but like those tall mountains to be conquered, they are there. We have so much to...

### Economics Nobel: Terms of stability
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

Robert E Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were awarded this year's Nobel Prize for Economics for their insights on how governments and central banks can stabilise economies in uncertain times.

The Nobel citation mentions their contributions “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their work has informed measures that stabilised economies in times of disruption caused by external events – from rising energy prices to changes in retail demand patterns. This assumes greater significance at a time when central banks across the world are using rate changes as an effective monetary tool to counter inflation. Last week, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised repo rates after nearly four years, joining other central banks on a tightening drive. This followed a rise in crude prices, a fallout of the war in West Asia, and a spike in inflation.

These stabilisation ideas can be traced to the work of John Maynard Keynes, one of the world’s most eminent economists in the last century. Keynesian models helped major economies in the 1930s to navigate the Great Depression. He countered the idea that economies could automatically correct themselves and address issues such as loss of employment.

US economists Robert Hall, Michael Woodford awarded 2026 Nobel economics prize Keynes proposed that governments raise expenditure, change taxation policies, and effect monetary easing to support and induce demand when economic activity declined. This is particularly so at a time of recession, when falling private consumption and investment adversely impact demand and production, leading to a decline in employment. Keynes’ ideas helped disrupted economies to regain balance and stability. But they came to be questioned later, when economies faced simultaneous challenges of inflation and unemployment. The idea of State intervention did not find favour in a liberalising world.

But Keynesian economics found traction this century. Hall and Woodford have adapted these traditional models to present situations. They have demonstrated how appropriate monetary policies can help reduce volatility. This has been seen in many cases where central banks turned to interest rates for solutions. The idea that expectations of the people and the markets about future interest rates can provide important inputs is accepted now. The Nobel committee said the laureates’ theoretical foundation enabled the world to deal with shocks in the economy, such as a sudden shift in household consumption. Economists rarely agree, so some of their ideas remain contentious. But there is no disagreement on the contemporary relevance of the economic thought they have shaped.

### Missing footage, eroding trust
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s inability to produce the video recording of vote counting in Karnataka’s Sringeri Assembly constituency, now sought by the Supreme Court in an election dispute, raises serious concerns about its capacity to safeguard electoral integrity. At a time when the poll body is already facing criticism over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and allegations of large-scale voter exclusion, such lapses further erode public confidence. Citizens cannot be expected to trust an electoral process when the institution overseeing it cannot account for crucial evidence.

The Sringeri controversy dates back to the 2023 Assembly election, when Congress candidate T D Rajegowda defeated Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) candidate D N Jeevaraj by 201 votes. Following Jeevaraj’s election petition, the Karnataka High Court ordered a recount of postal ballots. The recount in May 2026 reversed the result, giving Jeevaraj a 52-vote victory. Rajegowda challenged the order in the Supreme Court, arguing that the returning officer had exceeded the court’s directions by re-verifying 1,251 votes declared valid during the original count. The Supreme Court has allowed Rajegowda to continue as MLA pending its decision.

Sringeri recounting row| 'Won't accept lame excuses': Supreme Court pulls up Election Commission over missing 2023 counting video The missing footage is significant because it could help establish what transpired during the original counting. Questioning how an institution responsible for conducting elections could lose its records, the bench rejected the poll body’s explanation, saying it would not accept such “lame excuses”. ECI guidelines require videography and CCTV recordings of the counting process to be preserved for 45 days after results are declared. Where an election petition or related legal proceeding is pending, however, relevant records must be retained until the dispute is resolved. Therefore, the failure to preserve footage in an ongoing election dispute points to either serious negligence or a breakdown in established safeguards. Either way, the poll body cannot claim ignorance of its preservation rules.

The Court’s warning that it may draw an adverse inference if the footage is not produced is justified. But this alone will not address the institutional failure. The authorities must establish how the recording went missing, identify the officials responsible for its custody and preservation, and initiate appropriate disciplinary action. As the constitutional authority entrusted with conducting free and fair elections, the Commission must meet a higher standard of accountability. In electoral disputes, evidence is the foundation of legitimacy. When critical material disappears while a contest remains sub judice, it is not merely an administrative lapse; it strikes at the credibility of the electoral process itself.

### Case closed, dispute unresolved: SC leaves questions on press freedom and legislative privilege unanswered
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

The Supreme Court of India recently disposed of a two-decade-old case in just 14 minutes. The case raised a consequential question: Can a legislative assembly use its privilege powers to punish the press for criticising its members? The dispute arose in 2003, when the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly passed a resolution ordering the arrest of certain journalists of The Hindu over reports criticising the then Chief Minister J Jayalalitha and the conduct of proceedings in the Assembly.

When the Court finally heard the case this month, it found that the Assembly had already withdrawn the resolution in 2004. Consequently, it did what courts do when disputes cease to exist: it declared the case ‘infructuous’ and left the larger question open for another day. In a Court beset by rising pendency, this may seem entirely sensible. But the decision reveals something troubling about how the Supreme Court functions as a constitutional court and what it means for our rights.

First, the case, N Ravi v. Speaker, had been pending before a constitution bench since 2004. The delays before constitution benches are hardly news. According to Vidhi’s Constitution Bench Pendency Project, cases currently pending before constitution benches have remained so for close to eight years. But 21 years is egregious even by this standard. Constitution benches are constituted precisely because the questions before them matter beyond the parties in the case. Indefinite delays in such cases are therefore a cause for concern.

Freedom of press cannot shield irresponsible journalism: Delhi High CourtThe present case was also deciding something far beyond the fate of the journalists involved. Article 194 of the Constitution gives legislative assemblies certain powers and privileges, including the power to punish non-members with sanctions ranging from admonishment to imprisonment. This power traces its origins to the United Kingdom’s House of Commons, where parliamentary privilege is intended to protect the functioning of Parliament from obstruction.

In this instance, the proceedings were triggered by criticism of CM Jayalalitha’s conduct in the Assembly. The objection was to the use of phrases such as “stinging abuse”, “unrestrained attacks on the opposition”, “fumed”, “incensed”, and “chastisement” in reference to Jayalalitha’s speeches. The Assembly also objected to the suggestion that it was abusing its privilege powers to protect the reputation of individual legislators. None of this, however, obstructed the functioning of the Assembly. And the House of Commons, from which these powers are derived, has not used them to punish a journalist for criticising its MPs since 1957. The case thus raised important questions about press freedom and the broader fundamental right to freedom of speech.

These questions are far from ‘dead’ or ‘academic’, as some advocates have suggested. Comedian Kunal Kamra is currently facing breach of privilege proceedings in Maharashtra over a satirical portrayal of Eknath Shinde in his stand-up. Journalist Nikhil Wagle was jailed in 2004 after criticising the legislature for attacking an academician’s scholarly piece. In 2017, the Karnataka Assembly imposed a one-year imprisonment on two regional journalists. There was therefore no shortage of reasons for the Court to settle the question.

And it has chosen to do so in the past, even when the underlying dispute ceased to exist. In G S Parulekar v. Maharashtra (1964), the Court decided a habeas corpus petition even after the detention order had been revoked, noting that the questions were “of general importance and are likely to arise in many cases”. The Dawoodi Bohra case was referred to the nine-judge bench hearing the Sabarimala review on broader questions of constitutional interpretation even after the underlying Act had been repealed. And most recently, in Jai Bir Singh, the Court decided the meaning of “industry” even after the legislation under challenge had been replaced by the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. So why not this case?

When a bench refers a matter to a constitution bench, it acknowledges that the question is bigger than the dispute before it. The answer matters to how the Constitution is understood and applied. By failing to adjudicate these cases in time, the Court undermines its role as the final arbiter of the Constitution. The decision not to resolve the constitutional questions in N Ravi sets a troubling precedent. With constitution bench cases routinely delayed, what is to say that this question will not meet the same fate when it is raised again? For citizens whose rights are contingent on this question, an answer could well never come.

(The writer is a senior resident fellow, Judicial Reforms, at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy)

## 16 October 2026

### A necessary corrective: On the SSR, the special summary revision of electoral rolls
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s announcement of a special summary revision of electoral rolls in 14 States and three Union Territories is, on the face of it, a routine exercise. This annual exercise to enrol new electors was stalled last year due to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and resumes with January 1, 2027 as the qualifying date. Seen alongside what is simultaneously going on, however, the exercise is a corrective to the missteps in the SIR. The ECI is also conducting a “special drive” to re-enrol those “left out”, using the original Form 6 without the ancestry declaration. It has capped Form 7 objections amid reports of bulk filings in several States and will release searchable electoral rolls in text PDFs to parties and candidates. Together, these measures add up to an implicit admission about the severe flaws in the SIR. The drive is the most telling. By dispensing with mapping to older rolls and logical-discrepancy checks, it concedes that the SIR’s insistence on them was unnecessary. For States that are going to polls early next year — Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand – this is a welcome opportunity to repair the truncated rolls prepared by the SIR. Those wrongly deleted can now be re-enrolled, and newly eligible electors can be added, without recourse to “logical discrepancy” checks or quasi-citizenship tests. The ECI must report re-enrolments (after deletion) separately from fresh enrolments and the special drive’s house-to-house visits must ensure that the burden of re-enrolment does not fall on the electors again.

For States that have already voted on the basis of SIR rolls, however, a number of questions remain. In West Bengal, appellate tribunals have disposed of barely 3% of the 38 lakh appeals, 22 lakh of them by deleted electors, and restored the electors in 93% of the cases decided. The ECI has yet to say whether these appellants can also use the new drive or what becomes of the tribunals. In States such as Bihar, where the gender ratio fell from 907 in the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls to 892 in the SIR rolls, young married women who were struck off must be allowed the opportunity to re-enrol. The Supreme Court of India, which upheld the SIR in May and is now hearing petitions concerning West Bengal, Delhi and the Commission’s conduct, should ensure that genuine voters are reinstated on the electoral rolls. The ECI’s 2002-03 guidelines show that a revision need not shift the burden on to the elector. Any future intensive revision must revert to that model. The corrective steps owe much to the sustained protests against the SIR. But they are not enough for accountability. The two Election Commissioners objected on record to decisions taken by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India, and their questions remain unanswered. The appointment process laid down in Anoop Baranwal, which the government got overturned in Parliament in 2023 and on which a two-judge Bench delivered a split verdict last month, must also be settled. And the official who presided over the flawed process, CEC Gyanesh Kumar, must resign.

### Ripples from the future: On the Nobel Prize for Economics 2026
*The Hindu · Editorial*

This year’s Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded for work that is particularly crucial in the current global context. Implications from the work also have lessons for Indian policymakers, some of which have already been learnt, while others remain a work in progress. The crux of the research done by the laureates Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford is in quantifying the future-looking aspect of the consumption and pricing decisions made by households and companies, respectively. Bringing empirical backing and rigour to this aspect, as the laureates have done, has helped policymakers identify economically distressed segments of the population, implement more effective policies during supply shocks, and communicate their policies better. Mr. Hall’s research in particular has helped governments identify the exact proportion of consuming households that are living hand-to-mouth. This is of vital fiscal importance for countries such as India. At the moment, India provides free food to more than 81 crore people, based on estimates that are between 13 to 15 years old. Using data — as Mr. Hall’s research allows — to identify those who truly need help will streamline the government’s subsidy expenditure at a time when fiscal room is tight.

Mr. Woodford’s work brought to light the importance of companies’ future expectations when setting current prices. The private sector Purchasing Managers’ Index serves as a measure of companies’ expectations for a month ahead, but there is a need for a government survey for longer time periods. Another key aspect brought out by the laureates’ work is the need to effectively communicate policy decisions to the public. Apart from rare instances, the government has been sorely lacking in this regard. This lack has been seen time and again, such as during its attempts to pass the Farm Laws, Labour Codes, and Citizenship (Amendment) Act, to name a few. Households and companies feel more secure making economic decisions when there is medium term policy clarity and certainty. The framework developed by the Nobel laureates thus also highlights the sheer damage the war in West Asia is inflicting over and above the loss of life and asset damage. The future looks grim and uncertain, and its effects are rippling backwards in time to the present.

### A contested UNSC seat poses a test for India
*The Hindu · Opinion*

Following the conclusion of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), held from September 8 to 28, 2026, the government must double its efforts to secure a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) in next year’s election. India’s bid for the 2028-29 two-year term of the UNSC was launched by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar this year, with voting in the UNGA to take place in June 2027. As a result, Mr. Jaishankar was busier than usual during UNGA week, holding nearly 90 meetings over a 10-day stay in New York. Between now and next summer, India needs at least 129 affirmative votes in the 193-member Assembly to win.

The United Nations’ long road to restoring trustThis has not been as much of an issue on the eight occasions that India has won the seat over the past eight decades, becoming the Asia-Pacific grouping’s consensus choice once every decade. Even Pakistan votes for India at the UNGA in these elections, and India returns the favour. With the full backing of the 55-member group, India won a record 187 of 191 votes in 2010 and 184 of 192 votes in 2020.

The bid for a ninth termIndia’s ambition to win a ninth term is guided by several factors — its terms were in 1950-51, 1967-68, 1972-73, 1977-78, 1984-85, 1991-92, 2011-12 and 2021-22. Its last tenure, in 2021-22, was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Narendra Modi government felt it had been unable to meet all its objectives. New Delhi may want to complete these objectives, including resolutions on terrorism and United Nations reform, before the Modi government’s current term ends in 2029. With India’s push for permanent membership of the UNSC still elusive, the government may wish to increase the frequency of its non-permanent tenures, keeping India at the centrestage of geopolitics from the UNSC’s horseshoe table.

Russia backs India’s candidature for UNSC permanent seatThe difference this time, however, is that when India announced its candidacy for the 2027 election, Tajikistan was already in the fray and, according to the chart drawn up for the Asia-Pacific seat, was to be the consensus choice. On the two previous occasions when India had to contest an election — in 1975 against Pakistan and in 1996 against Japan — it lost. Decisions on consensus are made informally by diplomats at the UN, sometimes decades in advance for the 55-country Asia-Pacific grouping.

Like with all the other regional groups — African, Latin American and Caribbean (GRULAC), the Western European and Others Group (WEOG), and the Eastern European Group — a different number of seats fall vacant each year. When consensus breaks down, votes within the group are split, leading to a contest in the wider UNGA. From there it is a race for every country’s vote; the rule that contestants must also win two-thirds of the assembly, or more than 129 votes, complicates the task. Given that the course is set, the Modi government has three options, each opening a differently difficult path. The first is to battle it out against Tajikistan on the global stage; the second is to convince the Tajik government to withdraw its candidature; and the third is for India to withdraw its own. Another option — to divide the two-year term equally between the two candidates — has been tried in the past, but these cases have been countries that are evenly matched in other respects.

Battling it outAt first glance, India’s advantage over Tajikistan seems glaringly obvious, given its size, economic standing and past record on the Council. However, UN insiders know that these are not the only criteria by which UNSC elections are won. To begin with, India’s multiple terms on the UNSC may work against it, as there is a growing push within the UNGA to consider smaller countries that have never held council membership such as Tajikistan. In his UNGA speech, Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin said that, more than status, his country’s bid for a seat on the UNSC was about its responsibilities to the UN Charter and to “listen to all voices — large and small”. This David-versus-Goliath pitch is attractive to other smaller states, especially those from the Global South that feel their lack of representation is unfair. Japan, for instance, which has served 12 terms on the UNSC, announced its candidature for the 2043 election in 2024, having previously declared its intention to contest the 2032 election.

UNSC reform would border on failure if only non-permanent category expanded: IndiaThe next important factor is how subregional blocs are likely to vote within the Asia-Pacific grouping. Tajikistan already has the endorsement of its own region, Central Asia, and possibly, by extension, that of several neighbouring countries. It also has the endorsement of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a grouping of 57 member-states which would largely follow that position, although New Delhi may be able to win over some of its friends within the organisation. India is fairly confident of the votes of the Global North — the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and allied countries — as well as those of Southeast Asian countries (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations or ASEAN), Caribbean nations represented by the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), and Pacific island countries (PIC). This means the battle ground that matters most is the Global South — Africa, South America and also South Asia.

The current mood among Global South countries, as reflected in a number of UNGA resolutions over the past year, has been decidedly against the big powers, the U.S. and Russia, and has been inordinately critical of Israel. During the 80th session, member-states voted overwhelmingly in favour of at least 13 resolutions criticising Israel. The UNSC elections this year were particularly instructive. For the Asia-Pacific seat, the UNGA voted for first-timer Kyrgyzstan over the western-backed Philippines. For the WEOG, Germany, which had never lost a UNSC election, lost to Portugal and Austria, ostensibly due to its stance in support of Israel. In the election for the President of the UNGA, too, the Bangladesh Foreign Minister, Khalilur Rahman, defeated his rival from Cyprus, another western-backed candidate. While India’s assertion of strategic autonomy vis-à-vis the big powers may stand it in good stead, its diplomats may have to answer questions about India’s own ties with Israel in recent years, particularly following Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Israel in February 2026.

Tajikistan or India bowing outThe next option, which has worked in the past, is to persuade Tajikistan to withdraw its candidature — India was able to negotiate with Kazakhstan in 2010 for the 2011-12 term, and Afghanistan in 2013 to step aside for the 2021-22 tenure. However, despite meetings between Mr. Modi and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon on the sidelines of the SCO Summit in Bishkek, and between Mr. Jaishankar and his Tajik counterpart during the UNGA session (both in September 2026), there has been no such announcement. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will travel to Dushanbe next week for the SCO Heads of Government Council (October 19-20) and his meetings there will also be watched closely on this issue.

Even if Tajikistan decides to step aside after studying its chances, India must consider the message this would send to other Global South countries: that its second turn in a decade is more important than giving a smaller country its first opportunity to serve on the Council.

ALSO WATCH Watch: India’s UNSC bid | What are the challenges? | Worldview

This leaves the third alternative, which would certainly make the world sit up: India could agree to step aside for Tajikistan, in order to return to the UNSC a year or two later with the full backing of the Asia-Pacific grouping. Such a move would acknowledge Tajikistan’s special strategic relationship with India in the past, particularly its role in hosting an Indian Air Force base at Ayni and a medical base at Farkhor, strategically important in the Afghan conflict in the early part of this century, despite pushback from the U.S., China and even Russia. There is little evidence so far, however, that the Modi government, which announced its candidature with some fanfare, is considering backing down.

Before choosing an option, the government must undertake a cost-benefit analysis of the value of the UNSC non-permanent seat at a time the global body is seen, in the words of Mr. Jaishankar, as “largely irrelevant”. The last six years of this decade have witnessed shock after shock, but perhaps none have rendered its own significance into question as much as the violation of the UN charter by the Permanent members themselves. China’s refusal to share information on early cases of the COVID-19 pandemic with the World Health Organization, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, U.S. backing of Israel despite its violation of every UN covenant, the killing of UN personnel in Gaza and the visa ban on the UN Secretary-General, followed by the U.S.’s war on Iran — the assassination of its leaders, and the bombing of a girl’s school — are all examples of this.

The path to securing another non-permanent seat on the UNSC next year is not easy. India’s win can only be guaranteed by defeating the ambitions of its old friend and regional partner — the choice is between a Pyrrhic victory versus a tactical defeat. In the bigger war for India’s rightful place as a permanent member of the UNSC — one whose voice represents the aspirations of the Global South — this is a battle that could be avoided.

### Metrics to minds — restoring purpose to universities
*The Hindu · Opinion*

There was a time when a national examination served a clear and limited purpose in India: to find a few thousand officers, soldiers and engineers, and to do it fairly across a vast subcontinent. That restraint is gone. We have taken the logic of the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and stretched it across every discipline, every college and every career. A device designed for the few now governs the many. And the country is paying the price for this overreach.

The National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE), the University Grants Commission National Eligibility Test (UGC NET) and other examinations now test lakhs of candidates across disciplines ranging from oncology to organic chemistry and from history to Punjabi literature, all funnelled through the same multiple-choice format. Understandably, this method is designed for uniformity, when in fact it is being used to identify talent, reasoning ability and critical thinking. This precisely is what uniform testing misses out.

Let departments decideThe alternative is simple. Let institutions choose. No national agency can tell what a good student of literature or physics is made of better than the department that will admit her. Departmental examinations indeed, restore judgment to faculty, and freedom to students to apply where their aptitude lies, not where a single all-India rank deposits them. This is not nostalgia. It is the norm in the very systems in the West that we hold up as models.

Related StoriesCUET-UG set for a makeover. But can NTA deliver?

The importance of reform in higher education in India

NEET paper leak fallout: Why NTA must transform into a single digital testing authority

Professorial appointments were once based on discussions with people who knew the work. It was an examination of judgment through intellectual interchange, not of facts. Teachers, who were superb, often went beyond the syllabus and were always ready for a dialogue. None had sat the NET. Today, there are many students with far more talent than the test rewards. They fail not because they cannot think, but because the test does not ask them to. It merely asks them to master a technique. We have, in the name of standardisation, built a mechanism that rejects exactly what it claims to examine.

No education body appears to have ever conducted the historical comparison that would make this argument undeniable rather than anecdotal. I would wager what such a survey would find, having watched the change from the inside for decades. The quality of discussion in a classroom, the depth of a student’s reading, the willingness of a teacher to be genuinely questioned rather than merely quoted, has thinned considerably. What has replaced it is a generation arriving through memorisation-heavy, choice-based testing, showing little of the wide, unstructured reading that used to be simply assumed of anyone entering a classroom. The examination has indeed changed what the classroom was meant to be.

The numbers gameThe same malady runs through the procedures of recruitment. Selection committees increasingly lean on publication counts and research scores. Minimum publication requirements attached to promotions and appointments have created a market for papers rather than a market for ideas. Journals of no discernible academic standing exist largely to accept whatever applicants must publish to meet prescribed research-score requirements by a given deadline. The University Grants Commission’s 2018 Regulations discontinued the earlier API-based Performance Based Appraisal System (PBAS) and introduced a revised assessment framework incorporating research scores. Yet, the underlying problem persists. Academic achievement is still too often reduced to what can be counted.

How can India make quality higher education affordable?The same arithmetic has hollowed out the PhD itself — this is being said based on direct observation rather than hearsay. When a candidate’s doctorate is weighed for a teaching post, 30 marks are commonly set aside for it in the selection matrix. This is a substantial share of the total. Yet, almost none of that weight indicates the quality of the mind behind the thesis, the rigour of the argument, or the calibre of the papers the candidate drew from it. Getting the International Standard Book Number (ISBN) or an International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) is no evidence of scholarly merit. So-called authenticated journals publish across seven or eight disciplines under a single title, a “Journal of International Studies” that will print history, management, literature, and law in the same issue, with no serious process of sending submissions out to qualified referees. Whoever submits, gets published.

Moreover, the exercise of supervision has grown just as flimsy at the other end of the pipeline, something visible in a doctoral thesis dashed off with a report from a supervisor who has not properly read it. The viva voce sadly stands reduced to a formality so thin that those who sit through it treat it as something of a joke.

The skilling paradox in India’s universitiesThe absurdity reaches its peak at the vice-chancellor’s chair. Search committees have been observed asking candidates how many patents they hold — a question with no relevance whatsoever outside a narrow band of applied science. The answer has been observed to favour candidates from the Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) fields almost by design. This is because a scientist running a large laboratory can attach his name to every research candidate’s paper that passes through it, thus inflating a publication count which no humanities scholar working alone could ever match.

Such a candidate arrives at the vice-chancellor’s office having spent an entire career inside one laboratory, with no exposure to the university beyond it. It would not be incorrect at all to say that a vice-chancellor of this kind has, in many cases, never read a novel or a poem, and he is being asked to preside over an institution whose purpose is precisely the cultivation of minds beyond the laboratory.

Reimagining India’s universities: Lifelong learning as the blueprint for financial revivalNone of this can be fixed by adjusting the metrics alone, because a great many selections never really turn on metrics in the first place. Too many appointments in Indian universities are settled by networking rather than judgment. Merit, in such cases, was never actually the criterion being weighed.

This writer’s own interview for the post of associate professor had a committee of four of the most eminent professors in the country, headed by a genuinely learned vice-chancellor; the interview was conducted for over 40 minutes. It was a rigorous, unhurried conversation, and the selection that followed was entirely fair, without a single string pulled on anyone’s behalf. That is the standard against which today’s appointments, and for that matter today’s admissions, ought to be measured.

Let us be clear. Harsher laws will not repair a broken system. Penalties for examiners and testing agencies may punish a lapse, but they do nothing to prevent it. If we want universities that can compete globally, we must start where quality is actually made. This is happening in university departments through appointments made by peers who are willing to be answerable for their judgment. This is the operating logic observed at many universities of higher learning.

Not for reasons of nostalgiaDecentralising examinations back to faculties, and restoring appointments to peer scrutiny and not point-scoring, is not a wistful turn. It is a claim about what a university is for. It demands more time, more accountability, and the courage to defend a choice without a number to hide behind. In return, it gives institutions back their proper responsibility to select candidates not for “cracking” the examination, but for their intellectual competence. If we want universities that form minds rather than calculate scores, we must restore our trust in the academic judgement of those who work within them. Their integrity should be the measure of their decisions, and society must ultimately hold them accountable not for the scores they assign but for the quality of their judgement.

Shelley Walia has taught cultural and literary theory at Panjab University Chandigarh

### DC Edit | Govt Stays Determined To Stifle Anti-SIR protests
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

As ‘cockroach’ protesters took to the streets of New Delhi again on Friday, more questions have arisen over where the protests are heading and whether the government reaction to them, which has thus far been only about throttling the voices of dissent, will change at least to grant freedom of expression of disagreement in a highly regulated environment.

Sustained demonstrations of youth anger have evolved from starting as protests against the misconduct of entrance tests and the leaking of question papers to seeking the ouster of the chief election commissioner as a first step to electoral reforms and on to a wider fight over the fundamental right to protest after two CJP members were ordered into judicial custody for five days when they entered Jantar Mantar, by then denotified as a protest site.

The hostile attitude of the establishment has led to bizarre methods of strangling the protests rather than speaking to protesters as they did when question paper leaks were the leading cause of protests. A siege mentality was very much in evidence as forces brutalised sections of protesters — journalists were not spared either — to retain control of protest sites that were made off-limits to the public.

Protests the world over trigger different responses from governments but France, which is seeing countrywide student protests, may have found a kind of balance in keeping the space for expressing dissent open while cracking down on its excesses like rioting that often accompany large scale public protests.

There have been several examples of police excesses in India as law & order keeping forces demonstrate their power to muzzle and strength in handling protests. The fact that Opposition parties have swung into action to make capital out of youth anger — which is their democratic right too — and attempt to capture power has seen the situation explode into an incendiary political scenario.

The Supreme Court may have ticked off the Leader of the Opposition for leading a crowd towards the supreme seat of the judiciary to which people of a democracy must be respectful because it is considered a fair arbiter. But the courts are duty bound to examine the fundamental charge against the Election Commission of slanting the electoral system, which has been the fount of India in its democratic history, to facilitate the powers that be to consolidate their position.

The court did warn that the government was taking a hammer to kill a fly as it pursued the path of total opposition to protests, like converting the capital into a fortress and stopping all transport and diverting traffic to seal the regular protest sites. Curiously, some non-BJP governments, too, did take measures to curb protests.

The Bangladesh example being quoted of civil demonstrations bringing about a regime change militates against basic democratic principles since a nation in which parties opposed to the prevailing establishment either boycott the polls or are banned from participating in elections, as was the case with Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League party in the most recent polls, cannot be considered a “mother of democracy.”

The issue is not whether the CEC, seen as the arch villain who tweaked Form 6 to make staying on the rolls a problem for even legitimate voters, goes or not. It is up to the top court to say if he did indeed sully the process to the extent of casting serious doubts on the legitimacy of the revised poll rolls.

What must be decided upon soon is whether the entire SIR process, which had the blessings of the SC, should be considered illegal and the rolls handled now in such a way as to be inclusive of all save those who have either died or are ineligible to vote as they cannot prove they are genuine citizens of the country.

### DC Edit | Too ‘Other’ To Be ‘Backward’?
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

The Constitution-makers provided for reservation expressly for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as a form of affirmative action to bring the people who belonged to the dalit and adivasi communities to the mainstream of society by giving them opportunities and their due share in power.

In a sense, this was atonement for the injustice meted out to people who belonged to those communities by the rest of the Hindu community. And hence the provision covered only those people who were part of the Hindu community; those who converted to other religions moved out of its cover.

At the same time, the Constitution provided for the introduction of reservation for socially and educationally backward people irrespective of their religious faith. The implementation of the Mandal Commission report has extended the benefits accrued to the SC/ST communities to the Other Backward Classes.

Solving the matrix of castes and classes in India is a tough job as it does not take one linear approach. Hence the Supreme Court’s decision that converts from a Hindu backward community to a Muslim backward community cannot enjoy the benefits enjoyed by OBCs triggers more questions than they seek to answer.

The court is of the conclusive opinion that a person does not carry his backwardness when he moves from one religion to the other. In the instant case, a person converted from a backward Hindu community to a Muslim community which the government had already designated as a backward community. The court may be right in saying Islam does not approve of classes inside its community, but the situation on the ground and the spirit of the Constitution could be suggesting something else.

Backwardness is a social construct, and not a religious one. Especially in the instant case where more than 95 per cent of the Muslims are designated as OBCs in Tamil Nadu.

Reservations are not the end, but a means. And a powerful one at that. As long as the Constitution provides for OBC status for communities irrespective of their religion, the provision must be reflected in its implementation, irrespective of conversion. It is time society took up the matter for serious introspection.
