### AI in Cybersecurity | First real chance to level the battlefield
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

For three decades, cybersecurity has run on an uneven playing field. Attackers only need to get it right once; defenders must get it right every single time. I have watched threat actors innovate relentlessly, forcing defenders to stay perpetually on their toes. But the current moment feels different, and unprecedented.

AI is not just another control added to a long list of existing ones. It's a shift in how we find threats in the first place. We're already seeing frontier models surface dormant vulnerabilities that had gone undetected for years, and patterns that human analysts, however skilled, simply missed. That's the real disruption: machines catching what people, by nature, could not.

If this is happening with just one control, it's reasonable to expect the same disruption across the hundreds of others that make up a modern security stack.

Human-to-agent handoff needs guardrails

As agentic AI takes on more of the operational load in security, a new question emerges: how much control should agents have, and where should humans draw the line?

Human behaviour is shaped by years of conditioning: upbringing, education, codes of conduct, and standard operating procedures. These invisible guardrails define what we consider acceptable, and keep our actions within bounds. Agents don't carry this conditioning. Their core motivation is task completion, not constraint. Left unchecked, an agent optimising purely for output can behave in an ‘unhinged’ way, exceeding its intended remit and breaking policy in pursuit of a prompt's goal.

The solution is not to slow down adoption but to replicate human conditioning within the agent itself, building a control plane and governance framework with the same rigour we apply to functionality. For this, two things need to change.

First, the design conversation is currently skewed heavily toward capability and output, with far less attention paid to the control plane. That balance needs to shift.

Second, ‘secure by design’ has been cybersecurity's most quoted, and most consistently unmet, principle. Agentic AI gives us a genuine second chance to get this right. When agents are deployed at scale, embedding the security fabric at the design stage is dramatically cheaper than retrofitting it later. Security cannot be an afterthought bolted on post-deployment; it must be on the table from day one.

Levelling an asymmetric battlefield

Despite the risks, this is a very exciting period, and not just because of the technology.

Cybersecurity has never been purely a technical discipline. It is, at its heart, a change-management challenge. Success depends on engaging stakeholders across an organisation, helping them understand risk, and acting as a catalyst for change you can influence but rarely control outright.

AI now gives us a genuinely new lever to pull on the technical side of that equation. Cyber warfare has always been brutally asymmetric: attackers only need to succeed once, while defenders must get it right every single time. For the first time, AI offers a real chance to narrow that gap, and bring some balance to the fight.

Human error has historically been the weak link. ‘To err is human’, and it's precisely why so many attacks went undetected for years, with people sitting behind the monitoring dashboards. AI doesn't carry that same fallibility. Repeatable, mundane detection work can now be automated reliably, freeing human expertise for judgement calls that still need it.

That fusion of AI and cyber working in tandem, rather than AI simply as a tool cybersecurity teams use, is what makes this moment genuinely historic. There has never been a more exciting time to be in this field.

Vishal Salvi is Global Head of Cybersecurity Services at Cognizant

### No one loves a good drought, yet policy waits for one
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

P Sainath's Everybody Loves a Good Drought showed how a crisis releases money, machinery, and attention that ordinary years never see, and how little of it reaches the people it is meant for. The farmers' suffering recedes from public memory and those who briefly cared move on. We borrow it here for a related observation: India's food and farming policy tends to come alive in a crisis, and go quiet once it passes.

Every few years, a monsoon fails, a conflict disrupts a shipping route, or a commodity market swings sharply, making our plates and farmers vulnerable to forces far beyond the farm gate. In response, committees meet, imports are cleared, and subsidies are adjusted. Then the urgency eases.

Consider India’s fertiliser situation.

When the Strait of Hormuz shut in February, urea climbed past $850 a tonne by April, its highest in four years, threatening to double the subsidy bill. By late June, the price had halved to $445-449 a tonne only to start climbing again by July. In response, the Cabinet approved a new investment policy for urea after 14 years, incentivising additional gas-based urea production capacity.

Consider the impact of extreme heat on India’s crops.

In 2022, India’s hottest March on record hit wheat, forcing the ministry to slash its harvest estimate by six million tonnes. As wheat prices surged during the Russia-Ukraine conflict, exports were restricted in May, just days after India offered to help fill the global gap. Onions followed with repeated export curbs in 2023-2024. Extreme heat scorched harvests made crop losses a foreign policy issue within weeks.

These are different problems, and they require different instruments. But they expose a common weakness: India is better equipped to manage immediate shortages than to systematically reduce exposure to the risks that produce them.

Banning an export and pursuing an import are both legitimate ways to adjust for availability. So is subsidising a new urea plant. Whether India is short or long, buying or selling, the lever it reaches for usually moves supply. The framework is familiar: surplus opens the export tap; shortfall opens the import tender. Each intervention answers to the food security of millions.

Nevertheless, India has an extensive policy menu to manage the demand side of farming and agri-inputs. For example: The Crop Diversification Programme, the National Mission on Natural Farming, soil health cards, neem-coated urea, the millet mission — they all change how much fertiliser India needs. Because different ministries manage these efforts in silos, they remain disconnected from India’s broader crisis-response frameworks.

There is a straightforward reason. Supply can respond in weeks; demand and resilience-building take years. Simply, reactive governance and a supply-side reflex are two sides of the same problem. Then, if crisis should no longer be the principle of farm policy, what should replace it?

NITI Aayog’s recent Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero: Agriculture offers one possible answer: shift the farm policy framework from crisis response to long-term preparedness through planning. For policymakers, this means long-term risk-calibrated roadmaps for food systems. A long-term plan, however, cannot assume clear sailing. Some risks arrive abruptly, such as supply disruption from wars, and others accumulate almost invisibly, like soil degradation. Building these risk-calibrated roadmaps requires three things.

Risk intelligence for India’s food system

India can track individual risks; what it cannot yet see is how they compound. Soil degradation and climate stress may weaken a region’s productive base; drought or a supply-chain disruption can then trigger crop losses or fertiliser supply disruptions, with consequences for farm incomes, food prices, and national food security.

India needs national-to-district food-system risk intelligence that connects slow-onset climate vulnerabilities with immediate exposures, showing not just where risks lie, but where they converge and with what intensities.

Stress-test policies against risk intelligence

Agricultural strategies are usually tested against the baseline. They should also be tested against what happens when the baseline breaks: a drought, a heatwave, a trade disruption or a conflict. NITI Aayog’s emphasis on identifying long-term strategic pathways using Integrated food-system modelling creates an opportunity to do this. The question now should no longer be just about what a policy delivers, but what it protects us from, and what new vulnerabilities it may create.

Make roadmaps with spatial risk-calibration

A national target can tell the State what to scale, but not how much, when, and where it will deliver the greatest resilience. That requires combining risk exposure with suitability. Scaling natural farming, for instance, should consider not only its implications for food security, but also farmers’ capacity to transition. Spatio-temporal roadmaps can show where an intervention can reduce risk most because no intervention carries the same risk-reduction value everywhere.

Preparedness is, thus, needs to be more than the opposite of crisis management. It is what makes crisis management less costly. So, good planning is not about knowing the future. It is about being less exposed to its uncertainties. Because no one loves a good drought.

Nikhitha Jagadeesh is Programme Associate and Chandan Jha is Senior Programme Lead, Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW).

### Young India needs mental health action plans, not new policies
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Two weeks ago, India woke to a deeply disturbing news report involving a 19-year-old IIT Bombay student who had died by suicide. The circumstances of every such tragedy are complex, and alleged caste and discrimination-related angles are being widely reported and debated in the media. However, an important aspect not getting sufficient attention in this incident is the mental health of young Indians.

Children and young adults are now growing up in an always-on digital ecosystem of smartphones, social media, online gaming, OTT, cyberbullying, relentless comparison and, increasingly, generative AI. Digital technology blurs the boundaries between the classroom, peer group, and private life.

The WHO describes digital environments as important determinants of young people’s mental health, carrying both benefits and risks. It has been estimated that globally one in seven adolescents lives with a mental disorder, while suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29.

Precision psychiatry: The latest concept in mental health spaceThe issue is recognised and the Union Ministry of Education has reportedly also been working on a dedicated National Mental Health and Well-Being Policy for Schools. India also has a National Mental Health Policy of 2014, an ongoing National Mental Health Programme, and initiatives such as Tele-MANAS. Therefore, another policy is arguably not the solution.

Mental health is one area where the distance between policy and practice becomes especially consequential. A policy can recommend counselling in every school, but who will counsel? It can prescribe early identification, but which teacher has been trained to recognise persistent withdrawal, risk of self-harm, panic attacks, eating disorders or dangerous online behaviour? It can create referral pathways, but referral to whom, where, and within how many hours or days?

India has a genuine shortage of psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers, and trained counsellors. Simply issuing another set of national or state-level policy directives, therefore, risks producing an impressive document with limited implementation.

There is a useful lesson in history of India’s mental health care service delivery. The District Mental Health Programme of India started as a pilot in four districts in 1996 and expanded progressively. That approach recognised a basic public-health principle: when expertise is scarce, start locally, build workable systems, learn from implementation, adapt, and then scale.

There is another unlikely but valuable precedent: Heat Action Plans. Ahmedabad did not wait for every Indian city to have an identical national heat protocol. The model was subsequently adapted elsewhere because implementation was locally owned. Mental health now needs a similar shift — from broad aspiration to geographically specific action.

Delhi is developing a student-focused mental-health policy, potentially covering counselling, identification of vulnerable students, and institutional mechanisms. The intent is welcome, yet much of what is required already fits comfortably within the 2014 National Mental Health Policy and existing school-health, adolescent-health and mental-health programmes. The need is to develop an action plan and not new policies.

Mental health burden doubled since 1990, 1.2 billion people affected globally An action plan is different because it must answer practical questions. Every city should know how many school and college counsellors it actually has; which institutions have none; where the nearest psychologist or psychiatrist is; who responds after a suicide attempt; what a teacher should do when a student expresses hopelessness; how parents are contacted; how confidentiality is protected; and where a young person can seek help without fear of punishment, judgement, or stigma.

It must also address today’s rapidly changing realities: cyberbullying, problematic gaming, social-media comparison, sleep disruption, online sexual exploitation, AI-related academic anxiety, and excessive screen use. Schools need protocols for digital crises just as they have fire-safety procedures. Colleges need specific support systems for hostel residents, first-year students, examination periods, and those living away from their families. Coaching hubs require special attention because academic pressure, isolation, and intense competition can converge there.

India should begin with city-level mental health action plans in metros, as well as major education hubs such as Kota, Pune, and other coaching- and university-heavy towns. Each plan should be nested within existing government programmes, use available public and private capacity, train teachers in first-line recognition, create referral networks, involve parents and students, and publish measurable indicators of progress.

The first measure of success should not be how many counselling rooms are inaugurated. It should be whether a distressed student is recognised earlier, reaches appropriate help faster, and remains connected to care. A policy provides direction. But mental health is ultimately protected in classrooms, hostels, homes, clinics, and neighbourhoods. For Indians between five and 25 years of age, the challenge is local and immediate. Our response must become local too.

(Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician and author of ‘Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed’.)

### Bird islands: On India’s bustard conservation programme
*The Hindu · Editorial*

This week, at the Desert National Park in Jaisalmer, two male Great Indian Bustards were released into the wild. It was a ceremony with considerable bureaucratic pomp; the Union and the Rajasthan Environment Ministers were in attendance. The conservation plan now has 97 birds, with nine more awaiting release. Of these, 57 are captive-bred and have produced 29 chicks this year and 24 last year. These are notable numbers for a species with a population of around 120 that has teetered on the brink of extinction for nearly half a century. It is worth recounting the bird’s conservation travails. Ornithologist Salim Ali wanted it as the national bird, so that protection would follow; the Indian Board for Wildlife chose the peacock instead. Numbering about 1,260 in 1969, it dipped to 600 by 2000, and 140-175 in Rajasthan by the 2010s. Hunters, royal ones included, prized the bird, with shooting reportedly lasting into the late 1970s. The rise of irrigation in Rajasthan led to the grasslands, which were once dismissed as ‘wastelands,’ give way to irrigated, pesticide-soaked fields and roads making the bird more vulnerable. The most recent threat came in the form of high-tension power lines. As a heavy bird, the bustard tends to fly at the same height as power lines and has poor vision. The Supreme Court in 2021 ordered that low-voltage lines in priority habitats be underground. After opprobrium from renewable energy companies, on the grounds that this compromised the economics of solar power, the Court modified the order requiring that only a subset of the power lines — those part of the bird’s ‘critical’ habitat — be made underground.

While the cultural links of the ‘Godawan’ – the bird’s local name – to Rajasthan’s habitat are now part of government and private marketing efforts, there are several other birds that are not as fortunate. Nearly 1,256 bird species, about 11.5% of the world’s total, are classified as threatened. Skylark numbers have fallen nearly 80% and Indian rollers 30% in 12 years. India’s conservation policy is captive to symbolism. A tigress from Valmiki flown to Buxa; African cheetahs in enclosures; Gir’s lions, confined to Saurashtra and straying into human habitations stoking conflict; the Delhi Ridge, being planted with peepal and banyan that ecologists say do not belong to its dry ecology. The conservation ethos — on paper emphasising coexistence between the wild and human — is practically promoting islands and African-style reserves. These have merits but populations that thrive inside walls overflow into villages and fields, as India’s challenges with elephants show. Landscapes, not species, ought to be the unit of conservation.

### Good, not good enough: On India and the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026
*The Hindu · Editorial*

Aspiring to host the Olympic Games in 2036, India faced a harsh reality check at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Compared with the previous Hangzhou Games, where it won 106 medals with a 650-plus contingent, the country won 85 medals from around 500 athletes. The aggregate fell short of an internally projected figure of around 100 medals. It is likely to invite a thorough postmortem, given the hundreds of crores of public money spent on the athletes’ preparation. India laboured to 21 gold medals, seven fewer than in Hangzhou, after a late surge of 11 top honours in the last two days, driven by the exploits of archers, boxers, wrestlers, and hockey and cricket players. It tied with Uzbekistan but managed to retain its fourth spot on the strength of a bigger haul of silver. Thirteen of the gold medals came from team events, with cricket, kabaddi and hockey making a clean sweep of titles. It underscored a stark reality: the country needs to raise its bar in medal-fetching individual sports, such as athletics, swimming, gymnastics, fencing and cycling, which determine success in multi-disciplinary Games. China, the runaway winner with a massive aggregate of 341 medals, including 169 gold, secured 54 medals in swimming alone. Barring athletics, India stood nowhere.

On a brighter note, India fielded 310 debutants and recorded a marginal increase in its athlete-to-medal ratio ahead of Los Angeles 2028. Several historic performances provided reasons to rejoice. Seventeen-year-old rookie recurve archer Kumkum Mohod dismantling the Korean women’s hegemony to help the archery team contribute five gold medals was a defining moment. Trap shooter Neeru Dhanda, golfer Pranavi Urs, wrestler Sujeet Kalkal and the women’s hockey team, which upset Paris Olympics silver medallist China to clinch gold after 44 years, hogged the limelight. Lovlina Borgohain, Aman Sehrawat, Mirabai Chanu, Vithya Ramraj and Gulveer Singh lived up to their billing. Boxers, wrestlers and golfers registered noticeable improvement. Olympic quota places in archery and hockey added to the excitement. Indian women catching up with men — both genders delivered 38 medals apiece — was another encouraging sign. On the flip side, India’s two major contributors, athletics and shooting, which earned 24 and 15 medals, respectively, yielded 12 fewer medals than in 2023. The shuttlers slipped, while the tennis players returned empty-handed after 40 years. P.V. Sindhu and Manu Bhaker flopped. Stricter scrutiny of athletes’ funding and efficient implementation of the revamped Khelo India scheme, designed with a long-term vision, are essential for course correction. Without propelling India’s sporting standards, a bid to host the Olympics may become a countdown to international embarrassment.

### Courts must protect, not regulate free speech
*The Hindu · Opinion*

Freedom of speech is vital for any democracy. The suspect for any attack on the right to free speech is usually the executive or the legislature. However, the proceedings of the Supreme Court of India, in Ranveer Allahbadia vs Union of India and other cases have raised the worry that the potential risks of endangering speech could emerge from the Court itself. On November 27, 2025, the Court said that self-styled bodies are insufficient for regulation of online content and suggested the creation of neutral, autonomous bodies. It also suggested that the Government publish the draft regulatory guidelines and invite comments.

Existing laws and regulationIn India, the existing laws already regulate various aspects of speech. Section 67 of the Information Technology Act and Sections 294, 295 and 296 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) penalise obscenity. On online regulation in particular, Sections 66 of the Information Technology Act prohibits computer-related offences such as hacking and 66E of the Act prohibits publishing personal images of others. Section 66F of the same Act penalises cyber terrorism. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules were also promulgated in 2021 though they are criticised for their overreaching interference and penal provisions.

Related StoriesShould commercial speech on digital platforms be regulated?

What does the Supreme Court’s push to regulate social media mean for free speech?

The broadcasting services regulation bill: A threat to digital freedom and innovation

Under these rules, there is already an oversight mechanism by the Centre. These rules also impose prior restraint. To illustrate, as per clause II (c) under the appendix of the Rules, a publisher should take “ due caution and discretion” while dealing with “activities, beliefs, practices or views of any racial or religious group”. Despite the existence of these and other provisions, any attempt at further regulating the right to freedom of speech and expression must be subject to critical analysis, especially when it comes from the Court.

Privilege versus free speech case in Supreme Court disposed of in half an hour after two-decade waitThe first concern is about the nature of the case under consideration. The Bench was dealing with a plea challenging the First Information Reports at the instance of persons who are accused of improper or obscene content. The question of online content regulation was not originally the subject matter of such a case.

However, in the earlier proceedings on March 3, 2025, the Court said that it would “extend the scope” of the case to examine the question of what regulatory measures are required to prevent broadcasting which are “offensive to well-known moral standards of our society”. This expansion is problematic at the outset. Identifying the problems of content and regulation is something that falls in the legislative domain. In Common Cause vs Union of India (2008), the Court cautioned itself: “Apart from the doctrine of separation of powers, courts must realize that there are many problems before the country which courts cannot solve, however much they may like to.” When the Court takes on this task, it is limited by inherent institutional barriers, including that of technical expertise in the field of online media regulation. The Court’s obstinacy for regulations in the field also would be vitiated by the same limitations.

The second is about the thin line between regulation and unlawful restraint. A five judge Bench of the Court in Sahara India Real Estate Corp. Ltd.& Ors. vs Securities & Exch. Board Of India & Anr., (2012) had considered in detail the question whether regulation of media content is desirable. Being conscious of the dangers of blanket prohibition, the Court held that pre-censorship of the media must be avoided at all costs. In the context of court reporting, it was held that the postponement orders directed at the media must be done only as a last resort and must satisfy a high threshold of reasonableness.

An outline in the ConstitutionAlso, the grounds based on which the right to free speech can be restricted are laid down by the Constitution in Article 19(2). This consists of interests of sovereignty, security of the state, public order, defamation and others expressly enumerated. The Court itself, speaking through a five judge Bench in Kaushal Kishor (2023) held that additional restrictions beyond what is expressly laid down in Article 19(2) could not be imposed. It was categorically held: “The grounds lined up in Article 19(2) for restricting the right to free speech are exhaustive. Under the guise of invoking other fundamental rights or under the guise of two fundamental rights staking a competing claim against each other, additional restrictions not found in Article 19(2) cannot be imposed on the exercise of the right conferred by Article 19(1)(a) upon any individual.”

It is interesting to note that on previous occasions, the Court has effectively restrained itself from venturing into blanket prohibitory measures. In Adarsh Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. vs Union of India and Others (2018), when a suggestion was made by a counsel urging the court to direct the film-makers to add a disclaimer before the movie, the Court repelled it.

It said that it is for the Censor Board and not for the Court to decide it, and even the Censor Board could decide it only after hearing the producer or the director of the movie.

Validity of the laws are to be determined by the Court as the constitutional umpire. During the Constituent Assembly debates, Pandit Thakur Dass Bhargava said that “the Supreme Court should ultimately be the arbiter and should have the final say” in situations of challenging the restrictions on freedom, by saying whether “the restrictions put are reasonable” (Constituent Assembly Debates. December 1, 1948). This is the scheme of Article 19 of the Constitution as well. Therefore, constitutional propriety demands that the Court abstains not only from the process of law making but also from the deliberation on the requirement for a law touching the citizen’s freedom.

The case abroadThe Court’s persuasive demand for further stringent laws in a tricky area could instigate prior censorship or statutory gag. Almost all the major democracies across the world focus on removal of offensive content and penalisation in case of breaching the order for removal of content. The Digital Services Act, 2022 promulgated by the European Union prescribes content removal protocols. The Network Enforcement Act, 2017 in Germany ensures prompt action on harmful content, without adversely impacting free speech. The Online Safety Act, 2023 of the United Kingdom focuses on removal of harmful content and imposing a fine in case of breach. The Online Safety Act, 2021 in Australia imposes a fine on non-compliance with regulation. Unlike these practices in democracies, countries such as China and Russia are invoking draconian laws to restrict online content. Surveillance and pre-censorship also dominate the online content regulation in these jurisdictions. Sadly, even some of the democracies which transform into autocracies also follow suit. David Landau and Rosalind Dixon, in a research paper, demonstrated that “would- be authoritarians at times seek to capture courts and deploy them in abusive ways as part of a broader project of democratic erosion....” (Abusive Judicial Review: Courts Against Democracy, 53 UC Davis Law Review 1313 (2020).

When the Court repeatedly asks for stringent laws to regulate Internet content and when the Centre readily agrees, it is a serious concern in terms of a citizen’s freedom. Author Salman Rushdie, when censored, has put it succinctly — “Free Speech is the whole thing, the whole ball game. Free speech is life itself.”

Kaleeswaram Raj is a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India. Thulasi K. Raj is a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India

### The looming crisis of world unemployment
*The Hindu · Opinion*

A recent World Bank forecast reveals that the global economy stands at the precipice of a silent catastrophe. A recent warning issued by Bank President Ajay Banga is stark: over the coming decade, an astonishing 1.2 billion young men and women in the Global South will reach working age, but the global economy is projected to generate no more than 400 million viable jobs. This creates a staggering deficit of 800 million opportunities in the job market, a demographic chasm of such unprecedented magnitude that it threatens to convert what should be the greatest economic dividend of the 21st century into a catalyst for widespread instability.

For decades, economic theorists have championed the demographic dividend as the primary engine for lifting developing nations out of poverty. The formula appeared straightforward: as fertility rates decline, the proportion of working-age adults relative to dependents increases, creating a temporary window of high productivity, elevated domestic savings, and rapid capital accumulation that fuelled the East Asian economic miracle in the late 20th century. Today, however, that classic blueprint is failing. Developing nations such as India are experiencing their youth bulges at a historical moment when the traditional escalators of economic mobility are stalling. The sheer velocity of demographic growth in many countries is outstripping the rate at which domestic markets, infrastructure, and institutional frameworks can absorb new labour, turning the potential dividend into a looming crisis.

### DC Edit | Amid Global Shocks, India Must Revitalise Middle Class
*Deccan Chronicle · Editorial*

For nearly one month, crude oil price has remained above $100-barrel, testing India’s economic resilience and drawing attention to the country’s precarious dependence on foreign countries for its energy needs. Apart from affecting people at fuel stations, costly crude oil prices affect them through higher transportation costs and higher inflation.India imports close to 90 per cent of its crude requirement, making sustained increases in international prices particularly damaging. While the oil price remained comfortable till August, the escalation of US-Iran tensions and the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthis, a Shia Islamist terrorist organisation, kept the crude oil above $100 for almost the entire September.Though India managed higher crude oil prices through discount shopping in Russia, the country’s crude import bill reportedly jumped 48.4 per cent to $74.8 billion during April-August. The cushion that discounted Russian crude has provided India earlier has also largely disappeared. Russian oil, which at times was available at discounts of $10 a barrel or more, has recently been sold to Indian refiners at around parity with, and occasionally at a premium to, Brent.Higher crude oil price means higher transportation cost, which will have an inflationary effect on all prices. Since April, inflation has been on the rise steadily — 3.48 per cent in April, 3.93 per cent in May, 4.38 per cent in June, 4.45 per cent in July and 4.82 per cent in August.Though the inflation is still within the Reserve Bank of India’s target of four per cent with acceptable movement of plus or minus 200 basis points, the price scenario remains a grave concern for the policymakers. This will be one of the prime concerns that would be discussed by the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee, whose three-day meeting is underway now.Individually, India may manage the higher fuel price as it has been doing for some time through discounted Russian oil. However, the country is confronted by two more economic problems, whose roots are overseas — rising yield on US treasury bonds and isolationist policies by advanced economies, especially the United States.Together, they create an uncomfortable combination of imported inflation, pressure on the rupee, deterioration in the current account, a weaker rupee and higher domestic interest rates — the result is once again higher inflation. Companies may initially absorb some of the increase, but prolonged high prices inevitably get passed on to consumers.All these are external problems over which neither the RBI nor the government have little control. The RBI may increase repo rate, which could address yield differential between the US dollar and rupee. But it cannot bring down crude prices, end geopolitical conflicts or improve global trade. The government, therefore, needs to revitalise the Indian economy. Though the economy is growing on paper, it is said to be greatly contributed by premium products by affluent sections. India’s real strength was its middle class, which is languishing in debt in the wake of a multi-year freeze on salary hikes. Rising profits of companies that don't invest back cannot revive the economy. A part of profits must flow to direct and indirect stakeholders, only then the economy will get back into overdrive mode.

All good things must come to an end. And Harmanpreet Kaur has chosen to step down from the India captaincy across all three formats with perhaps the best possible view of the finish line. Dhoni to win the ICC ODI World Cup, remained the face and force of the transformation of women’s cricket.There is something fitting about the timing. ### Anil Tyagi | Who Runs ECI: A Political Duo, an Autonomous Trio, Admin Sextuplet?
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

Rahul Gandhi, Leader of Opposition in Parliament, alleged that the duo of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, and the chief election commissioner (CEC), were involved in a “conspiracy” to diminish the country’s electoral system. The aim was to run down the Election Commission of India (ECI), an autonomous institution under the Constitution. Constitutionally, the trio of election commissioners, headed by the CEC, who are all IAS officers, manages the affairs. Yet recent disclosures hint that three other civil servants are involved. The bureaucratic narrative begins in July 2021, when Ashwini Vaishnaw, the 1994-batch Odisha-cadre IAS, took charge of the ministry of electronics and Information Technology. In October 2022, Ajay Bhadoo, a 1999-batch Gujarat cadre IAS, became the deputy election commissioner in ECI. He had served as secretary to Gujarat chief minister Anandiben Patel. Along with Mr Bhadoo, two bureaucrats entered the picture: H.R. Srinivasa, a 1996-batch Bihar-cadre IAS, and Seema Khanna, DG (IT). They worked in tandem, or conflicted randomly, with some of the members of the “IAS” trio in ECI. Media seems to drag Seema Khanna’s name.Let us follow another tech-led trail of events. In 2018, ERONET was being rolled out as the electoral-roll technology management system. It was built by government institutions, including C-DAC. In 2019, the new, so-called efficient system was migrated across the country. Four years later, in 2023, came the next transformation as the ECI, as per its records, implemented the next tech phase, ERONET 2.0. By then, the electoral database of millions of Indian voters became a gigantic national digital infrastructure. The list of voters was handled and managed electronically, with names added and ejected.Around the six civil servants, three election commissioners and three others, a tech architecture stands as a private-sector partner. In 2022-23, a software leader and a Tata Group firm, TCS, was embedded inside the architecture of ERONET 2.0. The role of the state-owned C-DAC was reduced. ECI’s recruitment document (December 2023) explicitly stated that ERONET 2.0 and related applications were developed by TCS. The system has 1.05 million election officials, verified over 78 crore electors, and generated more than 25 crore EPICs, apart from nearly 125 crore voter information slips.It is time to ask a few questions: Who roped in TCS? Where are the minutes that record the decision? Who can add, and delete, names from the voters’ list? How did six IAS officers, including the three election commissioners, allow an outsider, TCS, to become central to the electoral machinery?Tata imbroglio: Vijay Singh’s secret ladderVijay Singh, a former civil servant, has emerged prominently in the ongoing boardroom battle for control over Tata Sons, the parent of the sprawling salt-to-software Tata Group. Until recently, he was an important cog in Tata Trusts, which together own two-thirds of Tata Sons’ equity, and a nominee director of the trusts in Tata Sons. Now, he and others wish to dilute the role of Noel Tata, the successor to the late Ratan Tata. Vijay Singh’s story is of an IAS who travelled from his state cadre of Madhya Pradesh to the commanding heights of India's largest business empire. His journey began in a state, where he was regarded as a protégé of the former chief minister Arjun Singh. Both hailed from the Thakur community, and maybe the social links translated into something else. In 1982, Mr Singh moved to Delhi, and entered the secretive machinery of the Festival of India. He found himself under the wings of S.K. Misra, a bureaucrat with deep political associations, and Pupul Jayakar, an influential figure in India's cultural establishment. After five years in the Capital, and several global assignments, Vijay Singh went back to the state, and became its chief secretary. This was followed by the ultimate prize: the post of central defence secretary in 2007. In October 2007, the ambitious Tata Group got seven defence industrial licences. Later, Mr Singh became an integral part of Tata Trusts and Tata Sons, and was chairman, Tata Advanced Systems.

Power shift behind DhamiUttarakhand has a bureaucratic mystery. Where does the power flow from? Anand Bardhan, chief secretary, heads the bureaucracy. But there is a powerful circle around chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, with Ramesh Kumar Sudhanshu, principal secretary to the CM, at the Centre. *Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

The on-again, off-again seesaw diplomacy that the Tarique Rahman-led BNP government resorted to over his proposed bilateral visit to Delhi at the invitation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi has brought the ties between the two closest neighbours to their nadir. ideals and values representing 1971. ### Tanvika Baru | The Acoustics of Audacity: The Insolence of Effluvia
*Deccan Chronicle · Opinion*

The decibel burden of urban habitation frequently necessitates recourse to law enforcement, the formal lodging of complaints, and the increasingly Sisyphean endeavour of addressing one’s neighbours with studied equanimity. One may exhaust every refinement of civility, marshal reason with deliberative restraint, and pursue the most conciliatory modalities of neighbourly diplomacy, yet such overtures become utterly nugatory when confronted by individuals inherently impervious to decorum and deficient in regard for the sanctity of shared domestic space. What ought to constitute an elementary compact of coexistence instead degenerates into an interminable contest between civic forbearance and sonic imposition.In Hyderabad, acoustic contamination now lies almost ineradicably embedded within the metropolitan soundscape: sirens cleave the ambient stillness; vehicular klaxons proffer their ceaseless metallic clamour; the resonant calls to prayer traverse densely inhabited neighbourhoods; children career through apartment corridors with exuberant abandon, occasionally accompanied by an indiscriminate barrage of invective; and festivals periodically transfigure residential precincts into theatres of amplified tumult. Each phenomenon, considered in isolation, may be rationalised as an incidental concomitant of urban existence; collectively, however, they constitute an unremitting auditory siege. The repercussions extend well beyond ephemeral irritation: persistent exposure to intrusive noise can exact an emotional and corporeal toll, engendering agitation, fatigue, querulousness and sustained sensory vigilance. When excessive decibels assume a quotidian character and consideration becomes conspicuously inaudible, quietude is transmuted from an elementary expectation of habitation into a recherché privilege.At certain conjunctures of domestic cacophony, the residential environment metamorphoses into an involuntary polyphonic totality of acoustic excess—an avant-garde opera to which nobody has purchased a ticket, yet everyone has been unwillingly conscripted into its audience. Windowpanes vibrate, crystalware quivers, doors resonate, and partition walls acquire an unsolicited percussive lexicon due to the unremitting reverberations of inverters, centrifugal pumps, drilling, exhausts, and compressors; one half anticipates the intervention of a coloratura soprano ascending into some vertiginous crescendo, while chandeliers oscillate with almost Wagnerian portent. Yet the denouement possesses none of the theatrical catharsis such a spectacle promises.Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie provides an especially apposite literary analogue: the accidental shattering of Laura’s unicorn transmutes fragility into auditory rupture, rendering vulnerability momentarily palpable through resonance. In lived reality, however, there is neither theatrical resolution nor intermission—only the physiological reverberations of relentless disturbance. What one household may construe as exuberance or quotidian conviviality may register within another as an unwelcome assault upon sensory equilibrium. Acoustic force, like fracture, possesses a threshold beyond which it ceases to be incidental and becomes injurious; the distinction is that shattered fragments are conspicuously visible, whereas the fragmentation of an overtaxed nervous system remains invisible yet corporeally consequential, perceptible principally to the individual compelled to endure it.What renders the predicament still more insidious is the manner in which religious observance and gendered assertions of ascendancy can serve as instruments of entitlement, converting differences of custom, conviction or conduct, into occasions for belligerence. Faith, when externalised through incessant amplification, can cease to constitute an inward article of conscience and assume the character of an unbidden imposition upon the acoustic commons; gender, likewise, may remain entangled with hierarchies of authority, performative machismo and the fallacious supposition that volume is a legitimate proxy for power. The consequence is not merely an increase in ambient tumult but a deterioration in the very phenomenology of convivial habitation, wherein reason is subsumed before it can be articulated and an appeal for restraint is misconstrued as an affront to prerogative.For those subjected to such conditions, the consequences can be profoundly debilitating. Sonic intrusion does not necessarily terminate when its immediate source subsides; its physiological reverberations may persist, compromising composure and the capacity for ordinary functioning.

It can likewise impede convalescence in adjacent hospitals and compromise students’ concentration during examinations.For an individual whose sensory apparatus has become exceptionally reactive to auditory stimuli, including misophonia and PTSD, the relentless barrage can render even quotidian responsibilities—bestirring oneself at daybreak,...

### KPSC rot demands reform at source
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) scam has exposed something far more disturbing than a mere question paper leak. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) have uncovered a network in which candidates were coached in resorts, marks systematically manipulated, and results withheld to demand bribes. In the recruitment of veterinary officers, candidates are alleged to have paid lakhs of rupees, with the ED tracing part of the illicit proceeds. The probe has since widened to the Karnataka Administrative Service (KAS) recruitment and other examinations. The controversy centres on suspended KPSC chairman Shivashankarappa S Sahukar and former controller of examinations, IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar. While Gangwar has been arrested, the role of other commission members is under investigation.

13 recruitments by KPSC in two years under ED scannerThe Congress government has repeatedly pointed out that Sahukar and other commission members were appointed during B S Yediyurappa's tenure. But that does not absolve the present administration of responsibility. The irregularities occurred under its watch. Responsibility for an appointment may lie with a previous regime, but the onus for oversight rests with the government in power. More importantly, the KPSC's deficiencies are hardly unknown. There has been no shortage of committees or recommendations. The Hota Committee identified most structural deficiencies years ago and proposed corrective measures. A reform agenda already exists, including an annual recruitment calendar, long-term manpower planning, safeguards modelled on those adopted by the Karnataka Examination Authority, elimination of interviews for Group C posts, digital OMR management, and parallel document verification. Two more committees, one headed by R V Deshpande, MLA, and another led by retired IAS officer S V Ranganath, are examining further reforms.

The deficiencies and remedies have largely been identified. What is lacking is the political will to implement them. The first and most critical reform concerns appointments. The chairman and members of a constitutional recruitment body must be chosen through an independent and transparent process based on integrity, competence, and administrative credibility, rather than political patronage. Equally, the KPSC investigation must not degenerate into a partisan contest. The ED’s inquiry should cover Sahukar's entire tenure instead of confining its focus to the period during which the Congress government has been in office. KPSC recruits personnel who ultimately run the state machinery. When merit is compromised at the point of entry, the integrity of governance is undermined. The state needs credible appointments, independent investigations, and, above all, the political courage to implement reforms on the table for years.

### SIR: Defending the indefensible
*Deccan Herald · Editorial*

The gross irregularities and undemocratic nature of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls demand accountability beyond mere course corrections. Media revelations have forced the Election Commission of India (ECI) to come out with explanations in its defence and take a few corrective steps. But the explanations do not justify the errors, primarily because these were not lapses that occurred in the normal course of implementing a national-scale programme involving many millions of people. These were predetermined actions intended to take the exercise in a particular direction and lead to an undemocratic outcome. The corrective measures do not neutralise the wrongs but only confirm them and strengthen the demand to establish greater accountability. The fundamental wrong of the SIR is more than the sum of all the individual wrongs exposed as part of its operation.

The ECI has ordered a special drive for the enrolment of voters left out and of young and first-time eligible voters in states and Union Territories where the revision has been completed. Form 6, prescribed for the registration of new voters, was illegally altered, as pointed out by Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu. This alteration had consequences, denying a large number of citizens their voting rights. Relaxation or cancellation of a wrong decision does not absolve an authority of its accountability for that decision, especially when the authority stuck to the decision even after the illegality was pointed out by a responsible official. The official in this case should also have had a role in the decision. The same is the case with the operationalisation of a software that took away the power of state-level officers to decide on the eligibility of voters and the appeals made in West Bengal against the inclusion of over 16 lakh voters in the rolls.

Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar took these and other crucial decisions without the concurrence of the two other election commissioners. That makes these decisions procedurally wrong, too, apart from being undemocratic in intent. This should render every action based on these decisions null and void. Kumar should be held accountable for the trauma and difficulties caused to millions of voters and the wastage of financial, material, and human resources in the exercise. Notably, the Commission has not addressed the nation on the controversy even in the face of credible evidence that its actions conflicted with its constitutional mandate and the essential principles of India’s electoral democracy.

### FPIs abandon India’s growth story
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs; foreigners investing in stock markets for financial returns) were net sellers (total of sales and purchases) of Rs 9,980 crore equity on September 29. On September 30, that figure rose to Rs 10,198 crore. The FPIs remained relentless on October 1 also, dumping Rs 9,570 crore equity.

Selling about Rs 30,000 crore worth of equity in three days was unprecedented and foreboding.

Recently, the FPIs have also been selling Indian government securities. They sold Rs 2,132 crore of fully accessible route (FAR; no restrictions on buying and selling) on September 30.

Are the FPIs running away from India’s equity and debt markets? Have they lost faith in the India story and the claims of high GDP and GST growth? Will they return soon? What does this mean for India’s foreign reserves?

Beyond GDP: Why India's missing informal sector numbers distort economic realityTreating India very differently

The nine months of 2026 have been very productive for the FPIs in most global markets. South Korean KOSPI has given a humongous return of 68%, Japan’s Nikkei has given 30%, and the United States’ NASDAQ delivered an impressive 15.6%. In a glaring contrast, India’s NIFTY delivered a (-)19.58% return in dollar terms during the same period.

The FPIs make investments in stock markets around the world seeking the best net dollar returns. Wherever they expect the stock markets (and individual listed companies) to do well, they go and buy, investing top dollars. Wherever they find that the listed companies are unlikely to make excellent profits or the markets might not rise, they sell and exit with their dollars. Their investment decisions are also hugely impacted by their view about appreciation/depreciation of the local currency.

At the moment, all these factors are signalling red for India.

Over the next 2-3 years, corporate profits are expected to be not very high, as Indian companies are neither technology leaders nor major investors in future industries, such as chips (most prominently GPUs), and digital, tech, and energy transition. India’s stock markets are performing poorly; NSE/BSE indices are -15% compared to September 2024, and valuations remain high. The rupee is depreciating despite the RBI stockpiling over $130 billion through FCNR deposits.

All this has sent shockwaves through the FPIs.

The FAR route was introduced in 2020 to entice the global bond market indices to include Indian government bonds therein. Two global bond market indices included Indian bonds as well. Despite all this, the FPIs are not enthusiastic because the difference in yields on their rupee and dollar bond investments has become too small to cover rupee depreciation, making their net return on rupee bonds much less in comparison to US bonds.

The FPIs are not in the business of charity. They do take some short-term losses when there is hope for making it up. That hope is vanishing. No wonder, they are dumping both equities and government bonds in India.

The US interest rates are a critical factor for the FPIs to return to the Indian stock market.

Yield on a 10-year US Treasury bond briefly crossed 5.3% (the highest in 20 years). There is enormous demand for debt from US corporates investing in AI and related industries and also from the US government to finance a huge fiscal deficit. The supply is, however, dwindling. Global investors (China, Japan, and others) are selling US securities and taking out their money.

In this scenario, it is highly unlikely that US interest rates would ease anytime soon; they may rise further. In such a situation, if India wants the FPIs to return to buy Indian bonds and invest in equity, the RBI must raise the interest rates.

Interest rates on government bonds are going up (crossed 7.2% on 10-year bonds). This, however, yields only 2% more than the US bonds. Considering likely rupee depreciation, unless the RBI creates a differential of 4% (raising yield to 9+%, which is nearly impossible for the bank to stomach), the FPIs are not going to buy the government bonds aggressively.

The dollar interest rates are used for discounting stock market returns globally.

As India’s stock markets are yielding negative returns and with no likelihood of the Narendra Modi government permitting Chinese to aggressively invest in India in future industries, including batteries and EVs, the FPIs are likely to keep away from India’s equity markets for some time.

Reserves under pressure

Foreign exchange reserves reached the high of $785.71 billion (foreign currency assets $648.17 billion) on September 4, riding over $130 billion FCNR(B) inflows.

The foreign exchange reserves have begun falling rapidly since then. In the week ending September 18, total reserves fell by $14.88 billion (currency reserves $14.82 billion) and on September 25 by $18.34 billion (currency reserves $15.57 billion). On September 25, the foreign reserves were down to $747.56 billion (currency reserves $615.41 billion).

Considering all factors (the current account deficit, NRIs encashing old FCNR and NRE deposits, the FPIs remaining reluctant, etc.), by the end of December, the reserves are likely to fall below their June 5 levels (total $681.61 billion, foreign currencies $543.44 billion). This may take the rupee to 100 per dollar, and that’s a scary scenario.

Subhash Chandra Garg is former Finance & Economic Affairs Secretary, and author of ‘The Ten Trillion Dream Dented’, ‘Commentary on Budget 2026-2027’, and ‘We Also Make Policy’.

### The high price of institutional capture: How backing the CEC is costing the BJP
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

A stage has been reached where the Union government seems almost incapable of thinking through the challenges it faces and how it responds. The handling of the largely peaceful protests against the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the extended Gandhi Jayanti weekend, when hundreds were detained at Jantar Mantar, is proof of this. The government appears unable to act even in its own narrow self-interest of protecting its reputation and political standing. What is gained politically by unleashing police force on those protesting against an already disgraced CEC, while BJP functionaries rally to his defence? The defence only proves the charge: that the CEC and the party in power are one in the exercise of targeted voter exclusion.

The national anger against the CEC, for his role in the widespread disenfranchisement of ordinary citizens, runs deep. His fellow election commissioners objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions taken without their knowledge, as reported. Given the depth of this anger, political survival dictates that the BJP maintain strategic silence on the issue, if not distance itself entirely. A formal dissociation would be a face-saving device for the party, but therein lies the bind: it would also raise questions about the legitimacy of recent state elections held on his watch, notably Bihar, where the BJP-led NDA won, and West Bengal, where the BJP came to power.

As matters stand, Kumar cannot continue in his role with any credibility for long. His continued defence, then, means spending political capital on a lost cause. Each detention at Jantar Mantar only reinforces the image of the CEC being in the service of the BJP.

‘Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao’: Congress announces nationwide campaign against CEC from October 10The Kumar affair, though, is a symptom, not the disease. There is little doubt that the Narendra Modi government is sinking deeper into a political quagmire. Even if it holds on, it will be a government with little political legitimacy. As developments have panned out, it will be very difficult to emerge from this crisis without extensive damage. This is a good time for the BJP to reflect on where it has landed under the Narendra Modi-Amit Shah capture. The question is even more urgent for the RSS, which, as the ideological root of the BJP, may face a bigger challenge. It runs the risk of being marked as a movement that enjoyed the spoils of power, built glamorous offices for itself, and watched silently as Indian institutions and the democratic framework were torn apart by the party it birthed and supported.

Historically, the RSS has been accused of not standing up to the British during the freedom struggle. It has been charged with propagating the communal hatred that led to the killing of Mahatma Gandhi. If that was history the RSS wanted to leave behind, here was a chance to build an agenda for growth and truly live the promise on which the BJP won its first full majority in the Lok Sabha: sab ka saath, sab ka vikas. What it oversaw instead was more communal hatred, a divisive agenda, renewed attacks on Gandhi, rising joblessness, a directionless foreign policy, and a new phase of unabashed crony capitalism. The slogan of development was, observers will argue, a well-thought-through ruse to grab power and play with India’s crown jewels, the ECI being just one among the many that have been vandalised.

India’s Preamble says the nation is constituted as a “sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.” Consider how each of those words has come under attack. The Indo-US trade deal, under which, by Washington’s account, India agreed to stop buying Russian oil in return for lower tariffs, undermines sovereignty. The socialist ideal has been under attack for some time now. The latest examples are the Delhi government’s decision to let private schools self-certify in place of the essentiality certificate, and the rapid march of private equity into hospitals across the nation. Unions have been marginalised and their leaders detained often. Secularism remains under attack internally, given the number of violations of minority rights. Democracy is threatened by the functioning of the ECI under Kumar.

Yet all of this has awakened and rekindled the republican spirit. “Republic” comes from the Latin res publica, “the public thing”, which holds that the nation belongs to the people, not to kings. India, as a republic, means its people, who must have a voice in how the nation’s affairs are run. People play an active part in shaping policy and driving direction. This is the part that has traditionally been weak in India, and which the government has tried to extinguish, but the protesters have brought alive.

What is the immediate way out of this entanglement? The CEC cannot be sacked. He can be removed only the way a Supreme Court judge is, which in effect means impeachment by Parliament. For that to succeed, the BJP has to dump him and ask its MPs to vote for his removal, or its allies [JD(U) and TDP] have to turn.

This appears unlikely: dumping Gyanesh Kumar means conceding the charge, along with questions over the mandates delivered on his watch. The other way involves backroom talks, in which the CEC is asked to resign voluntarily. How and why would he oblige? What price would he extract, and what secrets might he hold? Those become the levers in play if this option is pursued.

All of this only highlights the bind in which the government finds itself. The lasting lesson is that institutions must be left independent and due process respected. Playing with institutions is like playing with fire. The thrills of capture are short-term; the pain plays out in the longer run.

The writer is a journalist and faculty member at SPJIMR; Syndicate: The Billion Press.

### Why Keralam is right to reopen the Gyanesh Kumar case
*Deccan Herald · Opinion*

Keralam’s decision to reopen a two-decade-old vigilance inquiry involving Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar should not be dismissed as political retaliation. On the facts currently available, a fresh investigation is not only defensible; it is necessary.

The issue dates back to 2006, when Kumar, a Kerala-cadre IAS officer, served as secretary of the Public Works Department. Malaysian civil engineer Lee See Been, associated with the India-Malaysia PATI-BEL consortium working on the MC Road component of the Kerala State Transport Project, died by suicide that year. Contemporary and current reports say a purported suicide note named Kumar contained allegations connected to the clearing of project payments. Those allegations have never been judicially established, and Kumar is entitled to the presumption of innocence. But that is precisely why an unfinished inquiry is unsatisfactory: serious allegations require either substantiation or authoritative closure, not administrative oblivion.

Keralam’s Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala has now directed the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) to conduct a preliminary inquiry following a complaint by KPCC leader Malayinkeezhu Venugopal. Reports indicate the original inquiry began after Lee’s death but did not reach a conclusion; Kumar later moved to the Union government on deputation.

That history creates the strongest case for reopening the matter.

The relevant question is not why Keralam is investigating the 2006 case in 2026. The question is why a vigilance process arising from such grave allegations remained inconclusive for nearly 20 years.

A public servant’s career progression cannot substitute for a finding on the merits. Nor should the passage of time automatically convert an unresolved allegation into exoneration. If the original material was insufficient, an inquiry can establish that. If investigators found no wrongdoing, the record should show why. If, however, the investigation was abandoned because of administrative intervention or external pressure, that itself becomes a matter of legitimate public concern. The fact that Kumar is today India’s chief election commissioner makes the need for institutional clarity greater, not smaller.

The Election Commission of India occupies an exceptional place in India’s constitutional order. Article 324 entrusts it with the superintendence, direction, and control of elections. Its authority depends not merely upon statutory powers but upon public confidence that those exercising them meet exacting standards of independence and integrity.

Independence, however, cannot be confused with immunity from scrutiny.

The allegations being examined do not concern an act Kumar performed as chief election commissioner. They concern his tenure as Kerala’s PWD secretary almost two decades earlier. Constitutional protection for the independence of the ECI is intended to prevent governments from intimidating commissioners in the exercise of electoral functions. It cannot reasonably mean that a person appointed to constitutional office acquires retrospective insulation from scrutiny over unrelated conduct in an earlier administrative post.

This distinction matters, especially because criticism of Kumar’s stewardship of the ECI has intensified over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. A petition before the Supreme Court has also raised allegations concerning whether major ECI decisions were being taken collegially, while the ECI has rejected suggestions that its decisions lacked the concurrence required within the multi-member body.

None of this proves the 2006 allegations. Nor should the vigilance inquiry be used as a proxy trial of Kumar’s current performance as CEC.

But the contemporary political controversy cannot logically erase an older allegation merely because investigating it is politically inconvenient to Kumar. If anything, the correct response to accusations of political motivation is a transparent, evidence-based investigation — not abandonment of the inquiry.

Keralam’s government should proceed firmly but scrupulously. The VACB should retrieve the original case diary, correspondence, contractual records, payment files, and statements recorded in 2006. It should establish why the earlier inquiry stalled, whether officers recommended further action, whether records were suppressed or ignored, and whether any outside intervention affected the investigation.

The State should also make clear that political office-bearers will not dictate the outcome.

There is a larger democratic principle at stake here.

India often invokes institutional independence when powerful office-holders face scrutiny. But independence without accountability can easily become institutional exceptionalism. The credibility of constitutional bodies is strengthened — not weakened — when those who lead them can withstand legitimate examination of their public record.

Thus, the Keralam government is right to reopen the matter.

Twenty years is too long for serious allegations involving a major public project, a senior bureaucrat, and the death of an engineer to remain suspended between accusation and closure. The public interest now lies in finding out what really happened.

If Gyanesh Kumar has no case to answer, a professional investigation can establish that. If wrongdoing or interference is uncovered, accountability must follow irrespective of the office he currently holds. Neither outcome should frighten a democracy.

What should concern us far more is an unresolved vigilance file quietly surviving for two decades simply because the officer at its centre went on to occupy more powerful positions.

Amal Chandra is an author and policy analyst, serving as a core member of the policy department, Keralam PCC. X:@ens_socialis. (Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of DH.)

## 5 October 2026

### Outbound force: On the U.S. leaving Iraq
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The United States invaded Iraq in March 2003, saying that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and harboured terrorist groups. In 2011, then U.S. President Barack Obama announced America’s withdrawal, but its troops returned when the Islamic State captured huge swathes of territory in Iraq and Syria. On September 30, 2026, more than 23 years after the invasion, U.S. troops finally left Iraq, in the midst of another American war in the region. The war on Iraq has been one of the gravest strategic and humanitarian disasters of the 21st century. The WMD claim turned out to be false, if not an outright lie, while al-Qaeda built one of its most violent branches in post-war Iraq. The destruction of Saddam’s Ba’athist state and the abrupt rise of Shia parties widened social cleavages, triggering a deadly civil war, killing hundreds of thousands of Iraqis. The disastrous consequences of George W. Bush’s war did not end there. Al-Qaeda in Iraq transformed into the Islamic State by 2014 and spread terror across the region and beyond. The Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMFs, or Hashad al-Shabi), an umbrella of Iran-backed Shia militias, have since emerged as a state within the state.

Saddam’s Iraq, despite its hostile relations with Gulf monarchies, was a buffer between the Arab Gulf countries and Iran. When Saddam’s regime was toppled, Iran extended its influence across Iraq through Shia parties and militias. It is an irony that the U.S. is leaving Iraq at a time when it is trying to defeat Iran in a major regional war. But beneath the irony lies everything that went wrong with America’s regime-change wars, which destabilised parts of West Asia, gave rise to militias and jihadists and exposed the limits of American power in the region. When the U.S. and Israel began bombing Iran on February 28, Hashad joined the war. Since then, Iran and its allies have carried out at least 600 attacks on U.S. military and diplomatic facilities in Iraq, a stark reminder to Washington that maintaining troops there had become unsustainable. If in Afghanistan the U.S. exited after 20 years of war leaving the country in the hands of the same Taliban that it had toppled in 2001, in Iraq, America is leaving behind a war-ravaged country in the hands of a weak government and powerful militias backed by a resurgent Iran. Iran and its allies have vowed to push the U.S. out of West Asia. They may not have the wherewithal to achieve that goal, but they have managed to drive the U.S. out of Iraq.

### Two or three?: On the Court, students, three-language policy
*The Hindu · Editorial*

The Supreme Court, through its frequent interventions, is pointing to the various aspects of the three-language policy that the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) does not seem to have thought through. Regardless of its eventual judgment, the Court’s intent at this stage seems to be to point to the pitfalls of the policy and at least soften the rough edges. In its latest ruling, the Court has said that current Class 6 students should be given the same relief as students in Classes 7, 8 and 9, whose final Class 10 examination will only be an internal assessment, not a Board examination. The Court is seeking to lessen the load on the students, at least until schools are fully prepared. It had earlier asked if the policy could start from 2027, not 2026. The CBSE has stubbornly resisted compromise at various stages in the hearing. Earlier, the Court had intervened to point out that suddenly learning a new language in Class 9 would be too disruptive if the students had not studied a second “Indian” language until Class 8. The Court had also mooted careful consideration of treating English as indigenous, putting its categorisation as a foreign language under question.

English is a de facto Indian language. It has been in use in India for at least 300 years and is the leading language of education, courts, and professions widely practised by Indians; it also serves as the preferred link language for many. English knowledge has consistently given Indians an edge in employment in global industries such as the IT sector. Indians will want English to remain one of their unique selling points as the government looks to jobs in global industries as a pathway to prosperity. The National Education Policy 2020, though advocating for two Indian languages, also mentions the importance of learning foreign languages to facilitate the global mobility of Indians seeking employment. The Hindu’s reportage has shown that since English is the language of instruction in other subjects, it will become the only so-called foreign language students will take in CBSE schools. Many schools will stick to Sanskrit as the second Indian language all the way up to Class 10 while Hindi would be the first. Some schools, especially in the southern States, will continue with the regional language such as Tamil or Kannada as the other Indian language. The practical consequence of the current policy is removing Spanish, French and other foreign languages from schools. But any purported intent of promoting cross-regional language learning may just not be served though the Court has found merit in learning more Indian languages as a way of strengthening the federal structure. A strenuous learning of an additional Indian language serves little practical purpose though it may cater to the atavistic impulses of some. The two-language policy — English and mother tongue — would be best for India. Students can be tested on a third language of their choice through internal assessment, not through a Board examination.
